/-- Characterization of minimizers for the projection on a convex set in a real inner product
space. -/
theorem norm_eq_iInf_iff_real_inner_le_zero {K : Set F} (h : Convex ℝ K) {u : F} {v : F}
    (hv : v ∈ K) : (‖u - v‖ = ⨅ w : K, ‖u - w‖) ↔ ∀ w ∈ K, ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ ≤ 0 := by
  let : Nonempty K := ⟨⟨v, hv⟩⟩
  constructor
  · intro eq w hw
    let δ := ⨅ w : K, ‖u - w‖
    let p := ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ
    let q := ‖w - v‖ ^ 2
    have δ_le (w : K) : δ ≤ ‖u - w‖ := ciInf_le ⟨0, fun _ ⟨_, h⟩ => h ▸ norm_nonneg _⟩ _
    have δ_le' (w) (hw : w ∈ K) : δ ≤ ‖u - w‖ := δ_le ⟨w, hw⟩
    have (θ : ℝ) (hθ₁ : 0 < θ) (hθ₂ : θ ≤ 1) : 2 * p ≤ θ * q := by
      have : ‖u - v‖ ^ 2 ≤ ‖u - v‖ ^ 2 - 2 * θ * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ + θ * θ * ‖w - v‖ ^ 2 :=
        calc ‖u - v‖ ^ 2
          _ ≤ ‖u - (θ • w + (1 - θ) • v)‖ ^ 2 := by
            simp only [sq]; apply mul_self_le_mul_self (norm_nonneg _)
            rw [eq]; apply δ_le'
            apply h hw hv
            exacts [le_of_lt hθ₁, sub_nonneg.2 hθ₂, add_sub_cancel _ _]
          _ = ‖u - v - θ • (w - v)‖ ^ 2 := by
            have : u - (θ • w + (1 - θ) • v) = u - v - θ • (w - v) := by
              rw [smul_sub, sub_smul, one_smul]
              simp only [sub_eq_add_neg, add_comm, add_left_comm, add_assoc, neg_add_rev]
            rw [this]
          _ = ‖u - v‖ ^ 2 - 2 * θ * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ + θ * θ * ‖w - v‖ ^ 2 := by
            rw [@norm_sub_sq ℝ, inner_smul_right, norm_smul]
            simp only [sq]
            change
              ‖u - v‖ * ‖u - v‖ - 2 * (θ * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ) +
                absR θ * ‖w - v‖ * (absR θ * ‖w - v‖) =
              ‖u - v‖ * ‖u - v‖ - 2 * θ * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ + θ * θ * (‖w - v‖ * ‖w - v‖)
            rw [abs_of_pos hθ₁]; ring
      have eq₁ :
        ‖u - v‖ ^ 2 - 2 * θ * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ + θ * θ * ‖w - v‖ ^ 2 =
          ‖u - v‖ ^ 2 + (θ * θ * ‖w - v‖ ^ 2 - 2 * θ * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ) := by
        abel
      rw [eq₁, le_add_iff_nonneg_right] at this
      have eq₂ :
        θ * θ * ‖w - v‖ ^ 2 - 2 * θ * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ =
          θ * (θ * ‖w - v‖ ^ 2 - 2 * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ) := by ring
      rw [eq₂] at this
      exact le_of_sub_nonneg (nonneg_of_mul_nonneg_right this hθ₁)
    by_cases hq : q = 0
    · rw [hq] at this
      have : p ≤ 0 := by
        have := this (1 : ℝ) (by simp) (by simp)
        linarith
      exact this
    · have q_pos : 0 < q := lt_of_le_of_ne (sq_nonneg _) fun h ↦ hq h.symm
      by_contra hp
      rw [not_le] at hp
      let θ := min (1 : ℝ) (p / q)
      have eq₁ : θ * q ≤ p :=
        calc
          θ * q ≤ p / q * q := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right (min_le_right _ _) (sq_nonneg _)
          _ = p := div_mul_cancel₀ _ hq
      have : 2 * p ≤ p :=
        calc
          2 * p ≤ θ * q := by
            exact this θ (lt_min (by simp) (div_pos hp q_pos)) (by simp [θ])
          _ ≤ p := eq₁
      linarith
  · intro h
    apply le_antisymm
    · apply le_ciInf
      intro w
      apply nonneg_le_nonneg_of_sq_le_sq (norm_nonneg _)
      have := h w w.2
      calc
        ‖u - v‖ * ‖u - v‖ ≤ ‖u - v‖ * ‖u - v‖ - 2 * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ := by linarith
        _ ≤ ‖u - v‖ ^ 2 - 2 * ⟪u - v, w - v⟫_ℝ + ‖w - v‖ ^ 2 := by
          rw [sq]
          refine le_add_of_nonneg_right ?_
          exact sq_nonneg _
        _ = ‖u - v - (w - v)‖ ^ 2 := (@norm_sub_sq ℝ _ _ _ _ _ _).symm
        _ = ‖u - w‖ * ‖u - w‖ := by
          have : u - v - (w - v) = u - w := by abel
          rw [this, sq]
    · change ⨅ w : K, ‖u - w‖ ≤ (fun w : K => ‖u - w‖) ⟨v, hv⟩
      apply ciInf_le
      use 0
      rintro y ⟨z, rfl⟩
      exact norm_nonneg _

source.alignment: The source proves part (a), the characterization of nearest points by the inner product inequality. Parts (b) and (c) are not in this declaration.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Necessity in (a). Let v be a nearest point, w in K and θ in (0,1]. Then v+θ(w−v) is in K by convexity. So ‖u−v‖²≤‖u−v−θ(w−v)‖²=‖u−v‖²−2θ⟨u−v,w−v⟩+θ²‖w−v‖². Divide by θ and let θ→0. This gives ⟨u−v,w−v⟩≤0.

Sufficiency and uniqueness in (a). Suppose the inequality holds at v. For w in K, ‖u−w‖²=‖u−v‖²−2⟨u−v,w−v⟩+‖w−v‖²≥‖u−v‖²+‖w−v‖². So v is nearest, and equality forces w=v. Hence the nearest point is unique.
Existence in (a). The Hilbert projection theorem gives a nearest point in a nonempty closed convex set of a Hilbert space.

Part (b). Let p=P_K u and p′=P_K u′. Step 1 gives ⟨u−p,p′−p⟩≤0 and ⟨u′−p′,p−p′⟩≤0. Add them. The sum equals ⟨(u−u′)−(p−p′),p′−p⟩=−⟨u−u′,p−p′⟩+‖p−p′‖²≤0. So ‖p−p′‖²≤⟨u−u′,p−p′⟩. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality then gives ‖p−p′‖≤‖u−u′‖.

First-order condition. For convex differentiable f, v in K minimizes f over K if and only if ⟨∇f(v),w−v⟩≥0 for all w in K. Forward: g(θ)=f(v+θ(w−v)) has its minimum over [0,1] at θ=0, so g′(0)=⟨∇f(v),w−v⟩≥0. Backward: convexity gives f(w)≥f(v)+⟨∇f(v),w−v⟩≥f(v).

Part (c). Put u=v−η∇f(v). Then ⟨u−v,w−v⟩=−η⟨∇f(v),w−v⟩. This is at most 0 for all w in K exactly when the first-order condition holds. By part (a), that is exactly v=P_K u. So v is a minimizer if and only if v=P_K(v−η∇f(v)).

worked_application.title: Projection onto the simplex and a least squares fit
worked_application.goal: Project three points onto the probability simplex in ℝ³, test the inequalities, then run projected gradient steps for a least squares problem and check the fixed point.
hypotheses: K={x in ℝ³ : xᵢ≥0, Σxᵢ=1}. The projection has the form (x−θ)₊ with θ chosen so that the sum is 1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: K is closed, convex and nonempty. f is convex and differentiable. So parts (a) to (c) apply.

steps.text: Variational inequality. For x=(0.5,1.2,−0.3) and p=(0.15,0.85,0), x−p=(0.35,0.35,−0.3). The products ⟨x−p,eᵢ−p⟩ for the three vertices are 0, 0 and −0.65. All are at most 0. The inequality is linear in w, so it holds for the whole simplex.
Nonexpansiveness. For 20000 random pairs (x,y) in [−2,2]³, the ratio ‖P x−P y‖/‖x−y‖ never exceeds 0.999998, and the firm inequality of part (b) held in each case.

Projected gradient. L=λmax(AᵀA)=6.4115 and η=1/L. From x₀=(1/3,1/3,1/3) the iterates are (0.186,0.394,0.420) with f=0.72816 at step 1, (0,0.38591,0.61409) with f=0.58097 at step 5, and (0,0.250066,0.749934) with f=0.5625 at step 50. At step 200 the iterate is (0,0.25,0.75).

Fixed-point check. Take x*=(0,1/4,3/4). Then Ax*−b=(−0.25,−1,−0.25), f(x*)=9/16 and ∇f(x*)=(−0.75,−1.25,−1.25). For any η>0, x*−η∇f(x*)=(0.75η,0.25+1.25η,0.75+1.25η). Subtract θ=1.25η and clip: this gives (0,0.25,0.75), which sums to 1. So P_K(x*−η∇f(x*))=x*. By part (c), x* is the minimizer. The inner products ⟨∇f(x*),eᵢ−x*⟩ are 0.5, 0 and 0, all at least 0.

worked_application.result: The projected gradient iteration converges to x*=(0,1/4,3/4) with f=9/16, and the exact fixed-point test confirms optimality for every step size.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The Hilbert space must be real. In a complex space one uses the real part of the inner product.
The fixed-point test in (c) needs convexity of f. For a nonconvex f it is only necessary for a local minimum.
The application shows convergence of the iterates numerically. This entry does not prove a convergence theorem for projected gradient.
Closedness is needed for existence. In a nonclosed set the nearest point may not exist.

results.name: Metropolis-Hastings kernel satisfies detailed balance
results.statement: Let S be a finite set, π a probability vector on S with π(x)>0 for all x, and q a stochastic matrix on S such that q(x,y)>0 if and only if q(y,x)>0, for x≠y. Put a(x,y)=min{1,π(y)q(y,x)/(π(x)q(x,y))} when q(x,y)>0, and P(x,y)=q(x,y)a(x,y) for x≠y, and P(x,x)=1−Σ_{y≠x}P(x,y). Then P is a stochastic matrix, π(x)P(x,y)=π(y)P(y,x) for all x,y, and πP=π.
hypotheses: π is strictly positive on S. The weights may be known only up to a constant, because only ratios appear.
The proposal q is a stochastic matrix. It need not be symmetric, but it must be able to go back.
The result gives stationarity. Convergence of μPⁿ to π needs P irreducible and aperiodic, and that is not proved here.

/-- A reversible Markov kernel leaves the measure `π` invariant. -/
theorem IsReversible.invariant
    {κ : Kernel α α} [IsMarkovKernel κ] {π : Measure α}
    (h_rev : IsReversible κ π) : Invariant κ π := by
  ext s hs
  calc
    (κ ∘ₘ π) s = ∫⁻ x, κ x s ∂π := by rw [Measure.bind_apply hs (Kernel.aemeasurable _)]
             _ = ∫⁻ x in s, κ x Set.univ ∂π := by simpa [restrict_univ] using (h_rev hs .univ).symm
             _ = π s := by simp

steps.text: P is stochastic. For x≠y, P(x,y)≥0 because q and a are nonnegative. Also Σ_{y≠x}P(x,y)≤Σ_{y≠x}q(x,y)≤1, since a≤1. So P(x,x)≥0. Each row sums to 1 by the definition of P(x,x).
Off-diagonal pairs with q(x,y)=0. Then q(y,x)=0 by assumption, so P(x,y)=P(y,x)=0. Both sides of detailed balance are 0.
Pairs with q(x,y)>0. Put r=π(y)q(y,x)/(π(x)q(x,y))>0. Then a(x,y)=min{1,r} and a(y,x)=min{1,1/r}. The two sides of detailed balance are π(x)q(x,y)min{1,r} and π(y)q(y,x)min{1,1/r}.
Case r≥1. The left side is π(x)q(x,y). The right side is π(y)q(y,x)/r=π(x)q(x,y). They agree.
Case r<1. The left side is π(x)q(x,y)r=π(y)q(y,x). The right side is π(y)q(y,x)·1. They agree.
Diagonal pairs. For x=y the identity π(x)P(x,x)=π(x)P(x,x) is trivial. So detailed balance holds for all pairs.
Stationarity. For each y, Σ_xπ(x)P(x,y)=Σ_xπ(y)P(y,x)=π(y)Σ_xP(y,x)=π(y). This is πP=π.

results.statement: An urn holds a red and b black balls, with a,b positive integers. At each step draw a ball uniformly and return it with one more ball of the same colour. /-- **Almost everywhere martingale convergence theorem**: An L¹-bounded submartingale converges
almost everywhere to a `⨆ n, ℱ n`-measurable function. -/
theorem Submartingale.ae_tendsto_limitProcess [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hf : Submartingale f ℱ μ)
    (hbdd : ∀ n, eLpNorm (f n) 1 μ ≤ R) :
    ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, Tendsto (fun n => f n ω) atTop (𝓝 (ℱ.limitProcess f μ ω)) := by
  classical
  suffices
      ∃ g, StronglyMeasurable[⨆ n, ℱ n] g ∧ ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, Tendsto (fun n => f n ω) atTop (𝓝 (g ω)) by
    rw [limitProcess, dite_eq_left this]
    exact (Classical.choose_spec this).2
  set g' : Ω → ℝ := fun ω => if h : ∃ c, Tendsto (fun n => f n ω) atTop (𝓝 c) then h.choose else 0
  have hle : ⨆ n, ℱ n ≤ m0 := sSup_le fun m ⟨n, hn⟩ => hn ▸ ℱ.le _
  have hg' : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ.trim hle, Tendsto (fun n => f n ω) atTop (𝓝 (g' ω)) := by
    filter_upwards [hf.exists_ae_trim_tendsto_of_bdd hbdd] with ω hω
    simp_rw [g', dite_eq_left hω]
    exact hω.choose_spec
  have hg'm : AEStronglyMeasurable[⨆ n, ℱ n] g' (μ.trim hle) :=
    (@aemeasurable_of_tendsto_metrizable_ae' _ _ (⨆ n, ℱ n) _ _ _ _ _ _ _
      (fun n => ((hf.stronglyMeasurable n).measurable.mono (le_sSup ⟨n, rfl⟩ : ℱ n ≤ ⨆ n, ℱ n)
        le_rfl).aemeasurable) hg').aestronglyMeasurable
  obtain ⟨g, hgm, hae⟩ := hg'm
  have hg : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ.trim hle, Tendsto (fun n => f n ω) atTop (𝓝 (g ω)) := by
    filter_upwards [hae, hg'] with ω hω hg'ω
    exact hω ▸ hg'ω
  exact ⟨g, hgm, measure_eq_zero_of_trim_eq_zero hle hg⟩

steps.text: Probability of one sequence. Take a colour sequence with j red draws and n−j black draws. At each draw, the chance of red is (red count)/(total count). The red draws contribute the numerators a,a+1,…,a+j−1 in the order they occur, and the black draws contribute b,b+1,…,b+n−j−1. The denominators are a+b,a+b+1,…,a+b+n−1. So the probability is a^{(j)}b^{(n−j)}/(a+b)^{(n)}. It does not depend on the order. This gives exchangeability and the formula for P(Dₙ=j), by counting C(n,j) sequences. This proves (a).

Martingale. Let Tₙ=a+b+n and Rₙ=a+Dₙ. Given the first n draws, the red count after one more draw has mean Rₙ+Rₙ/Tₙ=Rₙ(Tₙ+1)/Tₙ. So E[X_{n+1}|Fₙ]=Rₙ(Tₙ+1)/(Tₙ(Tₙ+1))=Rₙ/Tₙ=Xₙ. Also 0≤Xₙ≤1. This proves (b).
Almost sure limit. A martingale bounded in [0,1] converges almost surely to a limit X_∞ in [0,1]. Since the sequence is bounded, the dominated convergence theorem gives E[Xₙᵏ]→E[X_∞ᵏ] for every k.

Moments of the red count. Fix k draw indices i₁,…,i_k. By step 1, the chance that all k are red equals the chance that the first k draws are red, which is a^{(k)}/(a+b)^{(k)}=:m_k. Count ordered k-tuples of distinct indices: there are n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1). So E[(Dₙ)_k]=(n)_k m_k.

From falling to ordinary powers. Write Dₙᵏ=(Dₙ)_k+Σ_{l<k}S(k,l)(Dₙ)_l, where S(k,l) are Stirling numbers of the second kind. Since (Dₙ)_l≤nˡ, we get |E[Dₙᵏ]/nᵏ−(n)_k m_k/nᵏ|≤C_k/n. Also (n)_k/nᵏ→1. So E[(Dₙ/n)ᵏ]→m_k.
Pass from Dₙ/n to Xₙ. Xₙ−Dₙ/n=(na−Dₙ(a+b))/(n(a+b+n)). Because 0≤Dₙ≤n, the absolute value is at most (a+b)/n. So |Xₙᵏ−(Dₙ/n)ᵏ|≤k(a+b)/n. Therefore E[Xₙᵏ]→m_k, and by step 3, E[X_∞ᵏ]=m_k.
Beta moments. For B with the Beta(a,b) law, E[Bᵏ]=B(a+k,b)/B(a,b)=Γ(a+k)Γ(a+b)/(Γ(a)Γ(a+b+k))=a^{(k)}/(a+b)^{(k)}, by the Beta-Gamma identity and Γ(x+k)=x^{(k)}Γ(x).

Moments determine the law. X_∞ and B are in [0,1] and have the same moments. So ∫p dμ=∫p dν for every polynomial p. Polynomials are uniformly dense in C[0,1] by the Weierstrass theorem, so ∫g dμ=∫g dν for all continuous g. Hence the two laws are equal. This proves (c).

results.name: Linear programming duality from the Farkas lemma
results.statement: Let A be a real m×n matrix, b in ℝᵐ and c in ℝⁿ. The primal problem is (P): maximize cᵀx subject to Ax≤b and x≥0. The dual problem is (D): minimize bᵀy subject to Aᵀy≥c and y≥0. (a) Weak duality: if x is feasible for (P) and y is feasible for (D), then cᵀx≤bᵀy. (b) Strong duality: if (P) is feasible and its supremum v* is finite, then (P) and (D) both have optimal solutions and the optimal values are equal. (c) Complementary slackness: feasible x and y are optimal if and only if yᵢ(b−Ax)ᵢ=0 for all i and xⱼ(Aᵀy−c)ⱼ=0 for all j.
hypotheses: All data are real. Inequalities between vectors hold in every coordinate.
In (b) the problem (P) has at least one feasible point and is bounded above.
If (P) is unbounded above then (D) is infeasible, by (a). If (D) is infeasible and (P) is feasible then (P) is unbounded. The second case is not proved here.

prerequisites.reason: The Farkas alternative produces the certificate x̃.

definitions.name: primal and dual program
definitions.text: (P) maximizes cᵀx over {Ax≤b, x≥0}. (D) minimizes bᵀy over {Aᵀy≥c, y≥0}.

definitions.name: Farkas alternative
definitions.text: For a matrix M and vector d, exactly one holds. Either Mz=d for some z≥0, or Mᵀw≥0 and dᵀw<0 for some w.

definitions.name: complementary slackness
definitions.text: A positive coordinate of one program forces the matching constraint of the other to be tight.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Weak duality. For feasible x and y, cᵀx≤(Aᵀy)ᵀx=yᵀ(Ax)≤yᵀb. The first step uses x≥0 and Aᵀy≥c. The last step uses y≥0 and Ax≤b. This proves (a).

Complementary slackness. If x and y are feasible, then bᵀy−cᵀx=yᵀ(b−Ax)+xᵀ(Aᵀy−c), and both terms are at least 0. The gap is 0 exactly when both terms are 0. Each term is a sum of nonnegative products, so each product is 0. This proves (c), once (b) is known. Also, if a feasible pair has gap 0, both are optimal by (a).

Set up the system for the dual. Let v* be the finite supremum of (P). Consider unknowns z=(y,s,t)≥0 with Aᵀy−s=c and bᵀy+t=v*. A solution gives y≥0 with Aᵀy≥c and bᵀy≤v*. Write the system as Mz=d with M=[[Aᵀ,−I,0],[bᵀ,0,1]] and d=(c,v*).

Apply the Farkas alternative. Suppose the system has no solution. Then there is w=(w₁,λ) with Mᵀw≥0 and dᵀw<0. Written out, Aw₁+λb≥0, −w₁≥0, λ≥0 and cᵀw₁+λv*<0. Put x̃=−w₁. Then x̃≥0, Ax̃≤λb, λ≥0 and cᵀx̃>λv*.
The case λ>0. The point x̃/λ is feasible for (P) and has value cᵀx̃/λ>v*. This contradicts the definition of v*.
The case λ=0. Then Ax̃≤0, x̃≥0 and cᵀx̃>0. Let x₀ be feasible for (P). For every τ≥0, x₀+τx̃ is feasible and has value cᵀx₀+τcᵀx̃, which tends to ∞. This contradicts v*<∞.

Dual optimum. Both cases are impossible, so the system has a solution. It gives y≥0, Aᵀy≥c and bᵀy≤v*. By weak duality bᵀy≥cᵀx for every feasible x, so bᵀy≥v*. Hence bᵀy=v*, and y is optimal for (D) because every dual feasible point has value at least v*.

Primal optimum. Rewrite (D) as a maximization problem: maximize −bᵀy subject to −Aᵀy≤−c and y≥0. It is feasible and bounded, with supremum −v*. Apply steps 3 to 7 to this program. Its dual is the minimization of −cᵀx subject to −Ax≥−b and x≥0, which is (P) in minimization form. The conclusion gives a feasible x with −cᵀx=−v*, that is cᵀx=v*. So (P) has an optimal solution. This proves (b).

worked_application.title: A two-variable program with a degenerate vertex
worked_application.goal: Solve a small LP, find two different dual optima, and use a Farkas certificate to refute a smaller dual value.
hypotheses: (P): maximize 3x₁+2x₂ subject to x₁+x₂≤4, x₁+3x₂≤6, 2x₁+x₂≤7 and x≥0.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: (P) is feasible at x=0 and bounded, because the feasible region is a bounded polygon. So strong duality applies.

steps.text: Primal vertices. Intersecting pairs of constraints and keeping feasible points gives the vertices (0,0), (7/2,0), (3,1) and (0,2), with values 0, 21/2, 11 and 4. The optimum is x=(3,1) with value 11. All three row constraints are tight at x: 3+1=4, 3+3=6 and 6+1=7.

Dual feasible points. The vertices of the dual region (with Aᵀy≥c, y≥0) are (0,1/5,7/5) with value 11, (1,0,1) with value 11, (3,0,0) with value 12, (0,3,0) with value 18 and (0,0,2) with value 14. The minimum is 11. So the optimal values agree, and the dual optimum is not unique.
Complementary slackness. Both x₁=3 and x₂=1 are positive, so Aᵀy=c must be tight in both coordinates. It is tight for both dual optima. The primal rows are all tight, so no condition falls on y.

Farkas certificate. Try to find y≥0 with Aᵀy≥c and bᵀy≤10. The certificate x̃=(3,1) with λ=1 satisfies x̃≥0, Ax̃=(4,6,7)≤λb=(4,6,7) and cᵀx̃=11>λ·10=10. So no such y exists, and the dual value cannot go below 11.

worked_application.result: The optimal value is 11 for both programs, with primal optimum (3,1) and dual optima (0,1/5,7/5) and (1,0,1).

limitations: The proof of (b) needs the Farkas alternative for the cone generated by the columns of M. Closedness of such cones is part of that lemma.
The case where (P) is unbounded and (D) is infeasible is only half proved, by weak duality. The converse needs another application of the alternative.
Duality gives the optimal value but not a fast algorithm. The simplex method or an interior point method still has to find the solution.
Integer programs do not have strong duality in general.

results.name: Cauchy-Binet formula for minors of a product
results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring. Let A be an m×n matrix and B an n×m matrix over R. For a subset S of {1,…,n} with m elements, let A_S be the m×m matrix of the columns of A in S, and let B_S be the m×m matrix of the rows of B in S. Then det(AB) = ∑_S det(A_S)·det(B_S), where the sum runs over all m-element subsets S. If n < m, the sum is empty and det(AB) = 0. More generally, for row sets I and column sets J of size k, det((AB)_{I,J}) = ∑_{|S|=k} det(A_{I,S})·det(B_{S,J}).
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with 1. No division is used.
A is m×n and B is n×m. The product AB is square of size m.
For the general form, I is a set of k rows of A and J is a set of k columns of B.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only multilinearity of the determinant and the Leibniz formula. No catalog theorem is cited.

definitions.name: minor
definitions.text: A k×k minor of a matrix is the determinant of the square submatrix on k chosen rows and k chosen columns.

definitions.name: compound matrix
definitions.text: The k-th compound matrix C_k(A) has one row and one column for each k-subset. Its entry at (I,S) is the minor det(A_{I,S}). The general form of the theorem says C_k(AB) = C_k(A)·C_k(B).

definitions.name: exterior power
definitions.text: The k-th exterior power Λ^k(f) of a linear map f has the compound matrix of f as its matrix in the wedge basis. The theorem is the statement that Λ^k respects composition.

      simp only [det_apply', mul_apply, prod_univ_sum, mul_sum, Fintype.piFinset_univ]

steps.text: Let a_1,…,a_n be the columns of A. Column j of AB is ∑_s B_{sj}·a_s, because (AB)_{ij} = ∑_s A_{is}B_{sj}.

The determinant is multilinear in the columns. Expand each of the m columns of AB. We get det(AB) = ∑_f (∏_{j=1}^m B_{f(j),j})·det(a_{f(1)},…,a_{f(m)}). The sum runs over all maps f from {1,…,m} to {1,…,n}.
If f is not injective, two of the columns a_{f(1)},…,a_{f(m)} are equal. A determinant with two equal columns is zero. So only injective f remain. If n < m, no injective f exists, and det(AB) = 0.
Let f be injective. Let S be its image. List the elements of S in increasing order as s_1 < … < s_m. There is a unique permutation τ of {1,…,m} with f(j) = s_{τ(j)}.
The matrix (a_{f(1)},…,a_{f(m)}) is the matrix A_S with its columns permuted by τ. Permuting columns multiplies the determinant by sgn(τ). So det(a_{f(1)},…,a_{f(m)}) = sgn(τ)·det(A_S).
Group the injective maps by their image S. We get det(AB) = ∑_S det(A_S)·∑_τ sgn(τ)·∏_j B_{s_{τ(j)},j}.

The inner sum is the Leibniz formula for det(B_S). Indeed the rows of B_S are rows s_1,…,s_m of B, and the term for τ is sgn(τ)∏_j (B_S)_{τ(j),j}. So the inner sum is det(B_S), and the first claim follows.

General minors. The submatrix (AB)_{I,J} equals A_{I,[n]}·B_{[n],J}, a product of a k×n matrix and an n×k matrix. Apply the first claim to this product. The column subsets S of A_{I,[n]} are the k-subsets of [n], and A_{I,[n]} restricted to S is A_{I,S}.
Thus every k×k minor of AB is a sum of products of a k×k minor of A and a k×k minor of B. This is the matrix identity C_k(AB) = C_k(A)·C_k(B), which is functoriality of the exterior power.

worked_application.title: Lagrange identity and a count of the spanning trees of K4
worked_application.goal: Use the formula to compute a Gram determinant and to count spanning trees by determinants.
hypotheses: Part 1: A is the 2×3 integer matrix with rows (1,2,0) and (0,1,3), and B = Aᵀ.
Part 2: M is the reduced vertex-edge incidence matrix of the complete graph K4.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Both parts apply the theorem to a product M·Mᵀ with n larger than m. The sum over m-subsets becomes a sum over a small set of column choices.

steps.text: Part 1. The product AAᵀ has entries 1+4 = 5, 2, 2 and 1+9 = 10. So det(AAᵀ) = 50 − 4 = 46.

The 2×2 minors of A for the column pairs {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3} are 1, 3 and 6. Since B_S = (A_S)ᵀ has the same determinant as A_S, the theorem gives det(AAᵀ) = 1² + 3² + 6² = 46. This agrees with the direct value. It is the Lagrange identity: the squared area of a parallelogram is the sum of the squared areas of its projections to the coordinate planes.

Part 2. Number the vertices of K4 as 1,2,3,4 and the edges as 12,13,14,23,24,34. The column of edge ij with i < j has +1 in row i and −1 in row j. Delete the row of vertex 4. This gives a 3×6 integer matrix M.
The product MMᵀ is the reduced Laplacian. It has 3 on the diagonal and −1 off the diagonal. Its determinant is 3·(9−1) − (−1)·(−3−1) + (−1)·(1+3) = 24 − 4 − 4 = 16.

Minor lemma. For a set T of 3 edges, the 3×3 minor M_T is ±1 if T is a spanning tree and 0 otherwise. If T has a cycle, the signed sum of the columns around the cycle is zero, so the columns are dependent. If T is a tree, it has at least 2 leaves, so it has a leaf other than vertex 4. The row of that leaf has a single nonzero entry ±1 in M_T. Expand along that row and repeat on the smaller tree.

By the theorem, det(MMᵀ) = ∑_T det(M_T)² = number of spanning trees. A computer check of all 20 edge triples finds 16 triples with minor ±1 and 4 triples with minor 0. The 4 zero triples are the 4 triangles. So K4 has 16 spanning trees, which agrees with Cayley formula 4² = 16.

worked_application.result: det(AAᵀ) = 46 = 1+9+36 for the 2×3 matrix. The complete graph K4 has 16 spanning trees, and the 16 equals the determinant of the reduced Laplacian.

limitations: The theorem is for commutative rings. For a noncommutative ring the determinant is not defined in this form.
The sum has C(n,m) terms. It is useful for theory and for small cases. It is a slow way to compute det(AB) for large n.
The formula needs both factors to have the shapes m×n and n×m. If A and B are square and of the same size, it reduces to det(AB) = det(A)det(B).

results.name: Smith normal form over a Euclidean domain and determinantal divisors
results.statement: Let R be a Euclidean domain, for example ℤ or k[x] with k a field. Let A be an m×n matrix over R of rank r. Then there are invertible matrices U (m×m) and V (n×n) over R such that UAV is the m×n matrix D with D_{ii} = d_i ≠ 0 for i ≤ r, all other entries 0, and d_1 | d_2 | … | d_r. The d_i are unique up to units. For 1 ≤ k ≤ r the product d_1⋯d_k equals, up to a unit, the gcd Δ_k(A) of all k×k minors of A. Consequently R^m/A·R^n ≅ R/(d_1) ⊕ … ⊕ R/(d_r) ⊕ R^{m−r}. If R = ℤ and m = n = r, then this quotient has exactly |det A| elements.
hypotheses: R is a Euclidean domain with Euclidean function δ. Division with remainder works.
Invertible means that the matrix has an inverse with entries in R. Equivalently, its determinant is a unit of R.
Uniqueness is up to multiplication of each d_i by a unit.

definitions.name: determinantal divisor Δ_k
definitions.text: Δ_k(A) is the gcd of all k×k minors of A. It is defined up to a unit.

definitions.name: invariant factors
definitions.text: The elements d_1 | d_2 | … | d_r of the Smith normal form.

source.excerpt:
/-- If `M` is finite free over a PID `R`, then any submodule `N` is free
and we can find a basis for `M` and `N` such that the inclusion map is a diagonal matrix
in Smith normal form.

See `Submodule.smithNormalFormOfLE` for a version of this theorem that returns
a `Basis.SmithNormalForm`.

This is a strengthening of `Submodule.basisOfPidOfLE`.
-/
theorem Submodule.exists_smith_normal_form_of_le [Finite ι] (b : Basis ι R M) (N O : Submodule R M)
    (N_le_O : N ≤ O) :
    ∃ (n o : ℕ) (hno : n ≤ o) (bO : Basis (Fin o) R O) (bN : Basis (Fin n) R N) (a : Fin n → R),
      ∀ i, (bN i : M) = a i • bO (Fin.castLE hno i) := by
  cases nonempty_fintype ι
  induction O using inductionOnRank b generalizing N with | ih M0 ih =>
  obtain ⟨m, b'M⟩ := M0.basisOfPid b
  by_cases N_bot : N = ⊥
  · subst N_bot
    exact ⟨0, m, Nat.zero_le _, b'M, Basis.empty _, finZeroElim, finZeroElim⟩
  obtain ⟨y, hy, a, _, M', M'_le_M, N', _, N'_le_M', y_ortho, _, h⟩ :=
    Submodule.basis_of_pid_aux M0 N b'M N_bot N_le_O
  obtain ⟨n', m', hn'm', bM', bN', as', has'⟩ := ih M' M'_le_M y hy y_ortho N' N'_le_M'
  obtain ⟨bN, h'⟩ := h n' bN'
  obtain ⟨hmn, bM, h''⟩ := h' m' hn'm' bM'
  obtain ⟨as, has⟩ := h'' as' has'
  exact ⟨_, _, hmn, bM, bN, as, has⟩

steps.text: Existence. Assume A ≠ 0. Among all matrices equivalent to A, choose a matrix B that has a nonzero entry b with the smallest possible value δ(b). Such a choice exists by well ordering of the values of δ. Swap rows and columns so that b is at position (1,1).

Claim: b divides every entry of the first row and of the first column. Take B_{1j} = qb + ρ with ρ = 0 or δ(ρ) < δ(b). Subtract q times column 1 from column j. The new matrix is equivalent to A and has ρ at position (1,j). If ρ ≠ 0, this contradicts the minimality of δ(b). So ρ = 0. The column case is the same.
Subtract suitable multiples of row 1 and column 1 to clear the rest of row 1 and column 1. The result is the block matrix diag(b, A′).

Claim: b divides every entry of A′. Suppose b does not divide the entry a at position (i,j) of A′. Add row i to row 1. Now row 1 contains b at (1,1) and a at (1,j). Write a = qb + ρ with ρ ≠ 0 and δ(ρ) < δ(b). Subtract q times column 1 from column j. We get a matrix equivalent to A with the nonzero entry ρ, and δ(ρ) < δ(b). This contradicts minimality.

Induction on the size. Apply the same argument to A′, which has smaller size. Row and column operations on A′ replace each entry by an R-linear combination of the old entries. So all entries stay multiples of b. This gives diag(b, d_2, …, d_r, 0, …, 0) with b | d_2, and the chain d_i | d_{i+1} holds by the same claim at each stage. Existence is proved.

Invariance of Δ_k. By Cauchy-Binet in its general form, every k×k minor of UAV is an R-linear combination of k×k minors of A. So Δ_k(A) divides Δ_k(UAV). Apply the same argument to A = U⁻¹(UAV)V⁻¹. We get Δ_k(UAV) divides Δ_k(A). So Δ_k(UAV) and Δ_k(A) agree up to a unit.

Determinantal divisors of D. A k×k minor of D with rows i_1<…<i_k and columns j_1<…<j_k is zero unless the row set equals the column set. Then it equals d_{i_1}⋯d_{i_k}. Because i_t ≥ t and the d_i form a divisibility chain, d_t divides d_{i_t}. So d_1⋯d_k divides every nonzero k×k minor, and it is itself the minor on the first k rows and columns. So Δ_k(D) = d_1⋯d_k up to a unit.
Uniqueness. By the last two steps, d_1⋯d_k ~ Δ_k(A) for all k ≤ r. Hence d_k ~ Δ_k(A)/Δ_{k−1}(A) with Δ_0 = 1. The d_k depend only on A. The rank r is the largest k with Δ_k(A) ≠ 0.

The quotient. The map x ↦ Ux sends the column space A·R^n onto UA·R^n = UAV·R^n = D·R^n, because V is invertible. So R^m/A·R^n ≅ R^m/D·R^n. The column space of D is d_1R ⊕ … ⊕ d_rR ⊕ 0. So R^m/D·R^n ≅ ⊕ R/(d_i) ⊕ R^{m−r}.
Order of the quotient over ℤ. For m = n = r, the group is ⊕ ℤ/(d_i). It has ∏|d_i| elements. Since det U and det V are ±1, |det A| = |det D| = ∏|d_i|.

worked_application.goal: Let A be the integer matrix with rows (2,4,4), (−6,6,12), (10,−4,−16). Find the invariant factors and the structure of ℤ³/Aℤ³.
hypotheses: R = ℤ and A is 3×3.

worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The ring ℤ is Euclidean. By the theorem, the invariant factors follow from the three gcds Δ_1, Δ_2, Δ_3. No row reduction is needed.

steps.text: Δ_1 is the gcd of the nine entries 2, 4, 4, −6, 6, 12, 10, −4, −16. It is 2.
The determinant of A is −144, so Δ_3 = 144.
The invariant factors are d_1 = 2, d_2 = 12/2 = 6 and d_3 = 144/12 = 12. The chain 2 | 6 | 12 holds. A computer algebra system returns the same Smith form diag(2, 6, 12).
By the theorem, ℤ³/Aℤ³ ≅ ℤ/2 ⊕ ℤ/6 ⊕ ℤ/12. It has 2·6·12 = 144 = |det A| elements.
Split into primary parts: ℤ/2 ⊕ (ℤ/2 ⊕ ℤ/3) ⊕ (ℤ/4 ⊕ ℤ/3). The elementary divisors are 2, 2, 4, 3, 3. The group has exponent 12. It has 2³ = 8 elements of order dividing 2.

results.name: Matrix similarity by invariant factors and the rational canonical form
results.statement: Let k be a field. Let A and B be n×n matrices over k. Then A and B are similar over k if and only if the matrices xI−A and xI−B over k[x] are equivalent. This holds if and only if xI−A and xI−B have the same invariant factors d_1 | d_2 | … | d_n, taken monic. The product d_1⋯d_n is the characteristic polynomial of A. The last factor d_n is the minimal polynomial of A. Also A is similar to the block diagonal matrix of the companion matrices of the nonconstant d_i. This block matrix is the rational canonical form of A. It depends only on the similarity class of A.
hypotheses: k is a field. Then k[x] is a Euclidean domain.
A and B are square matrices of the same size n.
Similar means B = PAP⁻¹ for an invertible matrix P over k.

prerequisites.reason: Steps 7 to 9 use the Smith normal form over k[x], the uniqueness of the invariant factors through the determinantal divisors, and the quotient decomposition.

definitions.name: k[x]-module V_A
definitions.text: V_A is the vector space k^n in which the polynomial x acts as the matrix A. A polynomial g acts as g(A). A k-linear map P from V_A to V_B is k[x]-linear exactly when PA = BP.

definitions.name: invariant factors of a matrix
definitions.text: The monic Smith diagonal entries d_1 | … | d_n of xI−A. The matrix xI−A has rank n, because its determinant is the monic characteristic polynomial. So all d_i are nonzero.

definitions.name: companion matrix
definitions.text: For a monic polynomial d = x^m + c_{m−1}x^{m−1} + … + c_0, the companion matrix C(d) is the m×m matrix with 1 on the subdiagonal and last column (−c_0, …, −c_{m−1}). It is the matrix of multiplication by x on k[x]/(d) in the basis 1, x, …, x^{m−1}.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Step 1. Similarity means isomorphism of modules. If P is invertible and PA = BP, then P is a k[x]-linear bijection from V_A to V_B. The converse is the same statement read backward. So A and B are similar if and only if V_A ≅ V_B.

Step 2. A presentation of V_A. Let e_1,…,e_n be the standard basis of k[x]^n. Define φ: k[x]^n → V_A by φ(∑ x^m v_m) = ∑ A^m v_m, with v_m in k^n. Then φ is k[x]-linear, because φ(x·v) = A·φ(v). It is onto, because φ(e_i) = e_i.

Step 3. The kernel of φ is the image of xI−A. First, (xI−A)e_j = x e_j − ∑_i A_{ij} e_i. Its image under φ is A e_j − A e_j = 0. So the image of xI−A lies in ker φ. For the other inclusion, take w in k^n. The identity (xI−A)·∑_{i+j=m−1} x^i A^j w = x^m w − A^m w shows that x^m w is congruent to the constant vector A^m w modulo the image of xI−A. Apply this to each term of v = ∑ x^m v_m. We get v ≡ φ(v) modulo the image. If φ(v) = 0, then v is in the image.
Step 4. Also xI−A is injective, because its determinant is a nonzero polynomial. So V_A ≅ k[x]^n / (xI−A)k[x]^n as k[x]-modules. This is the cokernel of xI−A.
Step 5. If A and B are similar, then B = PAP⁻¹. So P(xI−A)P⁻¹ = xI−B. The constant matrix P is invertible over k[x]. Hence xI−A and xI−B are equivalent.

Step 6. Suppose U(xI−A)V = xI−B with U and V invertible over k[x]. The map u ↦ Uu on k[x]^n sends the image of xI−A onto U(xI−A)k[x]^n = U(xI−A)V k[x]^n, which is the image of xI−B. So it induces a k[x]-linear bijection between the two cokernels. By Step 4, V_A ≅ V_B. By Step 1, A and B are similar.

Step 7. The Smith criterion. Two matrices over k[x] are equivalent exactly when they have the same Smith normal form. If the two forms are equal, both matrices are equivalent to one diagonal matrix. If the matrices are equivalent, the determinantal divisors agree, and the invariant factors are quotients of them. So A and B are similar if and only if they have the same monic invariant factors.
Step 8. The product. The determinantal divisor Δ_n of xI−A is its determinant, which is monic, up to a unit. Also Δ_n = d_1⋯d_n. So d_1⋯d_n = det(xI−A) = χ_A, the characteristic polynomial.

Step 9. The minimal polynomial. The quotient description of the Smith theorem gives V_A ≅ ⊕ k[x]/(d_i). Because d_i divides d_n, the polynomial d_n kills every summand. The summand k[x]/(d_n) is killed only by multiples of d_n. So the annihilator of V_A in k[x] is the ideal (d_n). By definition this annihilator is the ideal of all g with g(A) = 0. So d_n is the minimal polynomial of A. In particular the minimal polynomial divides χ_A, and χ_A divides d_n^n.

Step 10. The rational canonical form. For monic d of degree m, the classes of 1, x, …, x^{m−1} form a k-basis of k[x]/(d). In this basis x acts as C(d). Join these bases for the nonconstant d_i. The result is a k-basis of V_A in which A is the block diagonal matrix diag(C(d_i)). So A is similar to this matrix. By Step 7, matrices with the same similarity class have the same d_i, so the block matrix depends only on the class.

worked_application.title: Two 4×4 matrices with equal characteristic polynomial and equal rank data that are not similar
worked_application.goal: Decide whether A1 = J_2(1) ⊕ J_2(1) and A2 = J_3(1) ⊕ J_1(1) are similar over ℚ, and find the rational canonical form of A2.
hypotheses: J_m(1) is the m×m matrix with 1 on the diagonal and 1 on the superdiagonal.
The field is ℚ and the polynomial ring is ℚ[x].
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Both matrices are 4×4 over a field. The theorem reduces similarity to a comparison of the gcds of minors of xI−A.

steps.text: Both matrices have characteristic polynomial (x−1)^4, trace 4, determinant 1 and rank(A−I) = 2. So these simple invariants do not separate them.

In xI−A1 the diagonal entries are x−1 and the superdiagonal entries are −1 inside each block. Entries include the constant −1, so Δ_1 = 1. A 2×2 minor on the rows 1, 3 and columns 2, 4 equals (−1)(−1) = 1, so Δ_2 = 1. A computer algebra system computes all 3×3 and 4×4 minors. It returns Δ_3 = (x−1)^2 and Δ_4 = (x−1)^4 for A1.

For A2 the same computation returns Δ_1 = 1, Δ_2 = 1, Δ_3 = x−1 and Δ_4 = (x−1)^4. The invariant factors are the quotients Δ_k/Δ_{k−1}. For A1 they are 1, 1, (x−1)^2, (x−1)^2. For A2 they are 1, 1, x−1, (x−1)^3.

The invariant factors differ. By the theorem, A1 and A2 are not similar. The minimal polynomials confirm this: d_4 = (x−1)^2 for A1 and d_4 = (x−1)^3 for A2. Directly, (A1−I)^2 = 0, while (A2−I)^2 ≠ 0.

Rational canonical form of A2. The nonconstant invariant factors are x−1 and (x−1)^3 = x^3 − 3x^2 + 3x − 1. Their companion matrices are the 1×1 matrix (1) and the 3×3 matrix C with rows (0,0,1), (1,0,−3), (0,1,3). So A2 is similar to diag((1), C).
Check: the computer algebra system computes the invariant factors of diag((1), C). It returns 1, 1, x−1, (x−1)^3, the same list as for A2. So diag((1), C) is similar to A2 by the theorem.

results.name: Kronecker sum eigenvalues and solvability of the Sylvester equation
results.statement: Let A be an m×m complex matrix with eigenvalues λ_1,…,λ_m. Let B be an n×n complex matrix with eigenvalues μ_1,…,μ_n, counted with algebraic multiplicity. Let vec stack the columns of a matrix. Then vec(AX+XB) = K·vec(X), with K = I_n⊗A + Bᵀ⊗I_m. The mn eigenvalues of K, with multiplicity, are the sums λ_i+μ_j. Hence det K = ∏_{i,j}(λ_i+μ_j). The Sylvester equation AX+XB = C has exactly one solution X for every C if and only if A and −B have no common eigenvalue. If they have a common eigenvalue, the homogeneous equation AX+XB = 0 has a nonzero solution.
hypotheses: A is m×m and B is n×n over ℂ.
C and X are m×n.
The Kronecker product (P⊗Q) has block (i,j) equal to P_{ij}·Q.

definitions.name: vec
definitions.text: vec(X) is the column vector of length mn obtained by writing the columns of X one below the other.

definitions.name: Kronecker sum
definitions.text: The Kronecker sum of A and B is I_n⊗A + Bᵀ⊗I_m. It is the matrix of the linear map X ↦ AX+XB on m×n matrices.

definitions.name: Sylvester equation
definitions.text: The linear matrix equation AX+XB = C in the unknown X. The case B = Aᴴ is the Lyapunov equation.

/-- `Matrix.kroneckerMapBilinear` commutes with `*` if `f` does.

This is primarily used with `R = ℕ` to prove `Matrix.mul_kronecker_mul`. -/
theorem kroneckerMapBilinear_mul_mul [Semiring S] [Semiring R] [Fintype m] [Fintype m']
    [NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring α] [NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring β] [NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring γ]
    [Module R α] [Module R γ] [Module S β] [Module S γ] [SMulCommClass S R γ]
    (f : α →ₗ[R] β →ₗ[S] γ)
    (h_comm : ∀ a b a' b', f (a * b) (a' * b') = f a a' * f b b') (A : Matrix l m α)
    (B : Matrix m n α) (A' : Matrix l' m' β) (B' : Matrix m' n' β) :
    kroneckerMapBilinear f (A * B) (A' * B') =
      kroneckerMapBilinear f A A' * kroneckerMapBilinear f B B' := by
  ext ⟨i, i'⟩ ⟨j, j'⟩
  simp only [kroneckerMapBilinear_apply_apply, mul_apply, ← Finset.univ_product_univ,
    Finset.sum_product, kroneckerMap_apply]
  simp_rw [map_sum f, LinearMap.sum_apply, map_sum, h_comm]

/-- `determinant` of `Matrix.kroneckerMapBilinear`.

This is primarily used with `R = ℕ` to prove `Matrix.det_kronecker`. -/
theorem det_kroneckerMapBilinear [Semiring S] [Semiring R] [Fintype m] [Fintype n] [DecidableEq m]
    [DecidableEq n] [NonAssocSemiring α] [NonAssocSemiring β] [CommRing γ] [Module R α] [Module S β]
    [Module R γ] [Module S γ] [SMulCommClass S R γ]
    (f : α →ₗ[R] β →ₗ[S] γ) (h_comm : ∀ a b a' b', f (a * b) (a' * b') = f a a' * f b b')
    (A : Matrix m m α) (B : Matrix n n β) :
    det (kroneckerMapBilinear f A B) =
      det (A.map fun a => f a 1) ^ Fintype.card n * det (B.map fun b => f 1 b) ^ Fintype.card m :=
  calc
    det (kroneckerMapBilinear f A B) =
        det (kroneckerMapBilinear f A 1 * kroneckerMapBilinear f 1 B) := by
      rw [← kroneckerMapBilinear_mul_mul f h_comm, Matrix.mul_one, Matrix.one_mul]
    _ = det (blockDiagonal fun (_ : n) => A.map fun a => f a 1) *
        det (blockDiagonal fun (_ : m) => B.map fun b => f 1 b) := by
      rw [det_mul, ← diagonal_one, ← diagonal_one, kroneckerMapBilinear_apply_apply,
        kroneckerMap_diagonal_right _ fun _ => _, kroneckerMapBilinear_apply_apply,
        kroneckerMap_diagonal_left _ fun _ => _, det_reindex_self]
      · intro; exact LinearMap.map_zero₂ _ _
      · intro; exact map_zero _
    _ = _ := by simp_rw [det_blockDiagonal, Finset.prod_const, Finset.card_univ]

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Step 1. Vec identity. Column j of AXB equals A·X·(B e_j) = ∑_l B_{lj}·A x_l, where x_l is column l of X. So the block (j,l) of the matrix of X ↦ AXB, in the basis of vec, is B_{lj}A. This block is the block (j,l) of Bᵀ⊗A. Hence vec(AXB) = (Bᵀ⊗A) vec(X).
Step 2. Apply Step 1 twice. Use AX = A·X·I and XB = I·X·B. We get vec(AX) = (I_n⊗A)vec(X) and vec(XB) = (Bᵀ⊗I_m)vec(X). Add them to get vec(AX+XB) = K·vec(X).

Step 3. Mixed products. For matrices of fitting sizes, (P⊗Q)(R⊗S) = PR⊗QS. Indeed, the entry at row (i,a) and column (j,b) of the left side is ∑_{k,c} P_{ik}Q_{ac}R_{kj}S_{cb}. This equals (PR)_{ij}·(QS)_{ab}.

Step 4. Triangularization. Over ℂ every square matrix is similar to an upper triangular matrix. Proof by induction on the size. Take an eigenvector v of the matrix. Extend v to a basis. In this basis the matrix has a first column (λ,0,…,0)ᵀ. Apply the induction to the lower right block. The diagonal entries are the eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity, because similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial.

Step 5. Choose invertible P and Q with P⁻¹AP = S and Q⁻¹BQ = R, with S and R upper triangular. Their diagonals are (λ_i) and (μ_j). Then Bᵀ = Q⁻ᵀRᵀQᵀ. Put G = Q⁻ᵀ⊗P. By Step 3, G⁻¹ = Qᵀ⊗P⁻¹, and G⁻¹(I_n⊗A)G = (QᵀQ⁻ᵀ)⊗(P⁻¹AP) = I_n⊗S. Likewise G⁻¹(Bᵀ⊗I_m)G = (QᵀBᵀQ⁻ᵀ)⊗(P⁻¹P) = Rᵀ⊗I_m. So G⁻¹KG = I_n⊗S + Rᵀ⊗I_m =: T.

Step 6. T is triangular. Index the rows and columns of T by pairs (j,i), with j in {1..n} and i in {1..m}. The entry at row (j,i) and column (l,k) is δ_{jl}S_{ik} + (Rᵀ)_{jl}δ_{ik}. The first term is nonzero only if l = j and k ≥ i. The second is nonzero only if k = i and l ≤ j, because Rᵀ is lower triangular. Define the rank of (j,i) as i−j. In both cases the rank of the column index is at least the rank of the row index, with equality only when (l,k) = (j,i). Order the pairs by rank, and break ties in any way. Then T is upper triangular. Its diagonal entry at (j,i) is S_{ii}+R_{jj} = λ_i+μ_j.
Step 7. Since K is similar to T, the eigenvalues of K with multiplicity are the sums λ_i+μ_j. The determinant is the product of the diagonal entries of T, so det K = ∏(λ_i+μ_j).

Step 8. Solvability. By Step 2 the map X ↦ AX+XB is K in coordinates. It is bijective if and only if K is invertible. This holds if and only if no sum λ_i+μ_j is zero. That condition says that no eigenvalue λ_i of A equals −μ_j, an eigenvalue of −B. If the condition fails, K has a nonzero kernel vector, and it gives a nonzero X with AX+XB = 0. Then the range is a proper subspace, so some C give no solution.

worked_application.title: A 2×2 Sylvester equation, a solution and a singular case
worked_application.goal: Solve AX+XB = I for A = [[1,2],[0,3]] and B = [[1,0],[1,2]]. Then change B so that the equation becomes singular.
hypotheses: m = n = 2 over ℚ, which lies in ℂ.
C = I.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The eigenvalues of A are 1 and 3. The eigenvalues of B are 1 and 2. The eigenvalues of −B are −1 and −2. The sets share no number, so the theorem predicts a unique solution.

steps.text: The Kronecker sum is K = I⊗A + Bᵀ⊗I. Writing it out gives the 4×4 matrix with rows (2,2,1,0), (0,4,0,1), (0,0,3,2), (0,0,0,5).

K is upper triangular with diagonal 2, 4, 3, 5. These numbers are the sums 1+1, 3+1, 1+2, 3+2 in the order of the pairs. They are the four values λ_i+μ_j, and the theorem predicts them. So det K = 2·4·3·5 = 120.
Solve K·vec(X) = vec(I) = (1,0,0,1)ᵀ by back substitution. The result is vec(X) = (37/60, −1/20, −2/15, 1/5)ᵀ. So X = [[37/60, −2/15], [−1/20, 1/5]].
Check by hand. AX = [[31/60, 4/15], [−3/20, 3/5]] and XB = [[29/60, −4/15], [3/20, 2/5]]. The sum is [[1,0],[0,1]]. So the solution is correct and unique.

Singular case. Replace B by B′ = [[−1,0],[1,2]]. Its eigenvalues are −1 and 2. So −B′ has eigenvalues 1 and −2, and 1 is also an eigenvalue of A. The theorem predicts a nonzero solution of AX+XB′ = 0, and det K′ = 0.
Take X = [[1,0],[0,0]]. Then AX = [[1,0],[0,0]] and XB′ = [[−1,0],[0,0]]. Their sum is zero. A computer algebra system confirms that det K′ = 0 and that the kernel of K′ is spanned by vec of this X.

worked_application.result: The equation AX+XB = I has the unique solution X = [[37/60, −2/15], [−1/20, 1/5]] and det K = 120. For B′ the equation AX+XB′ = 0 has the nonzero solution E_11.

limitations: The proof uses triangularization over ℂ. Over ℝ the eigenvalues may be complex, but the statement about solvability is the same, because ℝ-solvability and ℂ-solvability agree for a real linear system.
The vec form has size mn×mn. Solving it directly costs O((mn)^3) operations. Numerical codes reduce A and B to Schur form instead, and cost O(m^3+n^3).
If A and −B have eigenvalues that are close, K is nearly singular. The solution is then sensitive to errors.
The theorem is about the eigenvalues of the Kronecker sum. The eigenvalues of A⊗B are the products λ_iμ_j. That statement has a similar proof but it is not proved here.

results.name: Galois group S_p for an irreducible polynomial of prime degree with two nonreal roots
results.statement: Let p be a prime. Let f be an irreducible polynomial of degree p in ℚ[x] that has exactly p−2 real roots. Then f has exactly two nonreal roots. The Galois group of f over ℚ is the full symmetric group S_p acting on the p roots. Its order is p!.
hypotheses: f is irreducible over ℚ, so f is separable and has p distinct roots in ℂ.
p is prime.
Exactly p−2 of the roots are real.

prerequisites.reason: The application needs the irreducibility of x^5 − 4x + 2, proved by the Eisenstein criterion.
Step 7 uses that the symmetric group is generated by transpositions.

definitions.name: Galois group of a polynomial
definitions.text: The group of automorphisms of the splitting field of f over ℚ. It acts faithfully on the set of roots, so it is a subgroup of the symmetric group on the roots.

definitions.name: transposition
definitions.text: A permutation that swaps two points and fixes all other points.

definitions.name: transitive action
definitions.text: A group G acts transitively on a set R if for all a and b in R some g in G has g(a) = b.

lemma galAction_isPretransitive [Fact ((p.map (algebraMap F E)).Splits)] (hp : Irreducible p) :
    MulAction.IsPretransitive p.Gal (p.rootSet E) := by
  refine ⟨fun x y ↦ ?_⟩
  have hx := minpoly.eq_of_irreducible hp (mem_rootSet.mp ((rootsEquivRootsAux p E).symm x).2).2
  have hy := minpoly.eq_of_irreducible hp (mem_rootSet.mp ((rootsEquivRootsAux p E).symm y).2).2
  obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ := (Normal.minpoly_eq_iff_mem_orbit p.SplittingField).mp (hy.symm.trans hx)
  exact ⟨g, (rootsEquivRootsAux p E).eq_symm_apply.mp (Subtype.ext hg)⟩

theorem prime_degree_dvd_card [CharZero F] (p_irr : Irreducible p) (p_deg : p.natDegree.Prime) :
    p.natDegree ∣ Nat.card p.Gal := by
  rw [Gal.card_of_separable p_irr.separable]
  have hp : p.degree ≠ 0 := fun h =>
    Nat.Prime.ne_zero p_deg (natDegree_eq_zero_iff_degree_le_zero.mpr (le_of_eq h))
  let α : p.SplittingField :=
    rootOfSplits (SplittingField.splits p) (by rwa [degree_map])
  have hα : IsIntegral F α := .of_finite F α
  use Module.finrank F⟮α⟯ p.SplittingField
  suffices (minpoly F α).natDegree = p.natDegree by
    let _ : AddCommGroup F⟮α⟯ := Ring.toAddCommGroup
    rw [← Module.finrank_mul_finrank F F⟮α⟯ p.SplittingField,
      IntermediateField.adjoin.finrank hα, this]
  suffices minpoly F α ∣ p by
    have key := (minpoly.irreducible hα).dvd_symm p_irr this
    apply le_antisymm
    · exact natDegree_le_of_dvd this p_irr.ne_zero
    · exact natDegree_le_of_dvd key (minpoly.ne_zero hα)
  apply minpoly.dvd F α
  rw [← eval_map_algebraMap, eval_rootOfSplits]

/-- `gal p` embeds as a subgroup of permutations of the roots of `p` in `E`. -/
theorem galActionHom_injective [Fact ((p.map (algebraMap F E)).Splits)] :
    Function.Injective (galActionHom p E) := by
  rw [injective_iff_map_eq_one]
  intro ϕ hϕ
  ext (x hx)
  have key := Equiv.Perm.ext_iff.mp hϕ (rootsEquivRootsAux p E ⟨x, hx⟩)
  change
    rootsEquivRootsAux p E (ϕ • (rootsEquivRootsAux p E).symm (rootsEquivRootsAux p E ⟨x, hx⟩)) =
      rootsEquivRootsAux p E ⟨x, hx⟩
    at key
  rw [Equiv.symm_apply_apply] at key
  exact Subtype.ext_iff.mp (Equiv.injective (rootsEquivRootsAux p E) key)

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Step 1. Let Σ be the splitting field of f in ℂ and let G = Gal(Σ/ℚ). Let R be the set of roots of f. Because f is irreducible over a field of characteristic 0, f and f′ are coprime, so |R| = p. An automorphism of Σ permutes R. It is determined by its action on R, because Σ is generated by R over ℚ. So G embeds in Sym(R) ≅ S_p.

Step 2. G is transitive on R. Let α and β be roots. Both have minimal polynomial f over ℚ, up to a scalar. So there is a field isomorphism ℚ(α) → ℚ(β) sending α to β. It extends to an automorphism of the normal extension Σ. This automorphism sends α to β.

Step 3. G contains a transposition. The coefficients of f are real, so complex conjugation c maps roots to roots. Hence c maps Σ to itself, and c restricted to Σ is in G. It fixes the p−2 real roots. The two nonreal roots are swapped by c, because a nonreal root α of a real polynomial has its conjugate ᾱ as another nonreal root, and there are only two. So c acts on R as a transposition τ = (a b).

Step 4. Lemma. Let G be a transitive subgroup of Sym(R) with |R| = p prime. Suppose G contains a transposition (a b). Then G = Sym(R). Proof. For x and y in R, write x ∼ y if x = y or the transposition (x y) lies in G. This is an equivalence relation. For three distinct points, (x z) = (x y)(y z)(x y), which lies in G when (x y) and (y z) lie in G.

Step 5. For g in G, g(x y)g⁻¹ = (gx gy). So x ∼ y implies gx ∼ gy, and g maps each class onto a class. Because G is transitive, for any two classes some g maps a point of the first class into the second. Then g maps the first class onto the second. So all classes have the same size s. The number of classes times s equals p, and p is prime. So s = 1 or s = p.
Step 6. Since (a b) lies in G, a ∼ b with a ≠ b. So s ≥ 2. Hence s = p. All points are equivalent. So every transposition of R lies in G.
Step 7. Every permutation is a product of transpositions. So G, which contains all transpositions, is equal to Sym(R). By Steps 1 to 3 and the lemma, G ≅ S_p, and |G| = p!.

worked_application.title: The quintic x^5−4x+2 has Galois group S_5
worked_application.goal: Show that the Galois group of f = x^5 − 4x + 2 over ℚ is the full symmetric group S_5.
hypotheses: f has integer coefficients.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: We check the two hypotheses of the theorem: f is irreducible of prime degree 5, and f has exactly three real roots.

steps.text: Irreducibility. Use Eisenstein criterion at the prime 2. The prime 2 divides the coefficients −4 and 2. It does not divide the leading coefficient 1. And 4 does not divide the constant term 2. So f is irreducible over ℚ.
At least three real roots. f(−2) = −22, f(−1) = 5, f(0) = 2, f(1) = −1 and f(2) = 26. The sign changes give a real root in each of (−2,−1), (0,1) and (1,2).

At most three real roots. The derivative f′(x) = 5x^4 − 4 has exactly two real zeros, ±(4/5)^{1/4}. By Rolle theorem, between two real roots of f there is a zero of f′. Four real roots would need three zeros of f′. So f has at most three real roots.
So f has exactly three real roots and two nonreal roots. Numerical values are −1.5185, 0.5085, 1.2436 and −0.1168 ± 1.4384i.

By the theorem, Gal(f/ℚ) ≅ S_5, of order 120. Check of consistency: a computer algebra system returns disc(f) = −212144. This is negative, so it is not a square in ℚ. Hence the group is not inside A_5, as the theorem requires.

worked_application.result: The Galois group of x^5 − 4x + 2 over ℚ is S_5 with 120 elements.

limitations: The theorem needs exactly two nonreal roots. A prime degree with four nonreal roots may have a smaller group.

The result gives the group only. It does not give the roots by formula. For p ≥ 5 the group S_p is not solvable, and this is a separate known fact. It shows that such roots cannot be written with radicals.
The proof uses the embedding of the splitting field in ℂ. For other base fields the argument needs another source of a transposition.
For p = 2 and p = 3 the statement is true and easy to check by hand.

results.name: Counting monic irreducible polynomials over a finite field
results.statement: Let q be a prime power and let N_q(n) be the number of monic irreducible polynomials of degree n in F_q[x]. Then x^{q^n} − x is the product of all monic irreducible polynomials over F_q whose degree divides n. Hence ∑_{d|n} d·N_q(d) = q^n, and N_q(n) = (1/n)·∑_{d|n} μ(n/d)·q^d. Also N_q(n) ≥ 1 for every n ≥ 1. In particular F_q has an extension of every degree n.
hypotheses: q is a prime power and F_q is the field with q elements.
n is a positive integer.
μ is the Möbius function.

definitions.name: Frobenius map

definitions.name: Möbius function
definitions.text: μ(1) = 1, μ(m) = (−1)^k if m is a product of k distinct primes, and μ(m) = 0 if a square greater than 1 divides m.

source.alignment: The source proves that a finite field K embeds in L over F if and only if [K:F] divides [L:F]. This is the field form of the criterion in Step 4: F_{q^d} sits inside F_{q^n} if and only if d divides n. The source does not count irreducible polynomials.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Step 1. The polynomial P = x^{q^n} − x is squarefree. Its derivative is q^n·x^{q^n−1} − 1 = −1, because q^n is zero in F_q. So gcd(P, P′) = 1. A repeated irreducible factor g of P would divide both P and P′. So no irreducible factor of P occurs twice. Hence P is the product of the distinct monic irreducible polynomials that divide it.

Step 2. Setup for a divisor test. Let f be monic irreducible of degree d. Let K = F_q[x]/(f). This is a field with q^d elements. Let α be the class of x. Then K = F_q[α]. Let φ(y) = y^q on K. It is a ring homomorphism. It fixes F_q, because a^q = a for a in F_q.

Step 3. The order of φ is d. Every y in K satisfies y^{q^d} = y, because K^× has order q^d − 1. So φ^d = id. Let r be the least positive integer with φ^r = id. Then r ≤ d. If φ^r = id, every element of K is a root of x^{q^r} − x, which has at most q^r roots. So q^d ≤ q^r and d ≤ r. Hence r = d. The set of integers m with φ^m = id is the set of multiples of d, because it is a subgroup of ℤ that contains d and no smaller positive number.

Step 4. f divides P if and only if d divides n. Indeed f | P if and only if P(α) = 0. This holds if and only if φ^n(α) = α. The map φ^n is a ring homomorphism that fixes F_q. The element α generates K as an F_q-algebra. So φ^n(α) = α if and only if φ^n = id. By Step 3, this holds if and only if d | n.
Step 5. By Steps 1 and 4, x^{q^n} − x = ∏_{d|n} ∏_{f monic irreducible, deg f = d} f. Compare degrees. We get q^n = ∑_{d|n} d·N_q(d).
Step 6. Möbius inversion. Put g(n) = q^n and h(d) = d·N_q(d). Step 5 says g(n) = ∑_{d|n} h(d) for all n. The inversion formula gives n·N_q(n) = ∑_{d|n} μ(n/d)·q^d.

Step 7. Positivity. For n = 1, N_q(1) = q ≥ 1. Let n ≥ 2 and m = ⌊n/2⌋. Step 5 for each d gives d·N_q(d) ≤ q^d. So n·N_q(n) = q^n − ∑_{d|n, d<n} d·N_q(d) ≥ q^n − ∑_{d=1}^{m} q^d. The geometric sum is (q^{m+1} − q)/(q − 1) ≤ q^{m+1} − q. Because m + 1 ≤ n for n ≥ 2, we get n·N_q(n) ≥ q^n − q^{m+1} + q ≥ q > 0.

results.name: Index of a principal ideal of the ring of integers equals the absolute norm
results.statement: Let K be a number field of degree n and let O_K be its ring of integers. For every nonzero α in O_K, the quotient O_K/αO_K is finite and its order is |N_{K/ℚ}(α)|. If M_α is the integer matrix of multiplication by α in a ℤ-basis of O_K, then O_K/αO_K ≅ ℤ/d_1 ⊕ … ⊕ ℤ/d_n, where d_1 | … | d_n are the invariant factors of M_α. Consequently α is a unit if and only if |N(α)| = 1, and α is irreducible whenever |N(α)| is a prime number.
hypotheses: K is a number field and O_K is a free ℤ-module of rank n = [K:ℚ].
α is a nonzero element of O_K.
N_{K/ℚ}(α) is the determinant of the ℚ-linear map x ↦ αx on K.

prerequisites.reason: Step 3 and the application use the Smith normal form over ℤ and the order formula for the quotient.

definitions.name: norm N_{K/ℚ}
definitions.text: N(α) is the determinant of multiplication by α on K as a ℚ-vector space. It is multiplicative. It equals the product of the conjugates of α.

definitions.name: absolute norm of an ideal
definitions.text: For a nonzero ideal I of O_K, N(I) = |O_K/I|. For I = αO_K the theorem says N(I) = |N(α)|.

definitions.name: irreducible element
definitions.text: A nonzero non-unit that has no factorization into two non-units.

steps.text: Step 1. Let w_1,…,w_n be a ℤ-basis of O_K. It is also a ℚ-basis of K. Multiplication by α maps O_K to O_K, because α is an algebraic integer in O_K. So αw_j = ∑_i (M_α)_{ij} w_i with an integer matrix M_α. By definition of the norm, det M_α = N_{K/ℚ}(α). The determinant does not depend on the basis.

Step 2. Because α ≠ 0 and K is a field, α is invertible in K, so det M_α ≠ 0. Hence M_α is injective as a map ℤ^n → ℤ^n. Under the identification O_K ≅ ℤ^n by the basis, the image of multiplication by α is the ideal αO_K. So αO_K corresponds to the column lattice M_α·ℤ^n.

Step 3. By the Smith theorem for ℤ, there are invertible integer matrices U and V with U·M_α·V = diag(d_1,…,d_n), with d_1 | … | d_n, all nonzero. The quotient ℤ^n/M_α ℤ^n is isomorphic to ⊕ ℤ/d_i. Its order is ∏|d_i| = |det M_α| = |N(α)|. So |O_K/αO_K| = |N(α)|, and O_K/αO_K ≅ ⊕ ℤ/d_i.
Step 4. Units. An element α is a unit of O_K if and only if αO_K = O_K. This holds if and only if the quotient has one element. By Step 3, this holds if and only if |N(α)| = 1.

Step 5. Irreducibility. Let |N(α)| = p be prime. Then α is not a unit, by Step 4. Suppose α = βγ with β and γ in O_K. The norm is multiplicative, and N maps O_K to ℤ, so |N(β)|·|N(γ)| = p. One of the two factors equals 1. By Step 4, one of β and γ is a unit. So α is irreducible.

worked_application.title: Quotients of ℤ[√−5] by principal ideals, and 6 has two factorizations
worked_application.goal: Compute the quotient ring ℤ[√−5]/(α) for α = 1+√−5, 2+√−5 and 3. Then show that ℤ[√−5] is not a unique factorization domain.
hypotheses: K = ℚ(√−5). The ring of integers is ℤ[√−5] with ℤ-basis 1, √−5.
For α = a + b√−5, the matrix M_α in this basis is [[a, −5b], [b, a]], and N(α) = a^2 + 5b^2.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each quotient is the cokernel of a 2×2 integer matrix. The theorem gives its order by the determinant and its structure by the Smith form.

steps.text: α = 1+√−5. The matrix is [[1,−5],[1,1]] with determinant 6. The entries have gcd 1, so the Smith form is diag(1,6). Hence ℤ[√−5]/(1+√−5) ≅ ℤ/6, of order 6 = N(α).
α = 2+√−5. The matrix is [[2,−5],[1,2]] with determinant 9 and entry gcd 1. The Smith form is diag(1,9). So the quotient is ℤ/9, of order 9.
α = 3. The matrix is 3I with determinant 9 and entry gcd 3. The Smith form is diag(3,3). So the quotient is ℤ/3 ⊕ ℤ/3, of order 9. Two elements of the same norm 9 give two different quotient groups.
There is no element of norm 2: a^2 + 5b^2 = 2 has no integer solution, because b = 0 gives a^2 = 2 and b ≠ 0 gives at least 5. Also a^2 + 5b^2 = 3 has no solution.

The element 2 has norm 4. A factorization into two non-units would need two factors of norm 2 by Step 4 and multiplicativity. There is none, so 2 is irreducible. In the same way 3 (norm 9) is irreducible, since a factorization needs two factors of norm 3. And 1±√−5 (norm 6) is irreducible, since a factorization needs factors of norms 2 and 3.

Now 6 = 2·3 = (1+√−5)(1−√−5). The norms of the four irreducible factors are 4, 9, 6 and 6. The only units of ℤ[√−5] are ±1, because a^2 + 5b^2 = 1 forces b = 0. So associated elements have the same norm. Hence 2 is not associated to 1±√−5. Hence ℤ[√−5] is not a unique factorization domain.

worked_application.result: The quotients have orders 6, 9 and 9. They are ℤ/6, ℤ/9 and ℤ/3 ⊕ ℤ/3. The two factorizations of 6 use irreducibles of different norms, so unique factorization fails in ℤ[√−5].
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The theorem is for the ring of integers. For a nonmaximal order, the quotient order is still |N(α)| when α lies in the order, but the proof here uses that O_K is a free ℤ-module of full rank.
The Smith form of M_α gives the group structure only. It does not give the ring structure of the quotient.
The statement that |N(α)| prime implies irreducible is not an equivalence. The element 1+√−5 has norm 6 and is irreducible.
Multiplicativity of the absolute norm for general ideals needs unique factorization of ideals. The theorem avoids it, because it treats principal ideals only.

results.name: Minkowski bound: every ideal class has an integral ideal of small norm
results.statement: Let K be a number field of degree n with r_2 pairs of complex embeddings and discriminant d_K. Let M_K = (n!/n^n)·(4/π)^{r_2}·√|d_K|. Then every ideal class of K contains an integral ideal I of O_K with N(I) ≤ M_K. Hence the class group is finite. It is generated by the classes of the prime ideals P with N(P) ≤ M_K, and each such P lies over a rational prime p ≤ M_K. If M_K < 2, then the class number is 1.
hypotheses: K is a number field with n = r_1 + 2r_2.
O_K is a Dedekind domain. An ideal J contains (α) if and only if J divides (α).
The absolute norm N(I) = |O_K/I| is multiplicative on ideals.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Step 1. Covolume of an ideal lattice. Let ω_1,…,ω_n be a ℤ-basis of O_K and let M = (σ_i(ω_j)) be the n×n matrix of all n embeddings. Then d_K = det(M)^2. Replace the rows of each complex pair, z and z̄, by Re z and Im z. These new rows are (z + z̄)/2 and (z − z̄)/(2i). Each pair changes the determinant by the factor of modulus 1/2. So the real matrix has |det| = 2^{−r_2}·√|d_K|. This is the covolume of σ(O_K). For a nonzero ideal I, σ(I) has index N(I) in σ(O_K). So its covolume is 2^{−r_2}·√|d_K|·N(I).

Step 2. A convex body. For t > 0, let B_t = {(x,z) : ∑|x_i| + 2∑|z_j| ≤ t}. It is compact, convex and symmetric about 0. Its volume is V(t) = t^n·V(1) by scaling. Claim: V(1) = 2^{r_1}·(π/2)^{r_2}/n!.

Step 3. Proof of the volume formula, by induction on r_1 + r_2. If r_1 = 1 and r_2 = 0, the set is [−1,1], with length 2. If r_1 = 0 and r_2 = 1, the set is the disc |z| ≤ 1/2, with area π/4. For the step, fix one real coordinate x. The slice is a body of the same kind with t replaced by 1 − |x|, so it has volume (1 − |x|)^m·V′, where m is the dimension of the rest and V′ its unit volume. Then V = V′·∫_{−1}^{1} (1 − |x|)^m dx = 2V′/(m+1). Likewise fix a complex coordinate z. Then V = V′·∫_{|z|≤1/2} (1 − 2|z|)^m dA = V′·2π·∫_0^{1/2} (1 − 2s)^m·s ds = V′·(π/2)·∫_0^1 (1 − u)^m·u du = V′·(π/2)/((m+1)(m+2)). These two recurrences give the formula.

Step 4. Choose t. By Step 1, the lattice σ(I) has covolume 2^{−r_2}√|d_K|·N(I). By Minkowski convex body theorem, a compact convex symmetric set of volume at least 2^n times the covolume contains a nonzero lattice point. Choose t with V(t) = 2^n·2^{−r_2}√|d_K|·N(I). By Step 3, t^n = n!·2^{n−r_1−r_2}·(2/π)^{r_2}·√|d_K|·N(I). Since n − r_1 = 2r_2, this gives t^n = n!·(4/π)^{r_2}·√|d_K|·N(I). So there is a nonzero α in I with σ(α) in B_t.

Step 5. Bound the norm. The absolute value |N(α)| is the product of the n numbers |x_i| (r_1 of them) and |z_j|, |z_j| (each repeated twice). The sum of these n numbers is ∑|x_i| + 2∑|z_j| ≤ t. By the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality, |N(α)| ≤ (t/n)^n = (n!/n^n)·(4/π)^{r_2}·√|d_K|·N(I) = M_K·N(I).

Step 6. Class representatives. Let C be an ideal class. Choose an integral ideal J in the class C^{−1}. Apply Steps 4 and 5 to I = J. We get a nonzero α in J with |N(α)| ≤ M_K·N(J). Because (α) ⊂ J, there is an integral ideal I′ with (α) = J·I′. The norm of a principal ideal is |N(α)|. By multiplicativity, N(J)·N(I′) = |N(α)|. So N(I′) ≤ M_K. In the class group, [J][I′] = [(α)] = 1, so [I′] = [J]^{−1} = C.

Step 7. Generation. Factor I′ into prime ideals. Each prime factor P divides I′, so N(P) divides N(I′) and N(P) ≤ M_K. A prime P over p has N(P) = p^f ≥ p, so p ≤ M_K. Hence every class is a product of classes of such primes. An ideal of norm N contains N, so it divides the ideal (N), which has finitely many divisors. So there are finitely many ideals of norm at most M_K, and the class group is finite.
Step 8. If M_K < 2, an integral ideal with N(I) ≤ M_K < 2 has N(I) = 1, so I = O_K. Then every class is trivial.

worked_application.title: Class groups of ℚ(i) and ℚ(√−5)
worked_application.goal: Use the bound to find the class number of ℚ(i) and of ℚ(√−5).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Both fields are imaginary quadratic. The bound is M_K = (2/4)·(4/π)·√|d_K| = (2/π)√|d_K|.

steps.text: For ℚ(i): M_K = (2/π)·2 = 4/π ≈ 1.273. This is less than 2. By the theorem, the class number is 1, so ℤ[i] is a principal ideal domain.
For ℚ(√−5): −5 ≡ 3 mod 4, so O_K = ℤ[√−5] and d_K = −20. M_K = (2/π)√20 ≈ 2.847. The only prime p ≤ 2.847 is p = 2. So every class contains an integral ideal of norm 1 or 2.

The polynomial x^2 + 5 ≡ (x+1)^2 mod 2. Let P = (2, 1+√−5). The lattice of P in the basis 1, √−5 is spanned by (2,0), (1,1), (0,2) and (−5,1). A computer algebra system returns the Smith form diag(1,2). So N(P) = 2.

P^2 is generated by 4, 2+2√−5 and (1+√−5)^2 = −4+2√−5. The difference of the last two is 6. Since gcd(4,6) = 2, the ideal P^2 contains 2. Also every generator is even, so P^2 ⊂ (2). Hence P^2 = (2). An ideal of norm 2 contains 2, so it divides P^2. The divisors of P^2 are O_K, P and P^2, with norms 1, 2 and 4. So P is the only ideal of norm 2.
If P = (α) for α = a + b√−5, then N(α) = a^2 + 5b^2 = N(P) = 2. This has no integer solution. So P is not principal, and [P] ≠ 1. But [P]^2 = [(2)] = 1.
By the theorem, every class is 1 or [P]. So the class group is {1, [P]} of order 2.

worked_application.result: The Minkowski bound is 1.273 for ℚ(i), so h = 1. For ℚ(√−5) it is 2.847, and the class group is ℤ/2, generated by the class of P = (2, 1+√−5).

limitations: The bound is not sharp. The real class number can be much smaller than the number of candidate ideals.
The finiteness part needs the lattice structure of O_K. The proof here uses facts about Dedekind domains and the covolume of the Minkowski lattice as stated in the hypotheses and Step 1.
To prove that a class group is trivial, one must show that every prime of norm at most M_K is principal. This is a finite check but it can be long.
For a field with large |d_K| the bound grows like √|d_K|, so the method is slow. Better bounds exist under extra assumptions, but they are not proved here.

results.statement: Let n ≥ 1 and let ζ be a primitive n-th root of unity in ℂ. Then the cyclotomic polynomial Φ_n is irreducible over ℚ. So [ℚ(ζ):ℚ] = φ(n). The field ℚ(ζ)/ℚ is Galois, and the map (ℤ/n)^× → Gal(ℚ(ζ)/ℚ), a ↦ σ_a with σ_a(ζ) = ζ^a, is a group isomorphism. In particular the extension is abelian.

ζ is a primitive n-th root of unity.
φ is Euler totient function.

definitions.name: primitive root of unity
definitions.text: A complex number ζ with ζ^n = 1 and ζ^k ≠ 1 for 0 < k < n. The powers ζ^a with gcd(a,n) = 1 are exactly the primitive n-th roots.

definitions.name: cyclotomic polynomial
definitions.text: Φ_n(x) = ∏(x − ζ^a), over a in (ℤ/n)^×. It has degree φ(n).

definitions.name: Frobenius on polynomials

/-- `IsCyclotomicExtension.autEquivPow` repackaged in terms of `Gal`.
Asserts that the Galois group of `cyclotomic n K` is equivalent to `(ZMod n)ˣ`
if `cyclotomic n K` is irreducible in the base field. -/
noncomputable def galCyclotomicEquivUnitsZMod : (cyclotomic n K).Gal ≃* (ZMod n)ˣ :=
  (AlgEquiv.autCongr
          (IsSplittingField.algEquiv L _ : L ≃ₐ[K] (cyclotomic n K).SplittingField)).symm.trans
    (IsCyclotomicExtension.autEquivPow L h)

/-- The `MulEquiv` that takes an automorphism `f` to the element `k : (ZMod n)ˣ` such that
  `f μ = μ ^ k` for any root of unity `μ`. A strengthening of `IsPrimitiveRoot.autToPow`. -/
@[simps]
noncomputable def autEquivPow (h : Irreducible (cyclotomic n K)) : Gal(L/K) ≃* (ZMod n)ˣ :=
  let hζ := zeta_spec n K L
  let hμ t := hζ.pow_of_coprime _ (ZMod.val_coe_unit_coprime t)
  { (zeta_spec n K L).autToPow K with
    invFun := fun t =>
      (hζ.powerBasis K).equivOfMinpoly ((hμ t).powerBasis K)
        (by
          have := IsCyclotomicExtension.neZero' n K L
          simp only [IsPrimitiveRoot.powerBasis_gen]
          have hr :=
            IsPrimitiveRoot.minpoly_eq_cyclotomic_of_irreducible
              ((zeta_spec n K L).pow_of_coprime _ (ZMod.val_coe_unit_coprime t)) h
          exact ((zeta_spec n K L).minpoly_eq_cyclotomic_of_irreducible h).symm.trans hr)
    left_inv := fun f => by
      simp only [MonoidHom.toFun_eq_coe]
      apply AlgEquiv.coe_toAlgHom_injective
      apply (hζ.powerBasis K).algHom_ext
      simp only [AlgEquiv.coe_toAlgHom]
      rw [PowerBasis.equivOfMinpoly_gen]
      simp only [IsPrimitiveRoot.powerBasis_gen, IsPrimitiveRoot.autToPow_spec]
    right_inv := fun x => by
      simp only [MonoidHom.toFun_eq_coe]
      generalize_proofs _ h
      have key := hζ.autToPow_spec K ((hζ.powerBasis K).equivOfMinpoly ((hμ x).powerBasis K) h)
      have := (hζ.powerBasis K).equivOfMinpoly_gen ((hμ x).powerBasis K) h
      rw [hζ.powerBasis_gen K] at this
      rw [this, IsPrimitiveRoot.powerBasis_gen] at key
      nth_rw 1 5 [← hζ.val_toRootsOfUnity_coe] at key
      simp only [← rootsOfUnity.coe_pow] at key
      replace key := rootsOfUnity.coe_injective key
      rw [pow_eq_pow_iff_modEq, ← Subgroup.orderOf_coe, ← orderOf_units, hζ.val_toRootsOfUnity_coe,
        ← (zeta_spec n K L).eq_orderOf, ← ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff] at key
      simp only [ZMod.natCast_val, ZMod.cast_id', id] at key
      exact Units.ext key }

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Step 1. Φ_n is monic with integer coefficients, has degree φ(n), and divides x^n − 1. Its roots are the primitive n-th roots of unity, each with multiplicity 1.

Step 2. Let f be the minimal polynomial of ζ over ℚ. Then f | Φ_n in ℚ[x]. Claim: f is in ℤ[x]. Factor Φ_n in ℤ[x] into monic irreducible polynomials g_1⋯g_s. By Gauss lemma, each g_i is irreducible in ℚ[x]. The polynomial f is monic and irreducible in ℚ[x] and divides the product. So f equals some g_i, and f is in ℤ[x]. The same argument shows that the minimal polynomial of any root of Φ_n lies in ℤ[x] and is monic.

Step 3. Key claim. Let η be any root of f and let p be a prime with p ∤ n. Then f(η^p) = 0. Proof. The number η^p is again a primitive n-th root, so a root of Φ_n. Let g be its minimal polynomial. By Step 2, g is monic and in ℤ[x]. Suppose g ≠ f. Two distinct monic irreducible polynomials in ℚ[x] are coprime, and both divide x^n − 1. So fg divides x^n − 1 in ℚ[x]. Because f and g are monic, the quotient lies in ℤ[x]: x^n − 1 = f·g·h with h in ℤ[x].

Step 4. Since g(η^p) = 0, the number η is a root of g(x^p). So f divides g(x^p) in ℚ[x], and in ℤ[x] since f is monic: g(x^p) = f·k with k in ℤ[x]. Reduce modulo p. By the Frobenius identity, ḡ(x)^p = ḡ(x^p) = f̄·k̄ in F_p[x]. Let π be an irreducible factor of f̄. It exists because f̄ is monic of positive degree. Then π divides ḡ^p, so π divides ḡ. Therefore π^2 divides f̄·ḡ, which divides x^n − 1 in F_p[x].

Step 5. But x^n − 1 is squarefree in F_p[x]. Its derivative is n·x^{n−1}, and n ≠ 0 in F_p. The only root of the derivative is 0, and 0 is not a root of x^n − 1. So gcd(x^n − 1, derivative) = 1. This contradicts π^2 | x^n − 1. Hence g = f, and f(η^p) = 0.

Step 6. Every primitive n-th root is ζ^k with gcd(k,n) = 1 and k ≥ 1. Write k = p_1⋯p_r as a product of primes. None divides n. Apply Step 3 to η = ζ, then to η = ζ^{p_1}, which is a root of f, and so on. We get that ζ^k is a root of f. Therefore all φ(n) primitive roots are roots of f. They are distinct, so Φ_n divides f. With f | Φ_n, we get f = Φ_n. So Φ_n is irreducible and [ℚ(ζ):ℚ] = φ(n).

Step 7. The field ℚ(ζ) contains all powers ζ^a, so it is the splitting field of x^n − 1 over ℚ. So the extension is Galois, and the group has order φ(n). An automorphism σ sends ζ to a root of f = Φ_n, which is a primitive root ζ^a with a in (ℤ/n)^×. It is determined by a. For the composition, σ_a(σ_b(ζ)) = σ_a(ζ^b) = ζ^{ab}. So a ↦ σ_a is an injective group homomorphism from (ℤ/n)^× to the Galois group. Both groups have order φ(n), so it is an isomorphism.

worked_application.title: The Galois group of ℚ(ζ_12) and its subfields
worked_application.goal: Describe Gal(ℚ(ζ_12)/ℚ) and all intermediate fields.
hypotheses: n = 12 and ζ = e^{2πi/12}.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem identifies the Galois group with (ℤ/12)^×. The subgroup lattice then gives the subfields.

steps.text: Φ_12 = x^4 − x^2 + 1, of degree φ(12) = 4. A computer algebra system confirms that it is irreducible over ℚ. So [ℚ(ζ):ℚ] = 4.
The group (ℤ/12)^× has 4 elements. Each element squares to 1: 5^2 = 25, 7^2 = 49 and 11^2 = 121 are all ≡ 1 mod 12. So the group is the Klein four-group, with three subgroups of order 2.
The subgroup {1,5}. The element ζ + ζ^5 = (√3/2 + i/2) + (−√3/2 + i/2) = i is fixed by σ_5, since σ_5(ζ + ζ^5) = ζ^5 + ζ^25 = ζ^5 + ζ. So the fixed field is ℚ(i), which has degree 2.

The subgroup {1,7}. The element ζ^2 = (1 + i√3)/2 is fixed by σ_7, since ζ^14 = ζ^2. So the fixed field is ℚ(√−3). The subgroup {1,11} is complex conjugation. The element ζ + ζ^{−1} = √3 is fixed. So the fixed field is ℚ(√3).
By the Galois correspondence, the intermediate fields of ℚ(ζ_12)/ℚ are ℚ, ℚ(i), ℚ(√−3), ℚ(√3) and ℚ(ζ_12) = ℚ(i,√3). There are no others.

worked_application.result: Gal(ℚ(ζ_12)/ℚ) ≅ (ℤ/12)^× ≅ (ℤ/2)^2. The proper subfields are ℚ(i), ℚ(√−3) and ℚ(√3).
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The proof is over ℚ. Over another base field the polynomial Φ_n can factor. For example, Φ_5 over F_11 splits into linear factors.
The map a ↦ σ_a is canonical. It does not depend on the choice of ζ.
The proof needs p ∤ n in Step 3. The primes dividing n do not give a root of f in the same way.
The abelian result is one half of the Kronecker-Weber theorem. The other half says every abelian extension of ℚ lies in a cyclotomic field. It is not proved here.

results.name: Discriminant of a power basis as the norm of f′(α), and the index formula
results.statement: Let α be an algebraic number of degree n with monic minimal polynomial f over ℚ. Let α_1,…,α_n be the roots of f in ℂ. Put L = ℚ(α). The discriminant of the basis 1, α, …, α^{n−1} is disc(f) = det(Tr(α^{i+j})) = ∏_{i<j}(α_i − α_j)^2 = (−1)^{n(n−1)/2}·N_{L/ℚ}(f′(α)). If α is an algebraic integer and ℤ[α] has finite index m in the ring of integers O_L, then disc(f) = m^2·d_L, where d_L is the discriminant of L.
hypotheses: f is monic and irreducible over ℚ, so its roots are distinct.
For the second claim, α lies in O_L, so f has integer coefficients, and O_L is a free ℤ-module of rank n.

prerequisites.reason: Step 2 evaluates the determinant of the embedding matrix as a Vandermonde determinant.
Step 6 uses the Smith theorem for the index of an integer lattice.

definitions.name: discriminant of a basis
definitions.text: For a basis b_1,…,b_n of L over ℚ, disc(b) = det(Tr(b_i b_j)).

definitions.name: discriminant d_L
definitions.text: The discriminant of any ℤ-basis of O_L. It does not depend on the basis, because a change of basis has determinant ±1.

definitions.name: index m
definitions.text: m = [O_L : ℤ[α]], the order of the finite quotient group.

/-- Formula for the discriminant of a power basis using the norm of the field extension. -/
theorem discr_powerBasis_eq_norm [Algebra.IsSeparable K L] :
    discr K pb.basis =
      (-1) ^ (n * (n - 1) / 2) *
      norm K (aeval pb.gen (minpoly K pb.gen).derivative) := by
  let E := AlgebraicClosure L
  let := fun a b : E => Classical.propDecidable (Eq a b)
  have e : Fin pb.dim ≃ (L →ₐ[K] E) := by
    refine equivOfCardEq ?_
    rw [Fintype.card_fin, AlgHom.card]
    exact (PowerBasis.finrank pb).symm
  have hnodup : ((minpoly K pb.gen).aroots E).Nodup :=
    nodup_roots (Separable.map (Algebra.IsSeparable.isSeparable K pb.gen))
  have hroots : ∀ σ : L →ₐ[K] E, σ pb.gen ∈ (minpoly K pb.gen).aroots E := by
    intro σ
    rw [mem_roots, IsRoot.def, eval_map_algebraMap, aeval_algHom_apply]
    repeat' simp [minpoly.ne_zero pb.isIntegral_gen]
  apply (algebraMap K E).injective
  rw [map_mul, map_pow, map_neg, map_one, discr_powerBasis_eq_prod'' _ _ _ e]
  congr
  rw [norm_eq_prod_embeddings, prod_prod_Ioi_mul_eq_prod_prod_off_diag]
  conv_rhs =>
    congr
    rfl
    ext σ
    rw [← aeval_algHom_apply, ← eval_map_algebraMap, ← derivative_map,
      (IsAlgClosed.splits _).eval_root_derivative ((minpoly.monic pb.isIntegral_gen).map _)
      (hroots σ), ← Finset.prod_mk _ (hnodup.erase _)]
  rw [Finset.prod_sigma', Finset.prod_sigma']
  refine prod_bij' (fun i _ ↦ ⟨e i.2, e i.1 pb.gen⟩)
    (fun σ hσ ↦ ⟨e.symm (PowerBasis.lift pb σ.2 ?_), e.symm σ.1⟩) ?_ ?_ ?_ ?_ (fun i _ ↦ by simp)
    <;> simp only [mem_sigma, mem_univ, Finset.mem_mk, hnodup.mem_erase_iff, IsRoot.def,
      mem_roots', mem_singleton, true_and, mem_compl, Sigma.forall, Equiv.apply_symm_apply,
      PowerBasis.lift_gen, implies_true, Equiv.symm_apply_apply,
      Sigma.ext_iff, Equiv.symm_apply_eq, heq_eq_eq, and_true] at *
  · simpa only [aeval_def, eval₂_eq_eval_map] using hσ.2.2
  · exact fun a b hba ↦ ⟨fun h ↦ hba <| e.injective <| pb.algHom_ext h.symm, hroots _⟩
  · rintro a b hba ha
    rw [ha, PowerBasis.lift_gen] at hba
    exact hba.1 rfl
  · exact fun a b _ ↦ pb.algHom_ext <| pb.lift_gen _ _

determinant of the matrix whose `(i, j)` coefficient is `σⱼ (b i)`, where `σⱼ : L →ₐ[K] E` is the

    algebraMap K E (discr K b) = (embeddingsMatrixReindex K E b e).det ^ 2 := by
  rw [discr_def, RingHom.map_det, RingHom.mapMatrix_apply,

source_references.alignment: The source proves that the discriminant equals the square of the determinant of the matrix of embeddings. This is Step 1.
