proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Step 1. Trace form as a square. The n embeddings of L into ℂ send α to α_1,…,α_n. For a basis b, Tr(b_i b_j) = ∑_k σ_k(b_i)σ_k(b_j). So the matrix (Tr(b_i b_j)) equals MᵀM, with M = (σ_k(b_i)). Hence disc(b) = det(M)^2.

Step 2. Vandermonde. For the basis b_i = α^{i−1}, the matrix M has entries M_{ki} = α_k^{i−1}. This is the Vandermonde matrix of the distinct nodes α_1,…,α_n. So det M = ∏_{k<l}(α_l − α_k). Therefore disc(f) = ∏_{k<l}(α_l − α_k)^2 = ∏_{k<l}(α_k − α_l)^2.

Step 3. The derivative at a root. Since f = ∏(x − α_j), we get f′(α_i) = ∏_{j≠i}(α_i − α_j). The norm N_{L/ℚ}(f′(α)) is the product of the conjugates of f′(α). The conjugates are f′(α_i), because f′ has rational coefficients. So N(f′(α)) = ∏_i ∏_{j≠i}(α_i − α_j) = ∏_{i≠j}(α_i − α_j).

Step 4. Sign. Each unordered pair {i,j} with i < j appears twice in ∏_{i≠j}, as (α_i − α_j)(α_j − α_i) = −(α_i − α_j)^2. There are n(n−1)/2 pairs. So ∏_{i≠j}(α_i − α_j) = (−1)^{n(n−1)/2}·∏_{i<j}(α_i − α_j)^2. With Step 2, disc(f) = (−1)^{n(n−1)/2}·N(f′(α)).

Step 5. Index formula. Let w_1,…,w_n be a ℤ-basis of O_L. Because ℤ[α] has finite index in O_L, the powers α^{i−1} have an expansion α^{i−1} = ∑_j T_{ij}·w_j with an integer matrix T of nonzero determinant. The trace matrices satisfy G(α) = T·G(w)·Tᵀ, because the trace form is bilinear. So disc(f) = det(T)^2·d_L.

Step 6. The order of the quotient. The lattice ℤ[α] is the row lattice of T inside ℤ^n = O_L. By the Smith theorem over ℤ, the index of the row lattice of an integer matrix of nonzero determinant is |det T|. So m = |det T|, and disc(f) = m^2·d_L.

worked_application.title: The cubic x^3 − x − 1 and the quadratic x^2 − 12
worked_application.goal: Compute disc(f), the norm of f′(α) and the index in two examples.
hypotheses: Example 1: f = x^3 − x − 1, irreducible over ℚ.
Example 2: f = x^2 − 12 with α = √12 = 2√3.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Both are monic with integer coefficients. The theorem links disc(f), N(f′(α)) and the field discriminant.

steps.text: Example 1. For x^3 + ax + b the discriminant is −4a^3 − 27b^2. With a = −1 and b = −1, disc(f) = 4 − 27 = −23. A computer algebra system confirms this.
Here n = 3, so (−1)^{n(n−1)/2} = (−1)^3 = −1. By the theorem, N(f′(α)) = N(3α^2 − 1) = 23. The resultant Res(f, f′) computed by a computer algebra system is also 23.
The number 23 is squarefree. So m^2 divides 23 forces m = 1. Hence ℤ[α] = O_L and d_L = −23.
Example 2. disc(x^2 − 12) = 48. The check by the theorem: n = 2, so the sign is (−1)^1. And N(f′(α)) = N(2α) = N(4√3) = −48. So disc = (−1)·(−48) = 48.
The field is ℚ(√3). Its ring of integers is ℤ[√3], since 3 ≡ 3 mod 4, and d_L = 12. The ring ℤ[2√3] has index 2 in ℤ[√3]. So 48 = 2^2·12, as the index formula says.

worked_application.result: disc(x^3 − x − 1) = −23, N(f′(α)) = 23 and the field discriminant is −23 with index 1. disc(x^2 − 12) = 48 = 2^2·12 with index 2.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The theorem is for the power basis of one generator. A general ℤ-basis of O_L gives d_L, and there may be no generator with index 1.
The index formula gives only that m^2 divides disc(f). A squarefree disc(f) gives m = 1. A non-squarefree one does not decide m.
The proof assumes that O_L is free over ℤ with rank n. This is a standard fact about rings of integers.
The sign of the discriminant is (−1)^{r_2}, where r_2 is the number of pairs of complex embeddings. This is not proved here.

results.name: Picard iteration with a factorial error bound for globally Lipschitz fields
results.statement: Let I=[t₀,t₀+T] and let f:I×ℝⁿ→ℝⁿ be continuous with ‖f(t,x)−f(t,y)‖≤L‖x−y‖ for all t∈I and x,y∈ℝⁿ, where L>0. Fix x₀∈ℝⁿ and put M=max_{t∈I}‖f(t,x₀)‖. Define φ₀≡x₀ and φ_{k+1}(t)=x₀+∫_{t₀}^t f(s,φ_k(s))ds. Write τ=t−t₀. Then (a) ‖φ_{k+1}(t)−φ_k(t)‖≤M L^k τ^{k+1}/(k+1)! for all k≥0 and t∈I. (b) The φ_k converge uniformly on I to a C¹ function φ with φ′(t)=f(t,φ(t)) and φ(t₀)=x₀. (c) Every continuous ψ:I→ℝⁿ with ψ(t)=x₀+∫_{t₀}^t f(s,ψ(s))ds equals φ. (d) ‖φ(t)−φ_k(t)‖≤(M/L)·(Lτ)^{k+1}/(k+1)!·e^{Lτ} for all k≥0 and t∈I.
hypotheses: The Lipschitz bound is global in x. It is not local near x₀. For this reason the solution exists on the whole interval I and no smallness condition on T is needed.
The estimate (d) is explicit and does not use any contraction constant below 1. The factorial makes the bound small for large k whatever the size of LT.
Every C¹ solution of x′=f(t,x) with x(t₀)=x₀ satisfies the integral equation by the fundamental theorem of calculus. So (c) gives uniqueness for the differential equation.

/-- A time-dependent bound on the distance between the `n`-th iterates of `next` on two curves -/
lemma dist_iterate_next_apply_le (hf : IsPicardLindelof f t₀ x₀ a r L K)
    (hx : x ∈ closedBall x₀ r) (α β : FunSpace t₀ x₀ r L) (n : ℕ) (t : Icc tmin tmax) :
    dist ((next hf hx)^[n] α t) ((next hf hx)^[n] β t) ≤
      (K * |t.1 - t₀.1|) ^ n / n ! * dist α β := by
  induction n generalizing t with
  | zero => simpa using!
      ContinuousMap.dist_apply_le_dist (f := toContinuousMap α) (g := toContinuousMap β) _
  | succ n hn =>
    rw [iterate_succ_apply', iterate_succ_apply', dist_eq_norm, next_apply,
      next_apply, picard_apply, picard_apply, add_sub_add_left_eq_sub,
      ← intervalIntegral.integral_sub (intervalIntegrable_comp_compProj hf _ t)
        (intervalIntegrable_comp_compProj hf _ t)]
    calc
      _ ≤ ∫ τ in uIoc t₀.1 t.1, K ^ (n + 1) * |τ - t₀| ^ n / n ! * dist α β := by
        rw [intervalIntegral.norm_intervalIntegral_eq]
        apply MeasureTheory.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le (Continuous.integrableOn_uIoc (by fun_prop))
        apply ae_restrict_mem measurableSet_Ioc |>.mono
        intro t' ht'
        -- Can `grind` do this in the future?
        have ht' : t' ∈ Icc tmin tmax :=
          subset_trans uIoc_subset_uIcc (uIcc_subset_Icc t₀.2 t.2) ht'
        rw [← dist_eq_norm, compProj_of_mem, compProj_of_mem]
        exact dist_comp_iterate_next_le hf hx _ ⟨t', ht'⟩ (hn _)
      _ ≤ (K * |t.1 - t₀.1|) ^ (n + 1) / (n + 1) ! * dist α β := by
        apply le_of_abs_le
        -- critical: `integral_pow_abs_sub_uIoc`
        rw [← intervalIntegral.abs_intervalIntegral_eq, intervalIntegral.integral_mul_const,
          intervalIntegral.integral_div, intervalIntegral.integral_const_mul, abs_mul, abs_div,
          abs_mul, intervalIntegral.abs_intervalIntegral_eq, integral_pow_abs_sub_uIoc, abs_div,
          abs_pow, abs_pow, abs_dist, NNReal.abs_eq, abs_abs, mul_div, div_div, ← abs_mul,
          ← Nat.cast_succ, ← Nat.cast_mul, ← Nat.factorial_succ, Nat.abs_cast, ← mul_pow]

steps.text: Continuity of each iterate. The function φ₀ is constant. If φ_k is continuous, then s↦f(s,φ_k(s)) is continuous on I. Its integral from t₀ to t is continuous in t, so φ_{k+1} is continuous. All φ_k are well defined.
First step of (a). For k=0, φ₁(t)−φ₀(t)=∫_{t₀}^t f(s,x₀)ds. The norm of the integrand is at most M, so ‖φ₁(t)−φ₀(t)‖≤Mτ. This is the claim for k=0.

Induction for (a). Assume ‖φ_{k+1}(s)−φ_k(s)‖≤M L^k σ^{k+1}/(k+1)! with σ=s−t₀. Then φ_{k+2}(t)−φ_{k+1}(t)=∫_{t₀}^t [f(s,φ_{k+1}(s))−f(s,φ_k(s))]ds. The Lipschitz bound gives the integrand norm at most L‖φ_{k+1}(s)−φ_k(s)‖. Integrate: ‖φ_{k+2}(t)−φ_{k+1}(t)‖≤M L^{k+1}∫_0^τ σ^{k+1}/(k+1)! dσ = M L^{k+1} τ^{k+2}/(k+2)!.

Uniform convergence. By step 3, sup_I‖φ_{k+1}−φ_k‖≤M L^k T^{k+1}/(k+1)!. The sum over k is (M/L)(e^{LT}−1), which is finite. By the Weierstrass M-test the series φ₀+∑(φ_{k+1}−φ_k) converges uniformly on I. So the partial sums φ_k converge uniformly to a continuous function φ.

The limit solves the integral equation. For all s∈I, ‖f(s,φ_k(s))−f(s,φ(s))‖≤L‖φ_k(s)−φ(s)‖. The right side tends to 0 uniformly. So ∫_{t₀}^t f(s,φ_k(s))ds→∫_{t₀}^t f(s,φ(s))ds for every t. Pass to the limit in the definition of φ_{k+1} to get φ(t)=x₀+∫_{t₀}^t f(s,φ(s))ds. The integrand is continuous, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus φ is C¹ with φ′=f(t,φ) and φ(t₀)=x₀. This proves (b).

Error estimate (d). Since φ−φ_k=∑_{j≥k}(φ_{j+1}−φ_j) pointwise, step 3 gives ‖φ(t)−φ_k(t)‖≤∑_{j≥k}M L^j τ^{j+1}/(j+1)! = (M/L)∑_{m≥k+1}(Lτ)^m/m!. For m=k+1+i, (k+1+i)!≥(k+1)!·i!. So the sum is at most (Lτ)^{k+1}/(k+1)!·∑_{i≥0}(Lτ)^i/i! = (Lτ)^{k+1}e^{Lτ}/(k+1)!. This is (d).

Uniqueness (c). Let ψ be a continuous solution of the integral equation. The function ‖φ−ψ‖ is continuous on the compact set I, so it has a maximum D. Subtract the two integral equations and use the Lipschitz bound: ‖φ(t)−ψ(t)‖≤L∫_{t₀}^t‖φ(s)−ψ(s)‖ds. By induction on k, ‖φ(t)−ψ(t)‖≤D(Lτ)^k/k!. The right side tends to 0 as k→∞ for fixed τ. So φ=ψ on I.

worked_application.title: Picard iterates and the a priori error for x′=t+x, x(0)=1 on [0,1]
worked_application.goal: Compute the first Picard iterates, compare them with the exact solution at t=1, and pick the number of iterates that guarantees an error below 10⁻³.
hypotheses: L=1, because |f(t,x)−f(t,y)|=|x−y|.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The field f is continuous and has a global Lipschitz constant 1 in x. So parts (a) to (d) apply on all of [0,1].

steps.text: Compute the iterates. φ₀=1. φ₁=1+∫₀^t(s+1)ds=1+t+t²/2. φ₂=1+∫₀^t(s+φ₁(s))ds=1+t+t²+t³/6. φ₃=1+t+t²+t³/3+t⁴/24.
The exact solution is x(t)=2eᵗ−t−1. It satisfies x′=2eᵗ−1=t+x and x(0)=1. At t=1 it equals 2e−2=3.436564.

Compare at t=1. The errors x(1)−φ_k(1) for k=0,1,2,3,4 are 2.436564, 0.936564, 0.269897, 0.061564 and 0.011564. They fall by factors 2.6, 3.5, 4.4 and 5.3. The factors grow, as the factorial predicts.
Check (a) at t=1. The differences φ_{k+1}(1)−φ_k(1) for k=0,1,2,3 are 1.5, 0.666667, 0.208333 and 0.05. The bounds M/(k+1)! are 2, 1, 0.333333 and 0.083333. Each difference is below its bound.
Check (d) at t=1. The bound 2e/(k+1)! gives 5.4366, 2.7183, 0.9061 and 0.2265 for k=0,1,2,3. These values are above the true errors 2.4366, 0.9366, 0.2699 and 0.0616.

Choose k. We need 2e/(k+1)!≤10⁻³, that is (k+1)!≥5436.6. Since 7!=5040 is too small and 8!=40320 is enough, k+1=8 and k=7 guarantee the error. The bound for k=6 is 2e/7!=1.08×10⁻³, which does not give the guarantee, although the true error 2.5×10⁻⁴ is already below 10⁻³.

worked_application.result: Seven Picard iterates give a certified error below 10⁻³ on all of [0,1]. The a priori bound is valid but 2 to 4 times larger than the true error at t=1.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The global Lipschitz condition is essential. For x′=x² the field has no global constant and solutions blow up in finite time, so the iterates do not converge on long intervals.
The bound (d) is an upper bound and is often far from the true error. In the application it is 2 to 4 times too large at t=1.

The theorem uses the maximum norm of the difference on a compact interval. For fields that are only continuous, solutions exist by the Peano theorem but are not unique and the iterates need not converge.

results.name: Global error bound for the explicit Euler method
results.statement: Let I=[t₀,t₀+T], let f:I×ℝᵈ→ℝᵈ satisfy ‖f(t,x)−f(t,y)‖≤L‖x−y‖ for all t∈I and x,y, and let y:I→ℝᵈ be a C² solution of y′=f(t,y) with ‖y″(t)‖≤M on I. Take a step h=T/N, put tₙ=t₀+nh, u₀=y(t₀) and uₙ₊₁=uₙ+h f(tₙ,uₙ). Then for n=0,…,N the error εₙ=‖y(tₙ)−uₙ‖ satisfies εₙ≤(M h/(2L))(e^{L(tₙ−t₀)}−1) if L>0, and εₙ≤M h(tₙ−t₀)/2 if L=0. In particular max_n εₙ≤C h with C=(M/(2L))(e^{LT}−1).
hypotheses: The solution y must be twice continuously differentiable with a bounded second derivative. The Lipschitz condition is needed in the second variable only.
The initial value is exact. With an initial error ε₀>0 the bound gains the term ε₀e^{L(tₙ−t₀)}.
Rounding errors are not modelled. They add a term that grows like 1/h.

steps.text: Taylor remainder. Fix n and write r=y(tₙ₊₁)−y(tₙ)−h y′(tₙ). Then r=∫₀^h [y′(tₙ+s)−y′(tₙ)]ds. Since y′ is C¹ with ‖y″‖≤M, the mean value inequality gives ‖y′(tₙ+s)−y′(tₙ)‖≤Ms. So ‖r‖≤M∫₀^h s ds=M h²/2.
Error identity. The exact solution has y′(tₙ)=f(tₙ,y(tₙ)). So y(tₙ₊₁)=y(tₙ)+h f(tₙ,y(tₙ))+r. Subtract the Euler step: y(tₙ₊₁)−uₙ₊₁ = (y(tₙ)−uₙ)+h[f(tₙ,y(tₙ))−f(tₙ,uₙ)]+r.
One-step inequality. Take norms and use the Lipschitz bound on the bracket and step 1 on r: εₙ₊₁≤εₙ+hLεₙ+M h²/2=(1+hL)εₙ+M h²/2.
Induction. Let q=1+hL and ε₀=0. Claim: εₙ≤(M h²/2)∑_{j=0}^{n−1}q^j. This holds for n=0. If it holds for n, then εₙ₊₁≤q(M h²/2)∑_{j<n}q^j+M h²/2=(M h²/2)∑_{j=0}^{n}q^j.
Sum the geometric series. For L>0, ∑_{j<n}q^j=(qⁿ−1)/(q−1)=(qⁿ−1)/(hL). So εₙ≤(M h/(2L))(qⁿ−1). For L=0, q=1 and ∑_{j<n}q^j=n, so εₙ≤n M h²/2=M h(tₙ−t₀)/2.

Exponential bound. The inequality 1+x≤eˣ holds for all real x. With x=hL we get q≤e^{hL}, so qⁿ≤e^{nhL}=e^{L(tₙ−t₀)}. Insert this in step 5 to obtain εₙ≤(M h/(2L))(e^{L(tₙ−t₀)}−1). The bound with C follows from tₙ−t₀≤T.

worked_application.title: Euler method for y′=y, y(0)=1 on [0,1]
worked_application.goal: Compute the Euler value at t=1 for four step sizes and compare the true error with the bound of the theorem.
hypotheses: f(t,y)=y, so L=1. The exact solution is y=eᵗ, so y″=eᵗ≤e=M on [0,1].
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The field is Lipschitz in y with L=1. The solution is C² with |y″|≤e on [0,1]. The initial value is exact.

steps.text: The Euler iterate has the closed form uₙ=(1+h)ⁿ because uₙ₊₁=uₙ+h uₙ. At t=1, u_N=(1+h)^{1/h}.
The true errors e−u_N are 0.124539, 0.064984, 0.033218 and 0.016797. Each error is below its bound. The bound is about 1.9, 1.8, 1.8 and 1.7 times the error.

First order. When h halves, the error falls by the factors 1.916, 1.956 and 1.978. The ratio error/h is 1.2454, 1.2997, 1.3287 and 1.3438. It approaches e/2=1.3591, so the error is asymptotically (e/2)h.

Check the bound at inner nodes for h=0.1. At t₁=0.1 the error is 0.005171 and the bound is 0.014294. At t₅=0.5 the error is 0.038211 and the bound is 0.088170. At t₁₀=1 the error is 0.124539 and the bound is 0.233539.

Use the bound to choose h. To guarantee error ≤10⁻³ at t=1 we need 2.33539 h≤10⁻³, so h≤4.28×10⁻⁴ and N≥2336 steps. The bound is not sharp, but its size is right: the true error at h=0.0125 (80 steps) is 0.0168 and the bound is 0.0292.

worked_application.result: The Euler error at t=1 is bounded by 2.33539 h and the true error is about 1.36 h. The method is first order and the theorem gives a certified step size.

limitations: The bound is pessimistic when the solution is stable. For y′=−10y the Lipschitz constant is 10 and the bound grows like e^{10T}, but the true error stays small.
A stiff problem needs h<2/L for Euler to be stable at all. The theorem is useful only when e^{LT} is moderate. See the entry on absolute stability for the stiff regime.
The estimate needs a bound on y″. For fields with only Lipschitz regularity in t the local error is O(h^{1+α}) and the order drops.

results.name: Exponential stability from a quadratic Lyapunov function and a small nonlinearity
results.statement: Let A be a real n×n matrix. Let P and Q be real symmetric positive definite n×n matrices with AᵀP+PA=−Q. Let g:ℝⁿ→ℝⁿ be continuous. Let r>0 and κ≥0 satisfy ‖g(x)‖≤κ‖x‖ for ‖x‖≤r (Euclidean norm), and assume 2κλ_max(P)<λ_min(Q). Put c=(λ_min(Q)−2κλ_max(P))/λ_max(P)>0 and ρ=r√(λ_min(P)/λ_max(P)). Let x:[0,T)→ℝⁿ be any C¹ solution of x′=Ax+g(x) with ‖x(0)‖<ρ. Then for all t∈[0,T) we have ‖x(t)‖≤r, xᵀ(t)Px(t)≤e^{−ct}x(0)ᵀPx(0), and ‖x(t)‖²≤(λ_max(P)/λ_min(P))e^{−ct}‖x(0)‖². Hence the origin is exponentially stable.
hypotheses: The matrix P is given. If all eigenvalues of A have negative real part, then for each symmetric positive definite Q one such P exists. This fact is not part of the claim and is used only as a remark.
The bound on g is a local bound near 0. It holds for a nonlinearity of order ‖x‖² or higher after a choice of small r.
The theorem does not assert that a solution exists. For locally Lipschitz g, a solution exists locally and the estimate shows that it continues to T=∞.

/-- A Grönwall-like inequality: if `f : ℝ → E` is continuous on `[a, b]`, has right derivative
`f' x` at every point `x ∈ [a, b)`, and satisfies the inequalities `‖f a‖ ≤ δ`,
`∀ x ∈ [a, b), ‖f' x‖ ≤ K * ‖f x‖ + ε`, then `‖f x‖` is bounded by `gronwallBound δ K ε (x - a)`
on `[a, b]`. -/
theorem norm_le_gronwallBound_of_norm_deriv_right_le {f f' : ℝ → E} {δ K ε : ℝ} {a b : ℝ}
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Icc a b)) (hf' : ∀ x ∈ Ico a b, HasDerivWithinAt f (f' x) (Ici x) x)
    (ha : ‖f a‖ ≤ δ) (bound : ∀ x ∈ Ico a b, ‖f' x‖ ≤ K * ‖f x‖ + ε) :
    ∀ x ∈ Icc a b, ‖f x‖ ≤ gronwallBound δ K ε (x - a) :=
  le_gronwallBound_of_liminf_deriv_right_le (continuous_norm.comp_continuousOn hf)
    (fun x hx _r hr => (hf' x hx).liminf_right_slope_norm_le hr) ha bound

source.alignment: The source proves that a function with norm of derivative at most K times its norm plus ε stays below gronwallBound. With ε=0 the bound is δe^{Kx}. This is the differential inequality step 4.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Norm equivalence. Since P is symmetric, the spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. In it xᵀPx is a sum of eigenvalues times squared coordinates. So λ_min(P)‖x‖²≤V(x)≤λ_max(P)‖x‖², where V(x)=xᵀPx. The same holds for Q.
Derivative of V. Let x be a solution and v(t)=V(x(t)). Because P is symmetric, v′=x′ᵀPx+xᵀPx′=xᵀ(AᵀP+PA)x+2xᵀPg(x)=−xᵀQx+2xᵀPg(x).

Bound on v′ while ‖x‖≤r. We have xᵀQx≥λ_min(Q)‖x‖². Also |xᵀPg(x)|≤‖P‖‖x‖‖g(x)‖≤λ_max(P)κ‖x‖², because the operator norm of a symmetric positive definite P is λ_max(P). So v′≤−(λ_min(Q)−2κλ_max(P))‖x‖². By step 1, ‖x‖²≥v/λ_max(P). The coefficient is positive, so v′≤−c v.

Differential inequality. From v′≤−c v on an interval, the function w(t)=v(t)e^{ct} has w′=(v′+cv)e^{ct}≤0. So w is non-increasing and v(t)≤v(0)e^{−ct}. This is the Grönwall comparison with the bound δe^{Kx} for K=−c and ε=0.

The solution stays in the ball. Let S={s∈[0,T): ‖x(σ)‖≤r for all σ∈[0,s]}. It contains 0 because ‖x(0)‖<ρ≤r. On S, steps 3 and 4 give ‖x(s)‖²≤v(s)/λ_min(P)≤v(0)/λ_min(P)≤(λ_max(P)/λ_min(P))‖x(0)‖²<(λ_max(P)/λ_min(P))ρ²=r². So on S we have ‖x‖<r strictly.

Closing the continuity argument. Suppose s*=sup S<T. Then ‖x(s*)‖<r by step 5 and by continuity ‖x(σ)‖≤r on [s*,s*+η] for some η>0. This contradicts the definition of s*. So S=[0,T) and the estimates of steps 3 and 4 hold for all t.

Conclusion. For all t∈[0,T), v(t)≤v(0)e^{−ct}. Using step 1 twice, ‖x(t)‖²≤v(t)/λ_min(P)≤e^{−ct}v(0)/λ_min(P)≤(λ_max(P)/λ_min(P))e^{−ct}‖x(0)‖². Given ε>0 choose δ=min(ρ,ε√(λ_min(P)/λ_max(P))). Then ‖x(0)‖<δ implies ‖x(t)‖<ε for all t and ‖x(t)‖→0.

worked_application.title: Damped pendulum x″+x′+sin x=0 near the rest position
worked_application.goal: Find an explicit basin of exponential decay and a decay rate, and test the bound by numerical integration.
hypotheses: State x=(x₁,x₂)=(θ,θ′). Then x′=Ax+g(x) with A=[[0,1],[−1,−1]] and g(x)=(0, x₁−sin x₁).
Take Q=I and r=1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The matrix A has the characteristic polynomial λ²+λ+1 with roots of real part −1/2. The Lyapunov equation has the solution P below. The bound on g is verified in step 3.

steps.text: Solve AᵀP+PA=−I for symmetric P. With P=[[p₁₁,p₁₂],[p₁₂,p₂₂]] the three entry equations give p₁₂=1/2, p₂₂=1 and p₁₁=3/2. Direct multiplication gives AᵀP=[[−1/2,−1],[1,−1/2]] and PA=[[−1/2,1],[−1,−1/2]]. The sum is −I.
The eigenvalues of P are (5±√5)/4, that is 1.809017 and 0.690983. So λ_max(P)/λ_min(P)=(3+√5)/2=2.618034 and √(λ_min/λ_max)=(√5−1)/2=0.618034. With r=1 the basin radius is ρ=0.618034.
The nonlinearity. By Taylor’s theorem for the alternating series of sin, |x₁−sin x₁|≤|x₁|³/6. For ‖x‖≤1 this gives ‖g(x)‖≤|x₁|³/6≤‖x‖/6. So κ=1/6.
Check the condition. 2κλ_max(P)=λ_max(P)/3=0.603006, which is below λ_min(Q)=1. The rate is c=(1−0.603006)/1.809017=1/λ_max(P)−1/3=0.219453.
The theorem gives for every solution with ‖x(0)‖<0.618034 the bound ‖x(t)‖²≤2.618034 e^{−0.219453t}‖x(0)‖². At ‖x(0)‖=0.6 this gives ‖x(10)‖≤0.32404 and ‖x(20)‖≤0.10816.

Test by numerical integration (Runge-Kutta, relative tolerance 10⁻¹¹) for x(0)=(0.6,0), (0,0.6), (−0.42,0.42) and (0.3,−0.5), over 0≤t≤40. In each case V(x(t))e^{ct}/V(x(0)) stays at most 1 and ‖x(t)‖ never exceeds ‖x(0)‖. For x(0)=(0.6,0) the true values are ‖x(10)‖=0.00359 and ‖x(20)‖=0.000036, below the bounds 0.324 and 0.108.

worked_application.result: Every solution that starts within 0.618 of the rest position decays at least like e^{−0.1097t}. The bound is safe but conservative, because the true rate is near 0.5.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The estimate gives only a local result and the basin radius ρ is not sharp. A better P, or a Q chosen to fit A, enlarges the basin.
The theorem needs a bound ‖g(x)‖≤κ‖x‖ with κ small compared with λ_min(Q)/λ_max(P). It cannot decide the case where A has an eigenvalue with zero real part.
A converse is not claimed. Failure of the inequality for one pair P,Q does not imply instability.

results.name: Liouville formula for the determinant of a fundamental matrix
results.statement: Let J be an interval and A:J→𝕂ⁿˣⁿ continuous, where 𝕂 is ℝ or ℂ. Let X:J→𝕂ⁿˣⁿ be a C¹ matrix function with X′(t)=A(t)X(t) for all t∈J. Then for all t,t₀∈J, det X(t)=det X(t₀)·exp(∫_{t₀}^t tr A(s)ds). In particular, det X vanishes at one point of J or at no point of J. If the columns of X are n solutions of x′=A(t)x, their Wronskian det X is either identically 0 or never 0.
hypotheses: The matrix A(t) may depend on t in any continuous way. No commutation property is needed.
Only the trace of A enters the formula. The other entries do not change the determinant.
For a scalar equation y⁽ⁿ⁾+a_{n−1}y⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾+…+a₀y=0 the companion matrix has trace −a_{n−1}. The Wronskian equals W(t₀)exp(−∫a_{n−1}).

prerequisites.reason: The singular case uses the Grönwall bound with zero initial value to show that a linear system has only the zero solution through a zero.

definitions.name: fundamental matrix
definitions.text: A matrix solution X of X′=A(t)X with det X(t)≠0 for all t. Its columns form a basis of the solution space of x′=A(t)x.

definitions.name: Wronskian
definitions.text: The determinant of the matrix whose columns are n solutions of a linear system of dimension n. For a scalar equation it is the determinant of the matrix of the functions and their derivatives.

definitions.name: trace
definitions.text: The sum of the diagonal entries of a square matrix.

/-- The first two terms of the Taylor expansion of `det (1 + r • M)` at `r = 0`. -/
lemma det_one_add_smul (r : R) (M : Matrix n n R) :
    det (1 + r • M) =
      1 + trace M * r + (det (1 + (X : R[X]) • M.map C)).divX.divX.eval r * r ^ 2 := by
  simpa [eval_det, ← smul_eq_mul_diagonal] using congr(eval r $(Matrix.det_one_add_X_smul M))

steps.text: Determinant near the identity. In the Leibniz expansion of det(I+E) the identity permutation gives ∏(1+E_ii)=1+tr E+(terms of degree at least 2 in the entries of E). Every other permutation moves at least two indices, so it contains at least two off-diagonal factors. Hence det(I+E)=1+tr E+R(E), where R is a polynomial with no terms of degree below 2. So |R(E)|≤C‖E‖² for ‖E‖≤1, with C depending only on n.

Derivative at an invertible point. Let w(t)=det X(t) and suppose X(t) is invertible. Write X(t+h)=X(t)+hA(t)X(t)+ρ(h) with ‖ρ(h)‖=o(h), because X is differentiable and X′=AX. Then X(t+h)=(I+hA(t)+E(h))X(t) with E(h)=ρ(h)X(t)⁻¹=o(h).

Multiplicativity of the determinant gives w(t+h)=w(t)det(I+hA(t)+E(h)). Step 1 with the matrix hA(t)+E(h), which is small, gives det(I+hA+E)=1+h tr A(t)+tr E(h)+O(h²)=1+h tr A(t)+o(h). So w′(t)=tr A(t)w(t) at every t where X(t) is invertible.

Singular case. Suppose det X(t₁)=0 for some t₁. Pick v≠0 with X(t₁)v=0 and put y(t)=X(t)v. Then y′=A(t)y and y(t₁)=0. On every compact subinterval ‖A(t)‖≤K, so ‖y(t)‖≤K|∫_{t₁}^t‖y‖|. The Grönwall bound with δ=0 and ε=0 gives y≡0. Hence X(t)v=0 for all t, det X(t)=0 for all t, and the formula holds with both sides equal to 0.

Invertible case. If det X(t)≠0 for all t∈J, then step 3 holds at every t. Let a(t)=∫_{t₀}^t tr A(s)ds. This function is C¹ with a′=tr A, since A is continuous. The product w(t)e^{−a(t)} has derivative (w′−a′w)e^{−a}=0.

A function with zero derivative on an interval is constant. So w(t)e^{−a(t)}=w(t₀), that is det X(t)=det X(t₀)exp(∫_{t₀}^t tr A). Together with step 4 this proves the formula for all t,t₀∈J. The dichotomy on the zeros of det X follows because the exponential factor never vanishes.

worked_application.title: Wronskian of y″+(2/t)y′+y=0 on t>0
worked_application.goal: Predict the Wronskian of two solutions from the trace alone, check it, and find the second solution by reduction of order.
hypotheses: Write the equation as x′=A(t)x with x=(y,y′) and A(t)=[[0,1],[−1,−2/t]].
Two solutions y₁=sin t/t and y₂=cos t/t.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The matrix A is continuous on t>0 and X=[[y₁,y₂],[y₁′,y₂′]] satisfies X′=AX. So the formula applies on J=(0,∞).

steps.text: Verify that y₁ and y₂ solve the equation. Direct differentiation gives y₁″+(2/t)y₁′+y₁=0 and the same for y₂. A symbolic check returns 0 for both.
The trace is tr A(t)=−2/t. So ∫₁^t tr A=−2 ln t and the theorem gives W(t)=W(1)·t⁻².
Compute W(1). We have y₁(1)=sin 1, y₂(1)=cos 1, y₁′(1)=cos 1−sin 1 and y₂′(1)=−sin 1−cos 1. So W(1)=sin 1(−sin 1−cos 1)−cos 1(cos 1−sin 1)=−sin²1−cos²1=−1. The formula gives W(t)=−1/t².
Reduction of order. For a second solution y=y₁u, the theorem gives W=y₁²u′, so u′=W/y₁²=−1/sin²t. Then u=cot t and y=y₁cot t=cos t/t. This recovers y₂ without solving a new equation.

worked_application.result: W(t)=−1/t². The two solutions are independent for every t>0, and the second solution follows from the first by one quadrature.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The formula involves only the trace. It says nothing about the individual solutions.
For a non-linear field the determinant of the flow Jacobian obeys a similar equation with the divergence in place of tr A. This is a different statement and is not proved here.
The formula holds for complex matrices. For operator-valued A in infinite dimensions the determinant does not exist in general.

results.name: Real eigenvalues, weighted orthogonality and simplicity for regular Sturm-Liouville problems
results.statement: Let a<b. Let p∈C¹[a,b] with p>0, and let q,w∈C[a,b] be real with w>0. For C² functions y:[a,b]→ℂ put Ly=−(py′)′+qy. Fix real pairs (α₁,α₂)≠(0,0) and (β₁,β₂)≠(0,0) and impose the boundary conditions α₁y(a)+α₂p(a)y′(a)=0 and β₁y(b)+β₂p(b)y′(b)=0. Call λ∈ℂ an eigenvalue if there is a non-zero C² function y that satisfies both conditions and Ly=λwy. Then (i) every eigenvalue is real. (ii) If y and z are eigenfunctions for eigenvalues λ≠μ, then ∫_a^b w y z̄ dx=0. (iii) For each eigenvalue the space of eigenfunctions has dimension 1.
hypotheses: The problem is regular: p>0 and w>0 on the closed interval and p,q,w are continuous. Singular endpoints are excluded.
The boundary conditions are separated and real. Periodic conditions are not covered.
The theorem does not claim that eigenvalues exist. Existence and completeness need a separate spectral argument.

prerequisites.reason: Simplicity uses the uniqueness part of the Picard-Lindelöf theorem for the linear first order system with zero data at a.

definitions.name: Sturm-Liouville operator

definitions.name: weighted inner product
definitions.text: ⟨y,z⟩_w=∫_a^b w y z̄ dx. Eigenfunctions with different eigenvalues are orthogonal for this product.

definitions.name: Lagrange identity
definitions.text: For C² functions u,v, (Lu)v̄−u·conj(Lv)=−d/dx[p(u′v̄−uv̄′)]. It turns the symmetry of L into a boundary term.

/-- The eigenvalues of a self-adjoint operator are real. -/
theorem conj_eigenvalue_eq_self (hT : T.IsSymmetric) {μ : 𝕜} (hμ : HasEigenvalue T μ) :
    conj μ = μ := by
  obtain ⟨v, hv₁, hv₂⟩ := hμ.exists_hasEigenvector
  rw [mem_eigenspace_iff] at hv₁
  simpa [hv₂, inner_smul_left, inner_smul_right, hv₁] using hT v v

/-- The eigenspaces of a self-adjoint operator are mutually orthogonal. -/
theorem orthogonalFamily_eigenspaces (hT : T.IsSymmetric) :
    OrthogonalFamily 𝕜 (fun μ => eigenspace T μ) fun μ => (eigenspace T μ).subtypeₗᵢ := by
  rintro μ ν hμν ⟨v, hv⟩ ⟨w, hw⟩
  by_cases hv' : v = 0
  · simp [hv']
  have H := hT.conj_eigenvalue_eq_self (hasEigenvalue_of_hasEigenvector ⟨hv, hv'⟩)
  rw [mem_eigenspace_iff] at hv hw
  refine Or.resolve_left ?_ hμν.symm
  simpa [inner_smul_left, inner_smul_right, hv, hw, H] using (hT v w).symm

steps.text: Lagrange identity. Since p,q are real, conj(Lv)=Lv̄. Put B(u,v)=p(uv̄′−u′v̄). A direct derivative gives B′=(pv̄′)′u+pv̄′u′−(pu′)′v̄−pu′v̄′=u(pv̄′)′−(pu′)′v̄. This equals (Lu)v̄−u(Lv̄) with the sign convention L=−(p·′)′+q, because the term quv̄ cancels. So ∫_a^b[(Lu)v̄−u·conj(Lv)]dx=B(u,v)(b)−B(u,v)(a).

The boundary terms vanish. Let u,v satisfy the boundary conditions. At a, the vectors (u(a),p(a)u′(a)) and (v̄(a),p(a)v̄′(a)) in ℂ² are both killed by the non-zero real functional (α₁,α₂). So both lie in its one-dimensional kernel and are linearly dependent. The determinant u(a)p(a)v̄′(a)−p(a)u′(a)v̄(a)=B(u,v)(a) is therefore 0. The same argument at b gives B(u,v)(b)=0. Hence ∫(Lu)v̄=∫u·conj(Lv).

Reality (i). Let y be an eigenfunction with eigenvalue λ. Apply step 2 with u=v=y: ∫λw|y|²=∫y·conj(λwy)=λ̄∫w|y|². So (λ−λ̄)∫_a^b w|y|²dx=0. Since y is continuous and not zero, and w>0, the integral is positive. So λ=λ̄ and λ is real.
Orthogonality (ii). Let Ly=λwy and Lz=μwz with λ,μ real and λ≠μ. Step 2 with u=y, v=z gives λ∫wy z̄=∫y·conj(μwz)=μ∫wy z̄ because μ is real. So (λ−μ)∫w y z̄=0 and the integral is 0.

Simplicity (iii). Let y,z be eigenfunctions for the same λ. The vectors (y(a),p(a)y′(a)) and (z(a),p(a)z′(a)) lie in the same one-dimensional kernel as in step 2. So some (c₁,c₂)≠(0,0) gives c₁y(a)+c₂z(a)=0 and c₁p(a)y′(a)+c₂p(a)z′(a)=0. The function u=c₁y+c₂z solves (pu′)′=(q−λw)u, which is the linear first order system (u,pu′)′=(pu′/p,(q−λw)u) with continuous coefficients. Its data at a are zero.

The linear system has the Lipschitz property in (u,pu′), so uniqueness for the initial value problem gives u≡0. Then c₁y+c₂z=0 with (c₁,c₂)≠0, so y and z are linearly dependent. The eigenspace has dimension at most 1, and it has dimension 1 because it contains y≠0.

worked_application.title: A Robin problem on [0,1]: y″=−λy, y′(0)=0, y(1)+y′(1)=0
worked_application.goal: Find the first four eigenpairs, and check orthogonality and the reality of the eigenvalues.
hypotheses: p=1, q=0, w=1, a=0, b=1. The condition at 0 is (α₁,α₂)=(0,1). The condition at 1 is (β₁,β₂)=(1,1).
Candidate eigenfunctions y=cos(μx), μ>0, λ=μ².
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The problem is regular. All hypotheses of the theorem hold.

steps.text: Boundary conditions. y′(0)=−μ sin 0=0 holds. The second condition y(1)+y′(1)=cos μ−μ sin μ=0 means μ tan μ=1 (cos μ≠0 because cos μ=μ sin μ would give sin μ=0 and cos μ=0 together).

Solve μ tan μ=1 numerically. The first four positive roots are μ₁=0.860334, μ₂=3.425618, μ₃=6.437298 and μ₄=9.529334. The eigenvalues are λ=μ²: 0.740174, 11.734862, 41.438808 and 90.808214. A residual check gives μ_k tan μ_k=1.000000 in each case.

Orthogonality (ii). The exact integral is ∫₀¹cos(μ_jx)cos(μ_kx)dx=½[sin(μ_j−μ_k)/(μ_j−μ_k)+sin(μ_j+μ_k)/(μ_j+μ_k)]. For all six pairs (j,k), a 30-digit evaluation returns a value of size below 10⁻³¹. The values are zero to working precision.

The mechanism is the Lagrange identity. For u=cos(μ_jx) and v=cos(μ_kx), (μ_k²−μ_j²)∫uv=μ_k cos μ_j sin μ_k−μ_j sin μ_j cos μ_k. Insert cos μ=μ sin μ for both: the right side is μ_kμ_j sin μ_j sin μ_k−μ_jμ_k sin μ_j sin μ_k=0. At x=0 the boundary term vanishes because sin 0=0.
Norms. ∫₀¹cos²(μx)dx=½(1+sin(2μ)/(2μ)) is 0.787328, 0.539262, 0.511782 and 0.505446 for k=1,…,4. The normalised functions cos(μ_kx)/√norm form an orthonormal family in L²(0,1).
Simplicity (iii). The eigenfunction through a given λ is fixed by y(0) and y′(0)=0, so it is c·cos(μx). The space has dimension 1.

worked_application.result: The eigenvalues 0.7402, 11.7349, 41.4388 and 90.8082 are real and simple, and the eigenfunctions cos(μ_kx) are orthogonal in L²(0,1).

The theorem does not show that the eigenfunctions span L²_w. That needs compactness of the inverse operator.
Simplicity holds for separated conditions. For periodic conditions each eigenvalue can have dimension 2.

results.name: Dirichlet kernel proof of pointwise Fourier convergence at jumps
results.statement: Let f:ℝ→ℂ be 2π-periodic and integrable on [−π,π]. Put c_n=(1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π}f(y)e^{−iny}dy and S_Nf(x)=∑_{|n|≤N}c_ne^{inx}. Let x₀∈ℝ. Assume that the one-sided limits f(x₀+) and f(x₀−) exist, and that there are C,δ>0 with |f(x₀+s)−f(x₀+)|≤Cs and |f(x₀−s)−f(x₀−)|≤Cs for 0<s<δ. Then S_Nf(x₀)→½(f(x₀+)+f(x₀−)) as N→∞.
hypotheses: The one-sided Lipschitz bound holds for every piecewise C¹ function. It also holds for any function with one-sided Hölder bound if the exponent is positive. Only the integrability of g(s)/s near 0 is used.
The value f(x₀) itself does not enter. At a jump the series converges to the midpoint.
The theorem is pointwise. It gives no rate and no uniform convergence.

/-- If the sequence of Fourier coefficients of `f` is summable, then the Fourier series of `f`
converges everywhere pointwise to `f`. -/
theorem has_pointwise_sum_fourier_series_of_summable (h : Summable (fourierCoeff f))
    (x : AddCircle T) : HasSum (fun i => fourierCoeff f i • fourier i x) (f x) := by
  convert! (ContinuousMap.evalCLM ℂ x).hasSum (hasSum_fourier_series_of_summable h)

steps.text: Convolution form. Insert the definition of c_n and exchange the finite sum with the integral: S_Nf(x)=(1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π}f(y)∑_{|n|≤N}e^{in(x−y)}dy. Substitute y=x−s and use the periodicity of f and of D_N to get S_Nf(x)=(1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π}f(x−s)D_N(s)ds.

Closed form of the kernel. For s∉2πℤ, D_N(s)=e^{−iNs}(e^{i(2N+1)s}−1)/(e^{is}−1), by the geometric sum. Multiply the numerator and denominator by e^{−is/2}: the numerator becomes e^{i(N+½)s}−e^{−i(N+½)s}=2i sin((N+½)s) and the denominator 2i sin(s/2). So D_N(s)=sin((N+½)s)/sin(s/2).
Mass of the kernel. For n≠0, ∫_{−π}^{π}e^{ins}ds=0, so (1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π}D_N=1. The kernel is even, because D_N(−s)=D_N(s). So (1/2π)∫_0^πD_N(s)ds=½.

Fold the integral. Split ∫_{−π}^{π} at 0 and substitute s→−s on [−π,0]. Since D_N is even, S_Nf(x₀)=(1/2π)∫_0^π[f(x₀−s)+f(x₀+s)]D_N(s)ds. By step 3, m=½(f(x₀+)+f(x₀−)) equals (1/2π)∫_0^π[f(x₀+)+f(x₀−)]D_N(s)ds.
Subtract. Put g(s)=f(x₀−s)+f(x₀+s)−f(x₀−)−f(x₀+). Then S_Nf(x₀)−m=(1/2π)∫_0^π h(s)sin((N+½)s)ds, with h(s)=g(s)/sin(s/2).

The function h is integrable on (0,π). Near 0, |g(s)|≤2Cs for s<δ. By concavity, sin(u)≥2u/π on [0,π/2], so sin(s/2)≥s/π on (0,π]. Hence |h(s)|≤2πC on (0,δ). On [δ,π] we have sin(s/2)≥sin(δ/2)>0 and g is integrable because f is. So h∈L¹(0,π).

Riemann-Lebesgue. Extend h by 0 outside (0,π) so that h∈L¹(ℝ). Write sin((N+½)s)=(e^{i(N+½)s}−e^{−i(N+½)s})/(2i). The Riemann-Lebesgue lemma gives ∫h(s)e^{±i(N+½)s}ds→0 as N→∞, since the frequencies tend to infinity. So S_Nf(x₀)−m→0.

worked_application.title: Sawtooth f(x)=x on (−π,π)
worked_application.goal: Compute the partial sums at x₀=π/2 and x₀=π, and recover the Leibniz series.
hypotheses: f(x)=x on (−π,π), extended 2π-periodically.
Fourier coefficients c_n=i(−1)ⁿ/n for n≠0 and c₀=0. The real form is S_Nf(x)=∑_{n=1}^N 2(−1)^{n+1}sin(nx)/n.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The function is C¹ off the points π+2πk. At these points the one-sided limits exist and the one-sided Lipschitz bound holds with C=1.

steps.text: Check the coefficients. For n=1,2,3 the integral (1/π)∫_{−π}^{π}x sin(nx)dx equals 2, −1 and 2/3. The formula 2(−1)^{n+1}/n gives the same.

At x₀=π/2, f is continuous with value π/2. At this point sin(nπ/2) is 0 for even n and (−1)^{(n−1)/2} for odd n. So S_Nf(π/2)=2∑_{n odd≤N}(−1)^{(n−1)/2}/n, which is twice a partial sum of the Leibniz series.
The theorem gives S_Nf(π/2)→π/2, so 1−1/3+1/5−…=π/4. Numerically S₁₀=1.669841, S₁₀₀=1.560797 and S₁₀₀₀=1.569796. The error π/2−S_N is 0.009999 for N=100 and 0.000999999 for N=1000.
At x₀=π, f(π−)=π and f(π+)=−π. The midpoint is 0. Every term sin(nπ) is 0, so S_Nf(π)=0 for every N. The partial sums converge to the midpoint 0, not to the value π of the generating formula.
Check the kernel formula for N=5 and s=0.7: 1+2∑_{n≤5}cos(0.7n)=−1.897432 and sin(5.5·0.7)/sin(0.35)=−1.897432. They agree.

limitations: The theorem needs a local one-sided regularity condition. For a merely continuous function the Fourier series can diverge at a point (du Bois-Reymond), so some condition is needed.
The convergence is not uniform near a jump. The Gibbs overshoot stays at about 9 percent of the jump size.
There is no rate in the statement. The observed rate 1/N in the application depends on the smoothness of f at x₀.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Coefficients of the derivative. Fix n≠0. The functions f and f′ are continuous on [0,2π], and f has derivative f′. Integration by parts, as in the Fourier-coefficient formula for derivatives, gives c_n(f)=(1/(−2πin))(e^{0}·(f(2π)−f(0))−2πc_n(f′)). Periodicity gives f(2π)=f(0), so c_n(f)=c_n(f′)/(in), that is c_n(f′)=in·c_n(f).
Mean zero. The coefficient c₀(f)=(1/2π)∫f=0 by hypothesis. So the series of squares for f runs over n≠0 only.

Parseval for f and for f′. Both functions are continuous, so they are square integrable on [0,2π]. Parseval gives (1/2π)∫f²=∑_{n≠0}|c_n|² and (1/2π)∫f′²=∑_n|c_n(f′)|²=∑_{n≠0}n²|c_n|², using step 1 and c₀(f′)=0.
The inequality. For n≠0 we have n²≥1. So ∑_{n≠0}n²|c_n|²≥∑_{n≠0}|c_n|². By step 3 this is ∫f′²≥∫f².

Equality implies a trigonometric form. By step 3, ∫f′²−∫f²=2π∑_{n≠0}(n²−1)|c_n|². All terms are non-negative. The sum is 0 only if c_n=0 for all |n|≥2, because n²−1≥3 for |n|≥2. So the only possible non-zero coefficients are c₁ and c₋₁=c̄₁ (f is real).

Identification of f. Put g(x)=c₁e^{ix}+c₋₁e^{−ix}=a cos x+b sin x with a=2Re c₁ and b=−2Im c₁. Then f−g is continuous and 2π-periodic, and all its Fourier coefficients vanish. By Parseval, ∫|f−g|²=2π∑|c_n(f−g)|²=0. A continuous function with zero integral of |f−g|² is 0. So f=g.
Converse. For f=a cos x+b sin x we have f′=−a sin x+b cos x. Then ∫₀^{2π}f′²=π(a²+b²)=∫₀^{2π}f². So equality holds.

The identity cos³x=(3cos x+cos 3x)/4.

steps.text: Fourier coefficients. From cos x=(e^{ix}+e^{−ix})/2 we get c_{±1}=3/8 and c_{±3}=1/8. All other coefficients are 0.
Numerical quadrature of 9cos⁴x sin²x and cos⁶x over [0,2π] gives 3.534292 and 1.963495. The ratio is 1.8, as 9/16 divided by 5/16.
The gap 9π/8−5π/8=π/2 equals 2π∑(n²−1)|c_n|²=2π·2·8·(1/64)=π/2. This confirms the identity in step 5. The gap comes only from the frequency 3.

The inequality is for real or complex f with mean 0 on the circle. For Dirichlet conditions f(0)=f(π)=0 the sharp constant is 1 on (0,π) and uses a sine series.

results.name: Beltrami identity for autonomous Lagrangians, with the catenoid
results.statement: Let F:ℝ×ℝ→ℝ, (u,p)↦F(u,p), be C². Let y:[a,b]→ℝ be C² and satisfy the Euler-Lagrange equation d/dx[F_p(y,y′)]=F_u(y,y′) on [a,b]. Then H(x)=F(y,y′)−y′F_p(y,y′) is constant on [a,b]. For F(u,p)=u√(1+p²) with y>0, the constant is c=y/√(1+y′²)>0. On any interval where y′≠0 this gives y″=y/c² and y(x)=c cosh(x/c+α) for some α∈ℝ.
hypotheses: The Lagrangian F does not depend on x explicitly. With an explicit x-dependence, H is not constant.
The extremal y is C² and satisfies the Euler-Lagrange equation. The theorem does not find extremals that are not C².
For the catenoid, y>0 on the interval and y′≠0 on the interval for the last claim.

definitions.name: Euler-Lagrange equation
definitions.text: For a Lagrangian F(y,y′), a smooth extremal of ∫F(y,y′)dx satisfies d/dx F_p(y,y′)=F_u(y,y′), where F_u and F_p are the partial derivatives of F in the first and second argument.

definitions.name: Beltrami identity
definitions.text: The first integral H=F−y′F_p of an autonomous Lagrangian. It replaces the second order Euler-Lagrange equation by a first order equation.

definitions.name: catenoid
definitions.text: The surface of revolution of the curve y=c cosh(x/c+α) about the x axis. Its area functional is 2π∫y√(1+y′²)dx.

source.alignment: The source gives the product rule for derivatives. It is the rule used in step 2 for the term y′F_p(y,y′).

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: The derivative of F along the curve. Since F is C² and y is C², the function x↦F(y(x),y′(x)) is C¹. The chain rule gives d/dx F(y,y′)=F_u(y,y′)y′+F_p(y,y′)y″.
The derivative of the second term. The function y′ is C¹ and F_p is C¹, so x↦F_p(y,y′) is C¹. The product rule gives d/dx[y′F_p(y,y′)]=y″F_p(y,y′)+y′·d/dx[F_p(y,y′)].
Subtract. H′=F_uy′+F_py″−y″F_p−y′ d/dx[F_p]=y′(F_u−d/dx[F_p]). The Euler-Lagrange equation says that the bracket is 0. So H′=0 on [a,b] and H is constant, because [a,b] is an interval.
The catenoid Lagrangian. For F(u,p)=u√(1+p²), F_p=up/√(1+p²). Then F−pF_p=u√(1+p²)−up²/√(1+p²)=u/√(1+p²). By steps 1 to 3, y/√(1+y′²)=c for a constant c. Since y>0, c>0.
The second order equation. Square the identity: y²=c²(1+y′²). Differentiate: 2yy′=2c²y′y″. On an interval where y′≠0, divide by 2y′ and obtain y=c²y″. So y″=y/c².

Solve. The ODE y″=y/c² is linear with constant coefficients. Its solutions are y=A cosh(x/c)+B sinh(x/c). Insert this into y²−c²y′²=c² and use cosh²−sinh²=1: the left side equals A²−B². So A²−B²=c²>0, hence |B|<|A|.

Sign of A. If A<0, then y=A cosh(x/c)+B sinh(x/c)≤A cosh(x/c)+|B| cosh(x/c)=(A+|B|)cosh(x/c)<0, which contradicts y>0. So A>0. Put α=artanh(B/A). Then A=c cosh α and B=c sinh α because A²−B²=c² and A>0. The addition formula gives y=c cosh(x/c+α).

worked_application.title: A soap film between two unit rings at distance 1
worked_application.goal: Find the surface of revolution with least area for y(0)=y(1)=1, and compare it with two flat discs.
hypotheses: F(u,p)=u√(1+p²). The boundary data are y(0)=y(1)=1.
By symmetry, the axis of the extremal is x=½. The ansatz is y=c cosh((x−½)/c), that is α=−1/(2c).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The Lagrangian does not depend on x. The curve y=c cosh((x−½)/c) is C², positive, and satisfies y/√(1+y′²)=c.

steps.text: Boundary condition. y(0)=y(1)=c cosh(1/(2c)). The condition y(0)=1 gives c cosh(1/(2c))=1.
The function g(c)=c cosh(1/(2c)) has two roots for g(c)=1. Numerically c₁=0.235095 and c₂=0.848338. The residuals are below 10⁻¹⁵.

Euler-Lagrange check at c₂. With u=(x−½)/c, y′=sinh u and √(1+y′²)=cosh u. Then F_u=cosh u. And F_p=y y′/√(1+y′²)=c cosh u sinh u/cosh u=c sinh u, so d/dx F_p=cosh u. The two sides agree. Also y/√(1+y′²)=c cosh u/cosh u=c.
Area. A(c)=2π∫₀¹y√(1+y′²)dx=(2π/c)∫₀¹y²dx=πc(1+c sinh(1/c)). So A(c₁)=6.845655 and A(c₂)=5.991797. A midpoint-rule sum with 200000 cells gives the same values to 6 digits.
Comparison. Two flat unit discs have total area 2π=6.283185. The catenoid with c₂ has the smaller area 5.991797. The catenoid with c₁ has the larger area 6.845655, so it is not a minimum.

worked_application.result: The first integral gives the family y=c cosh((x−½)/c). For rings at distance 1, there are two catenoids, with areas 5.991797 and 6.845655.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The identity is a first integral. It does not give existence of a minimiser, and it also holds for saddle points and maxima.
Beltrami loses information where y′=0. The step that divides by y′ needs y′≠0 on the interval.
For rings farther apart than about 1.3255 times their radius, the equation c cosh(L/(2c))=R has no real root. Then the extremal does not exist in this family.

results.name: Stability function and absolute stability region of one-step methods
results.statement: Apply a one-step method with step h to y′=λy, λ∈ℂ. Suppose that it gives y_{n+1}=R(z)y_n with z=hλ. (i) Then y_n=R(z)ⁿy₀. If |R(z)|<1, then y_n→0 for every y₀. If |R(z)|>1, then |y_n|→∞ for every y₀≠0. (ii) For explicit Euler, R(z)=1+z and {|R|<1} is the open disc |z+1|<1. For backward Euler, R=1/(1−z) and the set contains the left half plane Re z<0. For the trapezoidal rule, R=(1+z/2)/(1−z/2) and {|R|<1} equals {Re z<0} exactly. (iii) For an explicit s-stage Runge-Kutta method with ∑bᵢ=1, R is a non-constant polynomial. Then the set {|R|<1} does not contain the whole half plane Re z<0.
hypotheses: The analysis uses the linear test equation y′=λy. It describes the behavior of the method only for linear problems or for a linearisation.
The stage equations of the implicit methods must have a unique solution. For backward Euler and the trapezoidal rule this holds for z≠1 and z≠2.
The set {|R|<1} is the region of absolute stability. The set {|R|≤1} is not studied here.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only algebra of the stability function and the growth of a polynomial. It needs no earlier catalog result.

definitions.name: stability function
definitions.text: The function R(z) with y_{n+1}=R(hλ)y_n for the test equation y′=λy. For explicit methods it is a polynomial, and for implicit methods it is a rational function.

definitions.name: region of absolute stability
definitions.text: The set of z=hλ in ℂ with |R(z)|<1. For z in this set the numerical solution decays, as the exact solution does for Re λ<0.

definitions.name: A-stability
definitions.text: A method is A-stable if its region of absolute stability contains the left half plane {Re z<0}.

source.alignment: The source proves that |P(x)| tends to infinity as x tends to −∞ for a real polynomial of positive degree. It is the growth fact in step 6.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Powers. By the definition of R, y_{n+1}=R(z)y_n for each n with the same z=hλ. By induction y_n=R(z)ⁿy₀. If |R(z)|<1, then |y_n|=|R|ⁿ|y₀|→0. If |R(z)|>1 and y₀≠0, then |y_n|→∞. This proves part (i).
Explicit Euler. The method is y_{n+1}=y_n+hλy_n=(1+z)y_n, so R(z)=1+z. Then |R(z)|<1 is |z−(−1)|<1, the open disc of radius 1 about −1.
Backward Euler. The method y_{n+1}=y_n+hλy_{n+1} gives y_{n+1}=y_n/(1−z) for z≠1. Let z=x+iy with x<0. Then |1−z|²=(1−x)²+y²≥(1−x)²>1. So |R(z)|<1 on the left half plane.

Trapezoidal rule. The method y_{n+1}=y_n+(h/2)λ(y_n+y_{n+1}) gives R(z)=(1+z/2)/(1−z/2). With z=x+iy, |1+z/2|²−|1−z/2|²=(1+x/2)²−(1−x/2)²=2x. So |R(z)|<1 if and only if x<0. This is the exact left half plane.

Explicit Runge-Kutta methods. For the test equation, the stages are Yᵢ=y_n+z∑_{j<i}aᵢⱼYⱼ. By induction on i, each Yᵢ equals Pᵢ(z)y_n with Pᵢ a polynomial and Pᵢ(0)=1. Then y_{n+1}=y_n+z∑bᵢYᵢ=R(z)y_n with R(z)=1+z∑bᵢPᵢ(z). So R is a polynomial and R′(0)=∑bᵢ=1. Hence R is not constant.

No A-stability for polynomials. Let R be a polynomial of degree d at least 1. Put q(t)=|R(−t)|² for real t. This is a real polynomial of degree 2d with positive leading coefficient |a_d|². So q(t)→∞ as t→∞, which is the growth fact in the source for real polynomials. Hence q(t₀)>1 for some t₀>0. The point z=−t₀ has Re z<0 and is outside the region. This proves part (iii).

worked_application.title: The stiff test problem y′=−50y with step 0.05
worked_application.goal: Compare explicit Euler, backward Euler and the trapezoidal rule after 20 steps.
hypotheses: λ=−50, y₀=1, h=0.05, so z=−2.5. The final time is 1. The exact value is y(1)=e⁻⁵⁰=1.928750×10⁻²².
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: All three methods give y_{n+1}=R(z)y_n for the linear test equation. So y₂₀=R(z)²⁰y₀ by part (i).

steps.text: Explicit Euler. R_E(−2.5)=−1.5. Since |R_E|>1, the iterates grow. y₂₀=(−1.5)²⁰=3325.256730. The step is outside the disc |z+1|<1.
The stability limit for Euler. The condition |1+hλ|<1 for λ=−50 means 0<h<2/50=0.04. The step 0.05 is larger than 0.04.
Backward Euler. R_B(−2.5)=1/3.5=0.285714. Then y₂₀=(1/3.5)²⁰=1.314132×10⁻¹¹. The iterates decay for any h>0.
Trapezoidal rule. R_T(−2.5)=(1−1.25)/(1+1.25)=−0.111111. Then y₂₀=(−0.111111)²⁰=8.225263×10⁻²⁰. The iterates decay with alternating sign. The exact one-step factor is e^{−2.5}=0.082085.
Summary. The Euler method gives a value of size 3325 where the exact solution is of size 10⁻²². The two A-stable methods give a small positive value.

limitations: The analysis covers the linear test problem only. A-stability does not guarantee good behavior for nonlinear stiff problems.
The trapezoidal rule has |R(z)|→1 as z→−∞. It damps very stiff components only weakly, which is why L-stability is a stronger notion.
The region {|R|<1} does not give accuracy. It only shows that the numerical solution does not blow up.

results.name: Absolute and uniform Fourier convergence from a square integrable derivative
results.statement: Let f:ℝ→ℂ be continuous and 2π-periodic. Let there be 0=x₀<x₁<…<x_m=2π such that f is C¹ on each [x_{k−1},x_k]. Put σ²=(1/2π)∫₀^{2π}|f′|²dx and c_n=(1/2π)∫₀^{2π}f(x)e^{−inx}dx. Then ∑_{n≠0}|c_n|≤(π/√3)σ. The series ∑c_ne^{inx} converges absolutely and uniformly to f, and sup_x|f(x)−∑_{|n|≤N}c_ne^{inx}|≤σ√(2/N) for N≥1.
hypotheses: The function f is continuous and periodic. A jump destroys the result, because then c_n is of size 1/n.
The derivative is only piecewise defined. The values of f′ at the finitely many break points do not matter.
The bound uses σ, the normalised L² norm of f′. The constant π/√3 comes from ∑_{n≠0}1/n²=π²/3.

prerequisites.reason: Steps 2 and 5 use the Parseval identity for the piecewise continuous function f′ and for the continuous function f−g.
Step 3 uses the value ζ(2)=π²/6 to get the constant π/√3.

steps.text: Coefficients of the derivative. Fix n≠0. On each piece, integration by parts gives ∫_{x_{k−1}}^{x_k}f′(x)e^{−inx}dx=[f(x)e^{−inx}]_{x_{k−1}}^{x_k}+in∫_{x_{k−1}}^{x_k}f(x)e^{−inx}dx. Sum over k. The boundary terms telescope because f is continuous. The remaining terms f(2π)e^{−2πin}−f(0) cancel because f is periodic. So c_n(f′)=in c_n.
Parseval for f′. The function f′ is piecewise continuous and bounded, so it is square integrable. Parseval gives ∑_{n∈ℤ}|c_n(f′)|²=(1/2π)∫|f′|²=σ². By step 1, c_n(f′)=in c_n, so ∑n²|c_n|²=σ².

Cauchy-Schwarz. For M≥1, ∑_{0<|n|≤M}|c_n|=∑(1/|n|)(|n||c_n|)≤(∑_{0<|n|≤M}n⁻²)^{1/2}(∑n²|c_n|²)^{1/2}. The first factor is at most (2ζ(2))^{1/2}=(π²/3)^{1/2}, because ζ(2)=π²/6. The second is at most σ by step 2. Let M→∞ to get ∑_{n≠0}|c_n|≤(π/√3)σ.
Uniform convergence. The terms c_ne^{inx} have modulus |c_n|, and ∑|c_n| is finite by step 3. The Weierstrass M-test shows that the partial sums S_N converge uniformly to a continuous function g.

Identification g=f. Uniform convergence allows termwise integration, so c_n(g)=c_n(f) for all n. The function f−g is continuous with all Fourier coefficients 0. Parseval gives (1/2π)∫|f−g|²=∑|c_n(f−g)|²=0. A continuous function with zero integral of |f−g|² is 0, so f=g.
The tail bound. For N≥1 and every x, |f(x)−S_Nf(x)|≤∑_{|n|>N}|c_n|. As in step 3, this is at most (2∑_{n>N}n⁻²)^{1/2}σ. Since ∑_{n>N}n⁻²<∑_{n>N}1/(n(n−1))=1/N, the bound is σ√(2/N).

worked_application.title: The function f(x)=|x| on [−π,π]
worked_application.goal: Verify the bound on ∑|c_n|, the value f(π), and the tail estimate for N=10.
hypotheses: f(x)=|x| for x in [−π,π], extended 2π-periodically. It is continuous, with break points at 0 and ±π.
f′=±1 off the break points, so σ²=(1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π}1dx=1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The function is continuous, periodic and C¹ on [−π,0] and [0,π]. All hypotheses hold with σ=1.

steps.text: Coefficients. c₀=π/2. For n≠0, c_n=(1/π)∫₀^π x cos(nx)dx=((−1)ⁿ−1)/(πn²). So c_n=−2/(πn²) for odd n and c_n=0 for even n≠0.
Sum of moduli. ∑_{n≠0}|c_n|=2∑_{n odd, n>0}2/(πn²)=(4/π)(π²/8)=π/2=1.570796. A sum of 100000 odd terms gives 1.570793.
The bound of the theorem is (π/√3)σ=1.813799. The value 1.570796 is below it.
Value at π. The series at x=π is c₀+∑c_n(−1)ⁿ=π/2+π/2=π. This equals f(π)=π, as the theorem states.
Tail for N=10. S₁₀(π)=π/2+∑_{n odd≤9}(4/(πn²))=3.078140. The error at x=π is π−3.078140=0.063453. The bound σ√(2/N)=0.447214 holds.

worked_application.result: The series for |x| converges absolutely with ∑|c_n|=π/2, below the bound 1.8138. At N=10 the error 0.0635 at x=π is below the bound 0.4472.

limitations: A discontinuous f is excluded. For a function with a jump, c_n is of size 1/n, and the series ∑|c_n| diverges.
The rate σ√(2/N) is not sharp for smoother f. If f has two derivatives in L², the error is of order N^{−3/2}.
The theorem needs a derivative in L². A merely continuous function can have a Fourier series that is not absolutely convergent.

results.name: Existence and uniqueness for a nonlinear boundary value problem by Green function and contraction
results.statement: Let f:[0,1]×ℝ→ℝ be continuous and let |f(x,u)−f(x,v)|≤L|u−v| for all x,u,v with a constant L<8. Then the problem y″=f(x,y), y(0)=y(1)=0 has exactly one solution y∈C²[0,1]. Let y₀ be any continuous function and y_{k+1}=Ty_k, where (Ty)(x)=−∫₀¹G(x,t)f(t,y(t))dt, and G(x,t)=x(1−t) for x≤t and G(x,t)=t(1−x) for x≥t. Then ‖y_k−y‖_∞≤(L/8)^k(1−L/8)⁻¹‖y₁−y₀‖_∞.
hypotheses: The Lipschitz constant L is global in the second variable. A local Lipschitz condition gives only local existence.
The bound L<8 is a bound for the interval [0,1] and Dirichlet conditions. It is 8 because max_x∫|G(x,t)|dt=1/8.
The condition L<8 is sufficient, not necessary. For example, f(x,u)=−π²u has L=π². Then y=sin(πx) and y=0 both solve the problem.

steps.text: The solution formula for the linear problem. For continuous g put u(x)=−(1−x)∫₀^x t g(t)dt−x∫_x^1(1−t)g(t)dt. Differentiate: u′(x)=∫₀^x t g(t)dt−∫_x^1(1−t)g(t)dt, because the terms with g(x) cancel. Differentiate again: u″(x)=xg(x)+(1−x)g(x)=g(x). Also u(0)=0 and u(1)=0 from the formula. So u∈C² solves u″=g with u(0)=u(1)=0.
Uniqueness for the linear problem. If u₁ and u₂ both solve it, then w=u₁−u₂ has w″=0 and w(0)=w(1)=0. So w is affine with two zeros, and w=0. Hence u is the only solution, and u=−∫G g.

Equivalence. By steps 1 and 2, y∈C² solves the BVP if and only if y is continuous and y=Ty. Indeed, if y solves the BVP, then g=f(·,y) is continuous and y=−∫G g=Ty. If y=Ty with y continuous, then y∈C² by step 1 and y″=f(·,y).
The kernel integral. For x in [0,1], ∫₀¹|G(x,t)|dt=∫₀^x t(1−x)dt+∫_x^1 x(1−t)dt=(1−x)x²/2+x(1−x)²/2=x(1−x)/2≤1/8.

Contraction. T maps C[0,1] into itself, because the integral of a continuous function against the continuous kernel is continuous. For y,z in C[0,1], |(Ty−Tz)(x)|≤∫|G(x,t)|L|y(t)−z(t)|dt≤L‖y−z‖_∞x(1−x)/2≤(L/8)‖y−z‖_∞. So ‖Ty−Tz‖_∞≤q‖y−z‖_∞ with q=L/8<1.

Apply the Banach fixed-point theorem. The space (C[0,1],‖·‖_∞) is complete, and T is a contraction. So T has exactly one fixed point y, and y_k→y for every y₀. By step 3, y is the unique C² solution of the BVP. The a priori bound ‖y_k−y‖≤q^k(1−q)⁻¹‖y₁−y₀‖ is the standard estimate of the fixed-point theorem.

steps.text: First iterate. y₁(x)=−∫G(x,t)t dt=−x(1−x²)/6. Its sup norm is at x=1/√3 and equals 1/(9√3)=0.064150. So ‖y₁−y₀‖=0.064150 and y₁(½)=−0.062500.
Iteration with 2000 trapezoid cells for the kernel integral. y₂(½)=−0.059247, y₃(½)=−0.059412, y₄(½)=−0.059403, y₅(½)=−0.0594037 and y₆(½)=−0.05940371.
The sup norms of successive differences are 0.064150, 0.003259, 0.000165, 8.36×10⁻⁶, 4.2×10⁻⁷ and 2.1×10⁻⁸. Each ratio is about 0.051, which is below q=0.0625.

results.name: Möbius function of a locally finite poset: two-sided inversion and the product rule
results.statement: Let (P,≤) be a poset in which every closed interval [a,b] = {x : a ≤ x ≤ b} is finite. Define μ(a,b) = 0 if a ≰ b, μ(a,a) = 1, and μ(a,b) = −∑_{a≤x<b} μ(a,x) if a < b. Then: (1) ∑_{a≤x≤b} μ(a,x) = δ_{ab} and ∑_{a≤x≤b} μ(x,b) = δ_{ab}. (2) If every set {a : a ≤ b} is finite, and g(b) = ∑_{a≤b} f(a) for all b, then f(b) = ∑_{a≤b} μ(a,b)·g(a). (3) If every set {b : b ≥ a} is finite, and g(a) = ∑_{b≥a} f(b) for all a, then f(a) = ∑_{b≥a} μ(a,b)·g(b). (4) For the product order on P×Q, μ((a,c),(b,d)) = μ_P(a,b)·μ_Q(c,d). (5) On the Boolean lattice of subsets, μ(A,B) = (−1)^{|B∖A|} for A ⊆ B. On the divisor lattice of ℕ, μ(d,m) equals the number-theoretic Möbius function of m/d.
hypotheses: P is a partial order. Every interval [a,b] is finite, so P is locally finite.
The functions f and g take values in an abelian group, and μ takes values in ℤ.
For (2), each principal down-set is finite. For (3), each principal up-set is finite. For a finite poset, both hold.

definitions.name: incidence algebra
definitions.text: The set of functions h(a,b), defined for a ≤ b, with convolution (h*k)(a,b) = ∑_{a≤x≤b} h(a,x)·k(x,b). The unit is δ(a,b) = 1 if a = b and 0 otherwise.

definitions.name: zeta function
definitions.text: The element ζ of the incidence algebra with ζ(a,b) = 1 for all a ≤ b. Then (ζ*ζ)(a,b) = |[a,b]|.

definitions.name: Möbius function
definitions.text: The function μ defined by the recursion in the statement. By step 1 and step 2 it is the two-sided inverse of ζ in the incidence algebra.

definitions.name: product order
definitions.text: On P×Q, (a,c) ≤ (b,d) means a ≤ b and c ≤ d. Then [(a,c),(b,d)] = [a,b]×[c,d].

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Definition by recursion. For a < b every x with a ≤ x < b has [a,x] a proper subset of [a,b], so the interval [a,x] is smaller. Thus μ(a,b) is well defined by induction on |[a,b]|. For a = b the sum ∑_{a≤x≤b} μ(a,x) is μ(a,a) = 1. For a < b the recursion says ∑_{a≤x<b} μ(a,x) + μ(a,b) = 0. This proves the first identity in (1). In symbols, μ*ζ = δ.

Convolution is associative. Both (h*k)*l and h*(k*l) at (a,b) equal the sum of h(a,x)·k(x,y)·l(y,b) over all pairs x,y with a ≤ x ≤ y ≤ b. Also δ is a two-sided unit. These are finite sums, so the reindexing is valid.

Define μ′ by the dual recursion on the upper end: μ′(b,b) = 1 and μ′(a,b) = −∑_{a<x≤b} μ′(x,b) for a < b. The same induction shows that this is well defined. It gives ζ*μ′ = δ. Now μ = μ*δ = μ*(ζ*μ′) = (μ*ζ)*μ′ = δ*μ′ = μ′. Hence ∑_{a≤x≤b} μ(x,b) = δ_{ab}. This proves the second identity in (1).

Inversion from below, statement (2). Substitute g(a) = ∑_{c≤a} f(c) into ∑_{a≤b} μ(a,b)·g(a). The set of pairs (c,a) with c ≤ a ≤ b is finite, because {c : c ≤ b} is finite. Swap the sums to get ∑_{c≤b} f(c)·∑_{c≤a≤b} μ(a,b). By the second identity in (1), the inner sum is δ_{cb}. The whole sum is f(b).

Inversion from above, statement (3). Substitute g(b) = ∑_{c≥b} f(c) into ∑_{b≥a} μ(a,b)·g(b). Swap the finite sums to get ∑_{c≥a} f(c)·∑_{a≤b≤c} μ(a,b). By the first identity in (1), the inner sum is δ_{ac}. The whole sum is f(a).

Uniqueness of the recursion. Suppose a function h on pairs a ≤ b satisfies ∑_{a≤x≤b} h(a,x) = δ_{ab} for all a ≤ b. The case a = b gives h(a,a) = 1. The case a < b gives h(a,b) = −∑_{a≤x<b} h(a,x). By induction on |[a,b]|, h is equal to μ. So any such h is μ.

Product rule, statement (4). Put ν((a,c),(b,d)) = μ_P(a,b)·μ_Q(c,d). Since [(a,c),(b,d)] = [a,b]×[c,d], the sum of ν((a,c),(x,y)) over the interval factors as (∑_{a≤x≤b} μ_P(a,x))·(∑_{c≤y≤d} μ_Q(c,y)) = δ_{ab}·δ_{cd}. This is the unit of the product poset. By the uniqueness in step 6, ν = μ_{P×Q}.

Boolean lattice, statement (5). The chain 0 < 1 has μ(0,0) = μ(1,1) = 1 and μ(0,1) = −1. The subsets of an n-set form the product of n such chains, and the interval [A,B] is isomorphic to the product of |B∖A| copies of the chain. By step 7, μ(A,B) = (−1)^{|B∖A|}.

Divisor lattice, statement (5). The interval [d,m] of divisors is isomorphic to the product, over primes p, of the chains 0 < 1 < … < e_p with e_p = v_p(m/d). On a chain of length e, the recursion gives μ(i,i) = 1, μ(i,i+1) = −1 and μ(i,j) = −(1 − 1 + 0 + … + 0) = 0 for j ≥ i+2, by induction on j−i. By step 7, μ(d,m) is the product of these values. It is (−1)^k if m/d is a product of k distinct primes, and 0 otherwise. This is the number-theoretic Möbius function of m/d.

worked_application.title: Surjection count, divisor lattice of 360 and a poset that is not a product
worked_application.goal: Use the Möbius function of the Boolean lattice, of a divisor lattice and of a five-element poset to invert sums.
hypotheses: Part 1: f(S) counts the words of length 4 over {1,2,3} that use exactly the letters in S. Part 2: P is the lattice of divisors of 360 = 2³·3²·5.
Part 3: N is the poset with elements 0,a,b,c,1 and relations 0 < a < c < 1 and 0 < b < 1.
All posets are finite, so every hypothesis of the statement holds.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each part is an instance of the statement. Part 1 uses the Boolean lattice. Part 2 uses the divisor lattice. Part 3 uses the recursion directly, because N is not a product of chains.

steps.text: Part 1. Every word over S uses some set T ⊆ S of letters. So g(S) = |S|⁴ = ∑_{T⊆S} f(T). Inversion from below with μ(T,S) = (−1)^{|S∖T|} gives f({1,2,3}) = ∑_T (−1)^{3−|T|}·|T|⁴ = 3⁴ − 3·2⁴ + 3·1⁴ − 0⁴ = 81 − 48 + 3 = 36. A direct count agrees: the surjections from a 4-set onto a 3-set number 3!·S(4,3) = 6·6 = 36.

Part 2. The divisors of 360 are 24 in number. The exponent chains of 2, 3 and 5 have lengths 3, 2 and 1. The product rule gives μ(1,360) = μ_chain3(0,3)·μ_chain2(0,2)·μ_chain1(0,1) = 0·0·(−1) = 0. Also μ(1,30) = (−1)³ = −1 and μ(1,6) = 1 and μ(1,12) = 0. A computer evaluation of the recursion on all 24 divisors gives these four values.

Part 3. Use the recursion from the bottom element. μ(0,0) = 1. μ(0,a) = −1. μ(0,b) = −1. μ(0,c) = −(1 − 1) = 0. μ(0,1) = −(1 − 1 − 1 + 0) = 1. For the upper end, [x,1] is a chain for x = a,b,c, so μ(c,1) = −1, μ(b,1) = −1 and μ(a,1) = 0.

Take f(0)=2, f(a)=3, f(b)=5, f(c)=7, f(1)=11. Then g(0)=2, g(a)=5, g(b)=7, g(c)=12 and g(1)=28. Inversion from below at the top element gives f(1) = μ(0,1)g(0) + μ(a,1)g(a) + μ(b,1)g(b) + μ(c,1)g(c) + μ(1,1)g(1) = 2 + 0 − 7 − 12 + 28 = 11. This is the original value.

worked_application.result: The word count is 36. The Möbius values of the divisor lattice of 360 are μ(1,360) = 0 and μ(1,30) = −1. In the poset N, μ(0,1) = 1, and the inversion formula returns f(1) = 11.

limitations: The recursion for μ is easy to state, but the values can be hard to find. For the partition lattice or for the lattice of subspaces of a finite vector space, a product decomposition does not exist and other arguments are needed. This entry proves none of those values.

Inversion needs finiteness of the principal down-set or up-set. In an infinite poset such as the divisor lattice of ℕ, the formula for sums over divisors is fine, but sums over multiples need extra convergence.
The theorem inverts sums over order ideals. It does not invert sums over other families, for example over all subsets of a given size.

results.statement: Define S(0,0) = 1, S(n,0) = 0 for n ≥ 1, S(0,k) = 0 for k ≥ 1, and S(n+1,k+1) = (k+1)·S(n,k+1) + S(n,k). Write x^{\underline{k}} = x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1). Then: (1) In ℤ[x], x^n = ∑_{k=0}^n S(n,k)·x^{\underline{k}}, and the coefficients are unique. (2) S(n,k) is the number of partitions of an n-element set into k nonempty blocks. (3) The number of surjections from an n-set onto a k-set is k!·S(n,k) = ∑_{j=0}^k (−1)^{k−j}·C(k,j)·j^n. (4) For N ≥ 0 and k ≥ 0, ∑_{x=0}^{N−1} x^{\underline{k}} = N^{\underline{k+1}}/(k+1). Hence, for n ≥ 1, ∑_{x=0}^{N−1} x^n = ∑_{k=1}^n S(n,k)·N^{\underline{k+1}}/(k+1).
hypotheses: n and k are integers with n,k ≥ 0.
The identity (1) holds in the polynomial ring ℤ[x], so it holds for every integer x.
A block of a set partition is nonempty, and blocks are not ordered.

definitions.name: falling factorial

definitions.name: Stirling number of the second kind
definitions.text: The number S(n,k) of partitions of {1,…,n} into k nonempty unlabeled blocks. Step 4 shows that this number satisfies the recursion in the statement.

definitions.name: surjection
definitions.text: A map f : [n] → [k] such that every element of [k] has at least one preimage.

/-- Every power `n ^ k` is a linear combination of the descending factorials `n.descFactorial j`
with the Stirling numbers of the second kind `stirlingSecond k j` as coefficients. -/
theorem pow_eq_sum_stirlingSecond_mul_descFactorial (n k : ℕ) :
    n ^ k = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), stirlingSecond k j * n.descFactorial j := by
  induction k with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    have : ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), stirlingSecond k j * (j * n.descFactorial j)
        = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1),
            (j + 1) * (stirlingSecond k (j + 1) * n.descFactorial (j + 1)) := by
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ' (fun j ↦ stirlingSecond k j * (j * n.descFactorial j)) k,
        Finset.sum_range_succ (fun j ↦ (j + 1) * (stirlingSecond k (j + 1) *
          n.descFactorial (j + 1))) k,
        stirlingSecond_eq_zero_of_lt k.lt_add_one]
      simp [mul_left_comm]
    rw [pow_succ, ih, Finset.sum_mul,
      Finset.sum_range_succ' (fun j ↦ stirlingSecond (k + 1) j * n.descFactorial j) (k + 1)]
    simp only [mul_assoc, descFactorial_mul_self, mul_add, Finset.sum_add_distrib, this,
      stirlingSecond_succ_succ, add_mul, stirlingSecond_succ_zero, zero_mul, add_zero]
    exact add_comm _ _

steps.text: Falling factorials form a basis. The polynomial x^{\underline{k}} is monic of degree k. Monic polynomials of distinct degrees are linearly independent, and they span ℤ[x] by induction on the degree. So every polynomial has a unique expansion ∑ c_k·x^{\underline{k}}.
Key identity. Since x = (x − k) + k, we have x·x^{\underline{k}} = (x − k)·x^{\underline{k}} + k·x^{\underline{k}} = x^{\underline{k+1}} + k·x^{\underline{k}}.

Proof of (1) by induction on n. For n = 0 we have x^0 = 1 = S(0,0)·x^{\underline{0}}. Assume x^n = ∑_k S(n,k)·x^{\underline{k}}. Multiply by x and use step 2. Then x^{n+1} = ∑_k S(n,k)·x^{\underline{k+1}} + ∑_k k·S(n,k)·x^{\underline{k}}. The coefficient of x^{\underline{j}} for j ≥ 1 is S(n,j−1) + j·S(n,j), which is S(n+1,j) by the recursion. The coefficient for j = 0 is 0·S(n,0) = 0 = S(n+1,0). Uniqueness comes from step 1.

Proof of (2). Let T(n,k) be the number of partitions of [n] into k nonempty blocks. T(0,0) = 1, and T(n,0) = 0 for n ≥ 1, and T(0,k) = 0 for k ≥ 1. Take a partition of [n+1] into k+1 blocks. If {n+1} is a block, removing it leaves a partition of [n] into k blocks, which gives T(n,k) partitions. Otherwise, removing n+1 leaves a partition of [n] into k+1 blocks, and n+1 was in one of its k+1 blocks. This gives (k+1)·T(n,k+1) partitions. So T satisfies the recursion of S with the same start values, hence T = S.

Surjections. A surjection f : [n] → [k] has fibers f⁻¹(1),…,f⁻¹(k). They form a partition of [n] into k blocks, together with an order of the blocks. Conversely, a partition into k blocks and one of the k! orders of the blocks gives exactly one surjection. So the number of surjections is k!·S(n,k).

Explicit sum. Let Sur(n,k) be the number of surjections. For a set M ⊆ [k] the number of maps [n] → [k] whose image misses M is (k−|M|)^n. A map is a surjection if it misses no value. By inclusion-exclusion over the missed set, Sur(n,k) = ∑_{M⊆[k]} (−1)^{|M|}·(k−|M|)^n = ∑_{j=0}^k (−1)^{k−j}·C(k,j)·j^n.

Proof of (4). The forward difference of a falling factorial is (x+1)^{\underline{k+1}} − x^{\underline{k+1}} = (x+1)·x^{\underline{k}} − x^{\underline{k}}·(x−k) = (k+1)·x^{\underline{k}}. Sum over x = 0,…,N−1. The left side telescopes to N^{\underline{k+1}} − 0^{\underline{k+1}} = N^{\underline{k+1}}. Divide by k+1.

Power sums. Sum the expansion (1) over x = 0,…,N−1 and use step 7 term by term. The term k = 0 gives x^{\underline{0}} = 1, but S(n,0) = 0 for n ≥ 1, so this term vanishes. This gives ∑_{x<N} x^n = ∑_{k=1}^n S(n,k)·N^{\underline{k+1}}/(k+1) for n ≥ 1.

worked_application.title: Sum of fourth powers and a count of surjections
worked_application.goal: Compute 1⁴ + 2⁴ + … + 10⁴ and the number of surjections from a 5-set onto a 3-set.
hypotheses: The Stirling numbers S(4,k) for k = 1,…,4 are 1, 7, 6, 1.
The surjection count uses n = 5 and k = 3.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The power sum is statement (4) with n = 4 and N = 11. The surjection count is statement (3).

steps.text: Build the row. S(1,1) = 1. S(2,k) = 1, 1 for k = 1,2. S(3,k) = 1, 3, 1. S(4,1) = 1·S(3,1) + 0 = 1. S(4,2) = 2·S(3,2) + S(3,1) = 6 + 1 = 7. S(4,3) = 3·S(3,3) + S(3,2) = 3 + 3 = 6. S(4,4) = 1. This matches a direct count of 7 partitions of a 4-set into 2 blocks (3 of type 2+2 and 4 of type 3+1).

Apply statement (4) with N = 11. The falling factorials are 11^{\underline{2}} = 110, 11^{\underline{3}} = 990, 11^{\underline{4}} = 7920 and 11^{\underline{5}} = 55440. The four terms are 1·110/2 = 55, 7·990/3 = 2310, 6·7920/4 = 11880 and 1·55440/5 = 11088.

Surjections from a 5-set onto a 3-set. By statement (3) with the inclusion-exclusion sum, the number is 3⁵ − 3·2⁵ + 3·1⁵ − 0⁵ = 243 − 96 + 3 = 150. The other formula gives 3!·S(5,3) = 6·25 = 150, because S(5,3) = 3·S(4,3) + S(4,2) = 18 + 7 = 25. A brute force count over all 243 maps gives 150.

results.name: Walk counting by powers of the adjacency matrix, with closed walks, triangles and eigenvalues
results.statement: Let G be a finite simple graph on n vertices with adjacency matrix A, so A_{uv} = 1 if u and v are adjacent and 0 otherwise. Then: (1) For k ≥ 0, (A^k)_{uv} is the number of walks of length k from u to v. (2) tr(A^k) is the number of closed walks of length k, counted with a marked start vertex. In particular tr A = 0, tr A² = 2|E|, and tr A³ = 6·t where t is the number of triangles. (3) A is real symmetric. If λ_1,…,λ_n are its eigenvalues with multiplicity, then tr(A^k) = ∑_i λ_i^k. (4) If u ≠ v, the distance from u to v is the least k with (A^k)_{uv} > 0. The graph has diameter at most D if and only if every entry of (I+A)^D is positive and the graph is connected.
hypotheses: G is finite, undirected, without loops and without multiple edges.
A walk of length k is a sequence of vertices v_0,…,v_k with v_{i−1} adjacent to v_i for each i. Vertices may repeat.
A triangle is a set of 3 pairwise adjacent vertices.

prerequisites.reason: Steps 4 of the proof and 1 of the application use the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices to diagonalise the adjacency matrix.

definitions.name: walk
definitions.text: A sequence of vertices in which consecutive vertices are adjacent. Its length is the number of steps.

definitions.name: closed walk
definitions.text: A walk with v_k = v_0. A closed walk with a marked start vertex is counted once for each choice of start and direction.

definitions.name: adjacency matrix
definitions.text: The n×n matrix A with A_{uv} = 1 when u ~ v and 0 otherwise. It is symmetric with zero diagonal.

theorem adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_walk [DecidableEq V] [Semiring α] (n : ℕ) (u v : V) :
    (G.adjMatrix α ^ n) u v = Fintype.card { p : G.Walk u v | p.length = n } := by
  rw [card_set_walk_length_eq]
  induction n generalizing u v with
  | zero => obtain rfl | h := eq_or_ne u v <;> simp [finsetWalkLength, *]
  | succ n ih =>
    simp only [pow_succ', finsetWalkLength, ih, adjMatrix_mul_apply]
    rw [Finset.card_biUnion]
    · norm_cast
      simp only [Nat.cast_sum, card_map, neighborFinset_def]
      apply Finset.sum_toFinset_eq_subtype
    -- Disjointness for card_bUnion
    · rintro ⟨x, hx⟩ - ⟨y, hy⟩ - hxy
      rw [Function.onFun, disjoint_iff_inf_le]
      intro p hp
      simp only [inf_eq_inter, mem_inter, mem_map] at hp
      obtain ⟨⟨px, _, rfl⟩, ⟨py, hpy, hp⟩⟩ := hp
      cases hp
      simp at hxy

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Proof of (1) by induction on k. For k = 0 the matrix A⁰ = I counts the walk of length 0 from u to u and no other walk. Assume the claim for k. A walk of length k+1 from u to v is a walk of length k from u to some w, followed by a step from w to v. This step exists exactly when A_{wv} = 1. So the number of such walks is ∑_w (A^k)_{uw}·A_{wv} = (A^{k+1})_{uv}.

Proof of (2). A closed walk of length k with start u is a walk of length k from u to u. By (1) their number is (A^k)_{uu}. Sum over u to get tr(A^k). For k = 1, a closed walk of length 1 is a loop, so tr A = 0. For k = 2, a closed walk is u,w,u with w adjacent to u. The count is ∑_u deg(u) = 2|E|.

Triangles. A closed walk u,v,w,u of length 3 has u ~ v, v ~ w and w ~ u. There are no loops, so u ≠ v, v ≠ w and w ≠ u. Hence {u,v,w} is a triangle. Conversely, each triangle gives 6 closed walks of length 3, one for each of the 3 choices of start and the 2 directions. So tr A³ = 6t.

Proof of (3). A is real and A_{uv} = A_{vu}, so A is real symmetric. By the spectral theorem there is an orthogonal matrix Q with A = Q·diag(λ_1,…,λ_n)·Qᵀ. Then A^k = Q·diag(λ_i^k)·Qᵀ, and the trace is invariant under conjugation: tr(A^k) = ∑_i λ_i^k.

Proof of (4). The distance from u to v is the length of a shortest walk from u to v. A shortest walk exists exactly when some k has a walk of length k, and the least such k is the distance. By (1) this is the least k with (A^k)_{uv} > 0.

Diameter. Expand (I+A)^D = ∑_{j=0}^D C(D,j)·A^j. All terms have nonnegative entries, and C(D,j) > 0. So an entry is positive exactly when some A^j with j ≤ D has a positive entry there. By (1) and (4) this holds for all pairs exactly when every pair is at distance at most D. The pairs with u = v are covered by j = 0.

worked_application.title: Triangles in K4, five-walks in the Petersen graph and the spectrum of C5
worked_application.goal: Count closed walks and walks by trace and by eigenvalues, and check the counts by direct enumeration.
hypotheses: K4 is the complete graph on 4 vertices, with eigenvalues 3, −1, −1, −1.
The Petersen graph has 10 vertices, 15 edges and eigenvalues 3 (once), 1 (five times), −2 (four times). Its vertices are the 2-subsets of {1,…,5}, and two are adjacent when disjoint.
The cycle C5 has eigenvalues 2cos(2πj/5) for j = 0,…,4.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: All three graphs are finite and simple. The theorem applies. Each count in the steps below is compared to a direct enumeration.

steps.text: K4. By (3), tr A³ = 3³ + 3·(−1)³ = 24. By (2) this equals 6t, so K4 has t = 4 triangles. This agrees with C(4,3) = 4.

Petersen graph, closed walks. By (3), tr A^k = 3^k + 5 + 4·(−2)^k. This gives 0, 30, 0, 150, 120, 990 for k = 1,…,6. The value for k = 2 is 2·15 = 30 and the value for k = 3 is 0, so the graph has no triangle. These traces agree with matrix powers computed by computer.

Closed 5-walks. The value tr A⁵ = 243 + 5 − 128 = 120 counts closed walks of length 5. In a triangle-free graph, a closed walk of odd length 5 that repeats a vertex splits into a closed walk of odd length at most 3, which must be a loop or a triangle. Neither exists. So each such walk is a 5-cycle, and each 5-cycle gives 5·2 = 10 closed walks. The Petersen graph has 120/10 = 12 five-cycles, and an exhaustive search finds exactly 12.

Walk counts from one vertex. Row sums of A⁵ are 3⁵ = 243, because each vertex has degree 3. For a fixed vertex u, (A⁵)_{uu} = 12 and (A⁵)_{uv} = 22 for each neighbour v. Distances: A² has entry 1 at every vertex not adjacent to u, so every pair is at distance at most 2 by (4), and (I+A)² is positive.

C5. By (3), tr A⁵ = ∑_{j=0}^4 (2cos(2πj/5))⁵ = 10. A direct count agrees: the 5-cycle gives 5 starts and 2 directions, and no other closed 5-walk exists, because C5 is triangle-free and has no shorter odd cycle.

worked_application.result: K4 has 4 triangles. The Petersen graph has no triangle, 120 closed 5-walks and 12 five-cycles, and it has diameter 2. The graph C5 has 10 closed 5-walks.

limitations: The count in (2) treats a closed walk with different start vertices as different walks. To count cycles, divide by the start and direction symmetry only for cycles, and only when no shorter closed walk exists.
Statement (3) needs real symmetric matrices. For directed graphs the adjacency matrix is not symmetric, and the trace formula holds only with complex eigenvalues of A.
The formula tr A³ = 6t is special to three steps. For longer cycles, closed walks include degenerate walks, and a correction term is needed.

results.name: Finite projective planes: constant line size n+1 and n²+n+1 points and lines
results.statement: Let a finite projective plane be a finite set of points and a finite set of lines, with an incidence relation, such that: (A1) two distinct points lie on exactly one common line, (A2) two distinct lines meet in exactly one common point, (A3) there are four points, no three on a common line. theorem card_points [Fintype P] [Finite L] : Fintype.card P = order P L ^ 2 + order P L + 1 := by
  cases nonempty_fintype L
  obtain ⟨p, -⟩ := @exists_config P L _ _
  let ϕ : { q // q ≠ p } ≃ Σ l : { l : L // p ∈ l }, { q // q ∈ l.1 ∧ q ≠ p } :=
    { toFun := fun q => ⟨⟨mkLine q.2, (mkLine_ax q.2).2⟩, q, (mkLine_ax q.2).1, q.2⟩
      invFun := fun lq => ⟨lq.2, lq.2.2.2⟩
      right_inv := fun lq =>
        Sigma.subtype_ext
          (Subtype.ext
            ((eq_or_eq (mkLine_ax lq.2.2.2).1 (mkLine_ax lq.2.2.2).2 lq.2.2.1 lq.1.2).resolve_left
              lq.2.2.2))
          rfl }
  classical
    have h1 : Fintype.card { q // q ≠ p } + 1 = Fintype.card P := by
