steps.text: Symmetry of multiplication. For polynomials f and g, ⟨xf, g⟩ = ∫ x f g w = ⟨f, xg⟩. We use this in the next step.

The recurrence. The polynomial xπ_k − π_{k+1} has degree at most k. The π_0,…,π_k are orthogonal, nonzero and form a basis of the polynomials of degree at most k. So xπ_k − π_{k+1} = ∑_{j≤k} c_j π_j with c_j = ⟨xπ_k − π_{k+1}, π_j⟩/h_j = ⟨xπ_k, π_j⟩/h_j, because ⟨π_{k+1}, π_j⟩ = 0 for j ≤ k.

For j < k−1: ⟨xπ_k, π_j⟩ = ⟨π_k, xπ_j⟩ = 0, because xπ_j has degree j+1 < k. For j = k: c_k = α_k by definition. For j = k−1 with k ≥ 1: xπ_{k−1} = π_k + (terms of degree below k), so ⟨π_k, xπ_{k−1}⟩ = h_k and c_{k−1} = h_k/h_{k−1} = β_k. This proves (1).

The determinant recurrence. Let D_k(x) = det(xI_k − J_k), where J_k is the leading k×k block of J_n. Expand det(xI_{k+1} − J_{k+1}) along its last row. The row has the entry −√β_k in column k−1 and x − α_k in column k. The cofactor of the entry x − α_k is D_k. For the entry −√β_k, delete its row and column. The last column of the remaining matrix has the single nonzero entry −√β_k, in the row above. Expanding along it gives −√β_k·D_{k−1}. The cofactor sign of the entry is −1. The term is (−√β_k)·(−1)·(−√β_k)·D_{k−1} = −β_k D_{k−1}. So D_{k+1} = (x − α_k)D_k − β_k D_{k−1}.

Comparison. We have D_0 = 1 and D_1 = x − α_0. By (1) with k = 0, π_1 = x − α_0, and π_0 = 1. The polynomials π_k satisfy the same three-term recurrence by (1). By induction on k, D_k = π_k for all k ≥ 0. In particular det(xI − J_n) = π_n. This proves (2). The roots of π_n are real and simple, by the Gauss quadrature theorem.

The eigenvector. Divide the recurrence (1) by √h_k. We get x p_k = √β_{k+1}·p_{k+1} + α_k p_k + √β_k·p_{k−1}, because √(h_{k+1}/h_k) = √β_{k+1} and β_k·√(h_{k−1}/h_k) = β_k/√β_k = √β_k. Let P(x) = (p_0(x),…,p_{n−1}(x))ᵀ. Row k of J_n P(x) equals x p_k(x) for k < n−1. Row n−1 equals x p_{n−1}(x) − √β_n·p_n(x). At a root x_i of π_n, p_n(x_i) = 0. So J_n P(x_i) = x_i P(x_i). The first entry of P(x_i) is p_0 = h_0^{−1/2} ≠ 0, so P(x_i) ≠ 0.

Normalization. The eigenvalue x_i of the symmetric matrix J_n is simple, so its eigenspace is the line spanned by P(x_i). The unit vector is v_i = P(x_i)/‖P(x_i)‖, up to sign. So v_{i,1}² = p_0²/∑_k p_k(x_i)² = (1/h_0)/∑_k p_k(x_i)².

The Christoffel formula. The polynomial ℓ_i has degree n−1 and ℓ_i = ∑_{k<n} c_k p_k with c_k = ⟨ℓ_i, p_k⟩, because p_0,…,p_{n−1} is an orthonormal basis of that space. The product ℓ_i·p_k has degree at most 2n−2, so by exactness of the Gauss rule, c_k = ∑_j λ_j ℓ_i(x_j) p_k(x_j) = λ_i p_k(x_i). Evaluate ℓ_i at x_i: 1 = ℓ_i(x_i) = ∑_k c_k p_k(x_i) = λ_i ∑_k p_k(x_i)². So λ_i = 1/∑_k p_k(x_i)².
Conclusion. By the two last steps, λ_i = 1/∑ p_k(x_i)² = h_0·v_{i,1}². Since h_0 = ∫ w, this proves (3).

worked_application.title: Gauss-Legendre rule with three nodes from a 3×3 eigenvalue problem
worked_application.goal: Compute the nodes and weights of the three-point Gauss-Legendre rule from the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 3×3 matrix.
hypotheses: The monic polynomials are π_0 = 1, π_1 = x, π_2 = x² − 1/3.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The weight is even, so all α_k = 0. The recurrence coefficients follow from the norms h_k.

steps.text: The Jacobi matrix has zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries √(1/3) and √(4/15). Its characteristic polynomial is x³ − (β_1 + β_2)x = x³ − (3/5)x, because 1/3 + 4/15 = 3/5.
This is π_3 = x³ − (3/5)x, which the Gauss quadrature theorem gives from orthogonality. The eigenvalues are 0 and ±√(3/5), the three Gauss nodes.

Eigenvectors. By the proof, the vector P(x)/p_0 = (1, x/√β_1, (x² − β_1)/√(β_1β_2)) is an eigenvector. At x = 0 it is (1, 0, −√(β_1/β_2)). Its squared norm is 1 + β_1/β_2 = 1 + 5/4 = 9/4. So v_{1}² = 4/9 and the weight is 2·(4/9) = 8/9.

At x = ±√(3/5) the vector is (1, ±3/√5, (3/5 − 1/3)/√(4/45)) = (1, ±3/√5, 2/√5). Its squared norm is 1 + 9/5 + 4/5 = 18/5 = 3.6. So the first component squared is 5/18 and the weight is 2·(5/18) = 5/9. A computer eigenvalue routine gives the same eigenvalues and the weights 0.5556, 0.8889, 0.5556.

worked_application.result: The Jacobi matrix with off-diagonal entries √(1/3) and √(4/15) has eigenvalues 0 and ±√(3/5). The first components of its unit eigenvectors give the Gauss weights 8/9, 5/9, 5/9.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The statement assumes the hypotheses of Gauss quadrature. It does not treat weights whose orthogonal polynomials are not defined for all degrees.
The eigenvalue method gives nodes and weights in O(n²) work with the symmetric tridiagonal QR method. It is not an error bound for the rule.
The proof gives the first component of each eigenvector. It does not give a formula for the other components in closed form.

results.name: Legendre polynomials: Rodrigues formula, orthogonality, norm and three-term recurrence
results.statement: For n ≥ 0 let P_n(x) = (1/(2^n n!))·dⁿ/dxⁿ (x²−1)ⁿ. (a) P_n is a polynomial of degree n with leading coefficient k_n = (2n)!/(2^n (n!)²). It satisfies P_n(1) = 1 and P_n(−x) = (−1)ⁿP_n(x). (b) For all m, n ≥ 0, ∫_{−1}^{1} P_m P_n dx = 0 if m ≠ n and = 2/(2n+1) if m = n. (c) For n ≥ 1, (2n+1)·x·P_n = (n+1)·P_{n+1} + n·P_{n−1}. (d) Every polynomial f of degree at most N is the sum ∑_{k≤N} c_k P_k with c_k = ((2k+1)/2)∫_{−1}^{1} f P_k dx.
hypotheses: n, m are non-negative integers.
All integrals are Riemann integrals of polynomials over [−1,1].

definitions.name: Rodrigues formula
definitions.text: The formula P_n = (2^n n!)^{−1} dⁿ/dxⁿ (x²−1)ⁿ, which defines the Legendre polynomial by differentiation.

definitions.name: Legendre expansion
definitions.text: The expansion f = ∑ c_k P_k of a polynomial or of a function in L²[−1,1], with coefficients given by the inner products with P_k.

definitions.name: three-term recurrence
definitions.text: A relation that expresses xP_n by P_{n+1} and P_{n−1}. It allows a stable evaluation of P_n.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Notation. Put u_n(x) = (x²−1)ⁿ = (x−1)ⁿ(x+1)ⁿ. Then P_n = u_n^{(n)}/(2^n n!).

Degree and leading coefficient. The polynomial u_n has degree 2n and leading term x^{2n}. The n-th derivative of x^{2n} is ((2n)!/n!)xⁿ, and the n-th derivative of a polynomial of degree below 2n has degree below n. So P_n has degree n and k_n = (2n)!/(n!·2^n n!) = (2n)!/(2^n (n!)²).

Parity and value at 1. The polynomial u_n is even. Each derivative changes parity, so u_n^{(n)} has the parity of n, which gives P_n(−x) = (−1)ⁿP_n(x). By the Leibniz rule, u_n^{(n)}(x) = ∑_i C(n,i)·[(x−1)ⁿ]^{(i)}·[(x+1)ⁿ]^{(n−i)}. At x = 1 each term with i < n contains the factor (x−1)^{n−i}, which is zero. The term i = n is n!·(x+1)ⁿ, which is n!·2ⁿ at x = 1. So P_n(1) = n!·2ⁿ/(2ⁿ n!) = 1. This proves (a).

Vanishing at the ends. For 0 ≤ j < n, the same Leibniz expansion shows that u_n^{(j)} has the factor (x−1)^{n−i} (x+1)^{n−j+i} in each term, and both exponents are positive. So u_n^{(j)}(1) = u_n^{(j)}(−1) = 0.

Integration by parts n times. Let g be a polynomial. One integration by parts gives ∫_{−1}^{1} g·u_n^{(n)} dx = [g·u_n^{(n−1)}]_{−1}^{1} − ∫ g′·u_n^{(n−1)} dx. The boundary term is zero by the last step. Repeat n times. We get ∫ g·u_n^{(n)} dx = (−1)ⁿ ∫ g^{(n)}·u_n dx.
Orthogonality. Let m < n. Take g = P_m, which has degree m < n. Then g^{(n)} = 0 and ∫ P_m u_n^{(n)} dx = 0. So ∫ P_m P_n dx = 0. The case m > n follows by symmetry.

The norm. Take g = P_n. Its n-th derivative is k_n·n! = (2n)!/(2ⁿ n!), a constant. So ∫ P_n² dx = (1/(2ⁿ n!))·(−1)ⁿ·((2n)!/(2ⁿ n!))·∫ u_n dx = ((2n)!/(2ⁿ n!)²)·I_n, where I_n = ∫_{−1}^{1} (1−x²)ⁿ dx, because (−1)ⁿ u_n = (1−x²)ⁿ.

Computing I_n. Integrate by parts: I_n = [x(1−x²)ⁿ]_{−1}^{1} + 2n∫ x²(1−x²)^{n−1} dx = 2n∫ (1 − (1−x²))(1−x²)^{n−1} dx = 2n(I_{n−1} − I_n). So (2n+1)I_n = 2n·I_{n−1}, with I_0 = 2. Hence I_n = 2·∏_{k=1}^n 2k/(2k+1) = 2^{2n+1}(n!)²/(2n+1)!. Then ∫ P_n² dx = ((2n)!/(2ⁿ n!)²)·2^{2n+1}(n!)²/(2n+1)! = 2/(2n+1). This proves (b).

Recurrence. The polynomials P_0,…,P_{n+1} have degrees 0,…,n+1, so they form a basis of the polynomials of degree at most n+1. They are orthogonal, so xP_n = ∑_{j≤n+1} c_j P_j with c_j = ⟨xP_n, P_j⟩/⟨P_j, P_j⟩. For j < n−1: ⟨xP_n, P_j⟩ = ⟨P_n, xP_j⟩ = 0, because xP_j has degree below n. For j = n: ⟨xP_n, P_n⟩ = ∫ xP_n² dx = 0, because the integrand is odd by (a).

The two remaining coefficients. Compare leading coefficients: c_{n+1}·k_{n+1} = k_n, so c_{n+1} = k_n/k_{n+1} = (n+1)/(2n+1). For j = n−1, write xP_{n−1} = (k_{n−1}/k_n)P_n + (terms of degree below n). Then ⟨P_n, xP_{n−1}⟩ = (k_{n−1}/k_n)·⟨P_n,P_n⟩, and c_{n−1} = (k_{n−1}/k_n)·(2/(2n+1))/(2/(2n−1)) = (n/(2n−1))·((2n−1)/(2n+1)) = n/(2n+1). Here k_{n−1}/k_n = n/(2n−1) by the formula for k_n. Multiply xP_n = ((n+1)/(2n+1))P_{n+1} + (n/(2n+1))P_{n−1} by 2n+1. This proves (c).

Expansion. The P_0,…,P_N are orthogonal and nonzero, with degrees 0,…,N. So they form an orthogonal basis of the polynomials of degree at most N. The coefficient of f along P_k is ⟨f,P_k⟩/⟨P_k,P_k⟩ = ((2k+1)/2)⟨f,P_k⟩ by (b). This proves (d).

worked_application.title: Legendre expansion of x⁴ and a check by the value at x = 1
worked_application.goal: Expand x⁴ in Legendre polynomials and check the result.
hypotheses: f(x) = x⁴, N = 4.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The function is a polynomial of degree 4, so part (d) gives an exact finite expansion. Parity shows that only P_0, P_2, P_4 appear.

steps.text: From Rodrigues: d³/dx³ (x²−1)³ = d³/dx³ (x⁶ − 3x⁴ + 3x² − 1) = 120x³ − 72x. Divide by 2³·3! = 48 to get P_3 = (5x³ − 3x)/2. Its norm is ∫ P_3² = 2/7, which a direct integration confirms.
The recurrence (c) with n = 3 gives 7xP_3 = 4P_4 + 3P_2. So P_4 = (7xP_3 − 3P_2)/4 = (35x⁴ − 30x² + 3)/8. Its leading coefficient is 35/8. This matches k_4 = 8!/(2⁴(4!)²) = 40320/(16·576) = 35/8.

Coefficients. The odd coefficients vanish by parity. c_0 = (1/2)∫x⁴ = 1/5. c_2 = (5/2)∫ x⁴(3x²−1)/2 = (5/2)(3/7 − 1/5) = (5/2)(8/35) = 4/7. Because x⁴ = (1/k_4)P_4 + (lower terms), c_4 = 1/k_4 = 8/35.

Check by P_n(1) = 1: the coefficients sum to 1/5 + 4/7 + 8/35 = (7 + 20 + 8)/35 = 1 = 1⁴. Check by norms: the squared L² norm of x⁴ is 2/9. Parseval for the orthogonal basis gives ∑ c_k²·2/(2k+1) = 2/(25) + (16/49)(2/5) + (64/1225)(2/9) = 2/9. The numerical value is 0.08 + 0.130612 + 0.011610 = 0.222222.

worked_application.result: x⁴ = (1/5)P_0 + (4/7)P_2 + (8/35)P_4 on [−1,1]. The coefficients sum to 1 and satisfy Parseval: ∑ c_k²·2/(2k+1) = 2/9.

results.name: Bernstein polynomials: error bound by the modulus of continuity
results.statement: Let f be continuous on [0,1]. Let ω(δ) = sup{|f(s) − f(t)| : s, t in [0,1], |s − t| ≤ δ} be its modulus of continuity. Let B_n f(x) = ∑_{k=0}^n f(k/n)·C(n,k)·x^k(1−x)^{n−k}. Then for every n ≥ 1, every x in [0,1] and every δ > 0, |B_n f(x) − f(x)| ≤ ω(δ)·(1 + √(x(1−x)/n)/δ). Hence max |B_n f − f| ≤ ω(δ)(1 + 1/(2δ√n)), and with δ = n^{−1/2} we get max |B_n f − f| ≤ (3/2)·ω(n^{−1/2}). If f is Lipschitz with constant L, then |B_n f(x) − f(x)| ≤ L√(x(1−x)/n) ≤ L/(2√n). In particular B_n f converges to f uniformly on [0,1].
hypotheses: f is real and continuous on [0,1]. Then f is uniformly continuous and ω(δ) → 0 as δ → 0.
n ≥ 1 is an integer.

prerequisites.reason: The estimate of the mean absolute deviation by the standard deviation uses the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

definitions.name: Bernstein polynomial
definitions.text: The polynomial B_n f of degree at most n defined by the formula in the statement. Its coefficients are the values of f at k/n.

definitions.name: modulus of continuity
definitions.text: The function ω(δ) = sup{|f(s) − f(t)| : |s − t| ≤ δ}. It is non-decreasing and ω(δ) → 0 when f is continuous on [0,1].

definitions.name: binomial weights
definitions.text: b_k(x) = C(n,k)x^k(1−x)^{n−k}. They are non-negative on [0,1] and sum to 1.

source.excerpt:
/-- The Bernstein approximations
```
∑ k : Fin (n+1), f (k/n : ℝ) * n.choose k * x^k * (1-x)^(n-k)
```
for a continuous function `f : C([0,1], ℝ)` converge uniformly to `f` as `n` tends to infinity.

This is the proof given in [Richard Beals' *Analysis, an introduction*][beals-analysis], §7D,
and reproduced on wikipedia.
-/
theorem bernsteinApproximation_uniform [LocallyConvexSpace ℝ E] (f : C(I, E)) :
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => bernsteinApproximation n f) atTop (𝓝 f) := by
  let : UniformSpace E := IsTopologicalAddGroup.rightUniformSpace E
  have : IsUniformAddGroup E := isUniformAddGroup_of_addCommGroup
  /- Topology on a locally convex TVS is given by a family of seminorms `‖x‖_U = gauge U x`,
  where the open symmetric convex sets `U` form a basis of neighborhoods in this topology,
  and are the open unit balls for the corresponding seminorms.
  For technical reasons, we neither assume `U`s to be open, nor symmetric. -/
  suffices ∀ U ∈ 𝓝 (0 : E), Convex ℝ U →
      ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ x : I, gauge U (bernsteinApproximation n f x - f x) < 1 by
    rw [(LocallyConvexSpace.convex_basis_zero ℝ E).uniformity_of_nhds_zero_swapped
      |>.compactConvergenceUniformity_of_compact |> nhds_basis_uniformity |>.tendsto_right_iff]
    rintro U ⟨hU₀, hcU⟩
    filter_upwards [this U hU₀ hcU] with n hn x
    exact setOfPred_gauge_lt_one_subset_self hcU (mem_of_mem_nhds hU₀) (absorbent_nhds_zero hU₀)
      (hn x)
  intro U hU₀ hUc
  /- Choose a constant `C` such that `‖f x - f y‖_U ≤ C` for all `x`, `y`.
  For a normed space, this would be twice the norm of `f`. -/
  obtain ⟨C, hC⟩ : ∃ C, ∀ x y, gauge U (f x - f y) ≤ C := by
    have : Continuous fun (x, y) ↦ gauge U (f x - f y) := by fun_prop
    simpa only [BddAbove, Set.Nonempty, mem_upperBounds, Set.forall_mem_range, Prod.forall]
      using isCompact_range this |>.bddAbove
  have hC₀ : 0 ≤ C := le_trans (gauge_nonneg _) (hC 0 0)
  /- Use uniform continuity of `f` to choose `δ > 0` such that `‖f x - f y‖_U < 1 / 2`
  whenever `dist x y < δ`. -/
  obtain ⟨δ, hδ₀, hδ⟩ : ∃ δ > 0, ∀ x y : I, dist x y < δ → gauge U (f x - f y) < 1 / 2 := by
    have := CompactSpace.uniformContinuous_of_continuous (map_continuous f)
    rw [Metric.uniformity_basis_dist.uniformContinuous_iff
      (basis_sets _).uniformity_of_nhds_zero_swapped] at this
    exact this {z | gauge U z < 1 / 2} <| tendsto_gauge_nhds_zero hU₀
      |>.eventually_lt_const <| by positivity
  -- Take `n ≠ 0` such that `C / δ ^ 2 / n < 1 / 2`.
  have nhds_zero := tendsto_const_div_atTop_nhds_zero_nat (C / δ ^ 2)
  filter_upwards [nhds_zero.eventually_lt_const (half_pos one_pos), eventually_ne_atTop 0]
    with n nh hn₀ x
  -- The idea is to split up the sum over `k` into two sets,
  -- `S`, where `x - k/n < δ`, and its complement.
  set S : Finset (Fin (n + 1)) := {k : Fin (n + 1) | dist k/ₙ x < δ}
  calc
    gauge U (bernsteinApproximation n f x - f x)
      = gauge U (∑ k : Fin (n + 1), bernstein n k x • (f k/ₙ - f x)) := by
      simp [bernsteinApproximation.apply, smul_sub, ← Finset.sum_smul]
    _ ≤ ∑ k : Fin (n + 1), gauge U (bernstein n k x • (f k/ₙ - f x)) :=
      gauge_sum_le hUc (absorbent_nhds_zero hU₀) _ _
    _ = ∑ k : Fin (n + 1), bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x) := by
      simp only [gauge_smul_of_nonneg, bernstein_nonneg, smul_eq_mul]
    _ = (∑ k ∈ S, bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x)) +
          ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x) :=
      (S.sum_add_sum_compl _).symm
    -- We'll now deal with the terms in `S` and the terms in `Sᶜ` in separate calc blocks.
    _ < 1 / 2 + 1 / 2 := add_lt_add_of_le_of_lt ?_ ?_
    _ = 1 := add_halves 1
  · -- We now work on the terms in `S`: uniform continuity and `bernstein.probability`
    -- quickly give us a bound.
    calc
      ∑ k ∈ S, bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x) ≤ ∑ k ∈ S, bernstein n k x * (1 / 2) := by
        gcongr with k hk
        refine (hδ _ _ ?_).le
        simpa [S] using hk
      _ = 1 / 2 * ∑ k ∈ S, bernstein n k x := by rw [mul_comm, Finset.sum_mul]
      -- In this step we increase the sum over `S` back to a sum over all of `Fin (n+1)`,
      -- so that we can use `bernstein.probability`.
      _ ≤ 1 / 2 * ∑ k : Fin (n + 1), bernstein n k x := by gcongr; exact S.subset_univ
      _ = 1 / 2 := by rw [bernstein.probability, mul_one]
  · -- We now turn to working on `Sᶜ`: we control the difference term just using `C`,
    -- and then insert a `(x - k/n)^2 / δ^2` factor
    -- (which is at least one because we are not in `S`).
    calc
      ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x) ≤ ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, C * bernstein n k x := by
        simp only [mul_comm (bernstein n _ x)]
        gcongr
        apply hC
      _ = C * ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, bernstein n k x := by rw [Finset.mul_sum]
      _ ≤ C * ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, ((x : ℝ) - k/ₙ) ^ 2 / δ ^ 2 * bernstein n k x := by
        gcongr with k hk
        conv_lhs => rw [← one_mul (bernstein _ _ _)]
        gcongr
        simpa [one_le_div₀, hδ₀, sq_le_sq, S, abs_of_pos, ← Real.dist_eq, dist_comm (x : ℝ)]
          using! hk
      -- Again enlarging the sum from `Sᶜ` to all of `Fin (n+1)`
      _ ≤ C * ∑ k : Fin (n + 1), ((x : ℝ) - k/ₙ) ^ 2 / δ ^ 2 * bernstein n k x := by
        gcongr; exact Sᶜ.subset_univ
      _ = C * (∑ k : Fin (n + 1), ((x : ℝ) - k/ₙ) ^ 2 * bernstein n k x) / δ ^ 2 := by
        simp only [← mul_div_right_comm, ← mul_div_assoc, ← Finset.sum_div]
      -- `bernstein.variance` and `x ∈ [0,1]` gives the uniform bound
      _ = C / δ ^ 2 * x * (1 - x) / n := by rw [variance hn₀]; ring
      _ ≤ C / δ ^ 2 * 1 * 1 / n := by gcongr <;> unit_interval
      _ < 1 / 2 := by simpa only [mul_one]

source_references.alignment: The source proves the variance identity ∑ (x − k/n)² b_k = x(1−x)/n for Bernstein weights. This is the variance step of the proof.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Weights. Put b_k(x) = C(n,k)x^k(1−x)^{n−k} ≥ 0. By the binomial theorem ∑ b_k = (x + 1 − x)ⁿ = 1.
First moment. Since k·C(n,k) = n·C(n−1,k−1), we have ∑ k b_k = nx·∑_{k≥1} C(n−1,k−1) x^{k−1}(1−x)^{n−k} = nx.
Second moment. Since k(k−1)·C(n,k) = n(n−1)·C(n−2,k−2), the same argument gives ∑ k(k−1) b_k = n(n−1)x². So ∑ k² b_k = n(n−1)x² + nx.
Variance. ∑ (k − nx)² b_k = ∑ k² b_k − 2nx∑ k b_k + n²x² ∑ b_k = n(n−1)x² + nx − 2n²x² + n²x² = nx − nx² = n x(1−x). Divide by n²: ∑ (k/n − x)² b_k = x(1−x)/n.

Growth of ω. Let t > 0 and δ > 0. Take s, u in [0,1] with |s − u| ≤ t. Let m = ⌈t/δ⌉. Divide the segment between s and u into m equal parts. Each part has length at most t/m ≤ δ and its end points lie in [0,1]. Add the m differences along the parts. We get |f(s) − f(u)| ≤ m·ω(δ). Since m < 1 + t/δ, we get ω(t) ≤ (1 + t/δ)·ω(δ).

The main estimate. Since ∑ b_k = 1, B_n f(x) − f(x) = ∑ (f(k/n) − f(x)) b_k. So |B_n f(x) − f(x)| ≤ ∑ ω(|k/n − x|) b_k. The bound of the last step gives ω(|k/n − x|) ≤ ω(δ)(1 + |k/n − x|/δ). Hence |B_n f(x) − f(x)| ≤ ω(δ)(1 + (1/δ)∑ |k/n − x| b_k).

Cauchy-Schwarz. Write |k/n − x| b_k = (|k/n − x|·√b_k)·√b_k. Then ∑ |k/n − x| b_k ≤ (∑ (k/n − x)² b_k)^{1/2} (∑ b_k)^{1/2} = √(x(1−x)/n). This proves the main bound. Since x(1−x) ≤ 1/4, the uniform bound follows.
Special choices. For δ = n^{−1/2} we get 1 + √(x(1−x)/n)·√n = 1 + √(x(1−x)) ≤ 3/2. For f Lipschitz, ω(δ) ≤ Lδ, so the main bound is at most Lδ + L√(x(1−x)/n). Let δ → 0 to obtain L√(x(1−x)/n).
Uniform convergence. For every ε > 0 pick δ with ω(δ) < ε/2. Then max |B_n f − f| ≤ ω(δ)(1 + 1/(2δ√n)) < ε for n large. So B_n f → f uniformly.

results.name: Newton iteration: quadratic convergence near a simple root
results.statement: Let I be a closed interval. Let f be a real function of class C² on I. Let x* in I satisfy f(x*) = 0. Assume |f′(x)| ≥ m > 0 and |f″(x)| ≤ M for all x in I. Put c = M/(2m) and N(x) = x − f(x)/f′(x). Then (1) |N(x) − x*| ≤ c·|x − x*|² for all x in I. (2) Let ρ > 0 with [x* − ρ, x* + ρ] contained in I and cρ < 1. Let |x₀ − x*| ≤ ρ and x_{k+1} = N(x_k). Then every x_k lies in [x* − ρ, x* + ρ] and |x_k − x*| ≤ (1/c)·(c·|x₀ − x*|)^(2^k). (3) The sequence x_k converges to x*. If x_k ≠ x* for all k, then (x_{k+1} − x*)/(x_k − x*)² tends to f″(x*)/(2f′(x*)).
hypotheses: f is real, twice continuously differentiable on the closed interval I.
f(x*) = 0 with x* in I.
|f′| ≥ m > 0 and |f″| ≤ M on I.
The start point satisfies |x₀ − x*| ≤ ρ and cρ < 1, with [x* − ρ, x* + ρ] in I.

source.alignment: The source proves a Newton iteration doubles the nilpotency order, in a commutative ring with a nilpotent value of P and a unit derivative. This is the algebraic analogue of the quadratic convergence. The entry proves the real-analysis version, and the source does not.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Taylor expansion at the iterate. Let x be in I. By Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder, there is ξ between x and x* with 0 = f(x*) = f(x) + f′(x)(x* − x) + (1/2)f″(ξ)(x* − x)².
This is the order-1 Taylor formula with the Lagrange form of the remainder. It needs f of class C² on the segment between x and x*, and this segment lies in I.
Divide by f′(x). This is allowed because |f′(x)| ≥ m > 0. We get f(x)/f′(x) + (x* − x) = −f″(ξ)(x* − x)²/(2f′(x)).
Recognise the Newton step. The left side equals x* − (x − f(x)/f′(x)) = x* − N(x). So x* − N(x) = −f″(ξ)(x* − x)²/(2f′(x)).
Take absolute values and use the two bounds. |N(x) − x*| ≤ (M/(2m))·|x − x*|² = c·|x − x*|². This proves part (1).
Rescaled error. Put e_k = |x_k − x*|. Assume x_k lies in [x* − ρ, x* + ρ]. Part (1) gives c·e_{k+1} ≤ (c·e_k)².
Staying in the ball. Since c·e_0 ≤ cρ < 1, we get c·e_1 ≤ (c·e_0)² < c·e_0, so e_1 < e_0 ≤ ρ. By induction e_k is non-increasing and every x_k lies in the ball, where part (1) holds.
Explicit bound. By induction c·e_k ≤ (c·e_0)^(2^k). The case k = 0 is trivial. If it holds for k, then c·e_{k+1} ≤ (c·e_k)² ≤ (c·e_0)^(2^(k+1)). Divide by c to get part (2).
Convergence. Because c·e_0 < 1, the power (c·e_0)^(2^k) tends to 0. So e_k → 0 and x_k → x*.

Limit of the ratio. Let x_k ≠ x*. Apply the exact identity of the third step with x = x_k. Then (x_{k+1} − x*)/(x_k − x*)² = f″(ξ_k)/(2f′(x_k)) with ξ_k between x_k and x*. So ξ_k → x*. Continuity of f″ and f′ gives the limit f″(x*)/(2f′(x*)). This proves part (3).

results.name: Condition number: sharp perturbation bounds for linear systems
results.statement: Let A be an invertible n×n real matrix. Let ‖·‖ be the operator norm from a norm on R^n. Put κ(A) = ‖A‖·‖A⁻¹‖. Let b ≠ 0 and Ax = b. (a) If A(x + δx) = b + δb, then ‖δx‖/‖x‖ ≤ κ(A)·‖δb‖/‖b‖. (b) Let ε = ‖δA‖/‖A‖ with κ(A)ε < 1. Then A + δA is invertible, and if (A + δA)(x + δx) = b, then ‖δx‖/‖x‖ ≤ κ(A)ε/(1 − κ(A)ε). (c) For the Euclidean norm, (a) is sharp: for each b-perturbation size there are b and δb with equality. (d) For the Euclidean norm, min{‖δA‖₂/‖A‖₂ : A + δA is singular} = 1/κ₂(A) = σ_min/σ_max.
hypotheses: A is invertible and b ≠ 0.
Parts (c) and (d) use the Euclidean norm and the singular values of A.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Right-hand side perturbation. Subtract Ax = b from A(x + δx) = b + δb. We get Aδx = δb, so δx = A⁻¹δb and ‖δx‖ ≤ ‖A⁻¹‖‖δb‖.
Relative form. From b = Ax we get ‖b‖ ≤ ‖A‖‖x‖, so 1/‖x‖ ≤ ‖A‖/‖b‖. Multiply: ‖δx‖/‖x‖ ≤ ‖A‖‖A⁻¹‖·‖δb‖/‖b‖. This proves (a).
Invertibility. Write A + δA = A(I + B) with B = A⁻¹δA. Then ‖B‖ ≤ ‖A⁻¹‖‖δA‖ = κ(A)ε < 1. The Neumann series gives that I + B is invertible and ‖(I + B)⁻¹‖ ≤ ∑‖B‖^j = 1/(1 − ‖B‖).
Bound for the inverse. (A + δA)⁻¹ = (I + B)⁻¹A⁻¹, so ‖(A + δA)⁻¹‖ ≤ ‖A⁻¹‖/(1 − κ(A)ε).
Perturbed matrix. Subtract Ax = b from (A + δA)(x + δx) = b. We get (A + δA)δx = −δA·x. So ‖δx‖ ≤ ‖A⁻¹‖‖δA‖‖x‖/(1 − κ(A)ε).
Divide by ‖x‖ and use ‖A⁻¹‖‖δA‖ = κ(A)ε. We get ‖δx‖/‖x‖ ≤ κ(A)ε/(1 − κ(A)ε). This proves (b).

Singular value set-up. Let A v_i = σ_i u_i with orthonormal v_i and u_i and σ_1 ≥ … ≥ σ_n > 0, as in the singular value decomposition. Then ‖A‖₂ = σ_1 and A⁻¹u_i = v_i/σ_i, so ‖A⁻¹‖₂ = 1/σ_n and κ₂ = σ_1/σ_n.

Sharpness of (a). Take x = v_1 and b = σ_1u_1. Take δb = t·u_n for a number t > 0. Then δx = A⁻¹δb = t·v_n/σ_n. So ‖δx‖/‖x‖ = t/σ_n and ‖δb‖/‖b‖ = t/σ_1. The ratio is σ_1/σ_n = κ₂, so (a) is an equality. This proves (c).
Lower bound in (d). If ‖δA‖₂ < ‖A⁻¹‖₂⁻¹ = σ_n, then ‖A⁻¹δA‖ < 1, and step 3 shows that A + δA is invertible. So a singular A + δA needs ‖δA‖₂ ≥ σ_n, that is ‖δA‖₂/‖A‖₂ ≥ σ_n/σ_1 = 1/κ₂.

Attainment in (d). Put δA = −σ_n u_n v_nᵀ. Then ‖δA‖₂ = σ_n, and (A + δA)v_n = σ_n u_n − σ_n u_n(v_nᵀv_n) = 0. So A + δA has a non-zero kernel vector and is singular, with relative size exactly 1/κ₂. This proves (d).

steps.text: The condition number is κ₂ = 2.00005/4.99987e-05 = 40002.0. Also ‖A‖₂ = 2.00005 and ‖A⁻¹‖₂ = 20000.5.

Right side. Take δb = (0, 1e-4). Then x + δx = (0, 2), so δx = (−1, 1). The relative error ‖δx‖/‖x‖ is 1. The relative size of δb is 3.5355e-5. The bound (a) is 40002·3.5355e-5 = 1.4142. So 1 ≤ 1.4142 holds.
Matrix. Take δA = diag(0, −1e-5). Then ε = 5.0e-6 and κε = 0.2000 < 1. The perturbed solution is x′ = (8/9, 10/9), so ‖δx‖/‖x‖ = 1/9 = 0.111. The bound (b) is 0.2/0.8 = 0.25. So 0.111 ≤ 0.25 holds.

Singularity. The matrix δA = diag(0, −1e-4) makes A + δA singular. Its relative size is 5.0e-5. The minimum from (d) is 1/κ₂ = 2.5e-5. The SVD matrix −σ_n u_n v_nᵀ has relative size 2.4999e-5 and determinant 0 up to rounding.

limitations: The bounds are worst-case over all perturbations. A particular perturbation can give a much smaller error.
The condition number depends on the chosen norm. Different norms give condition numbers that differ by a factor that depends only on n.
Part (b) does not cover errors in both A and b together. A combined bound needs one more step.

results.name: Root bounds: the Cauchy, sum, Fujiwara and reciprocal bounds
results.statement: Let p(z) = z^n + a_{n−1}z^{n−1} + … + a_0 be a monic complex polynomial with n ≥ 1. Put a_n = 1. Let ζ be a root of p. Then: (i) Cauchy: |ζ| < 1 + max_{0≤k≤n−1}|a_k|. (iv) Lower bound: if a_0 ≠ 0, then |ζ| > 1/(1 + max_{1≤k≤n}|a_k|/|a_0|).

steps.text: Set-up. Let ζ be a root and r = |ζ|. From p(ζ) = 0 we get ζ^n = −∑_{k=0}^{n−1} a_kζ^k. So r^n ≤ ∑_{k=0}^{n−1}|a_k|r^k. All bounds follow from this inequality.

Cauchy. Let α = max|a_k|. If α = 0, then p = z^n and r = 0 < 1. Let α > 0. If r ≤ 1, then r ≤ 1 < 1 + α. Let r > 1. Then r^n ≤ α∑_{k<n}r^k = α(r^n − 1)/(r − 1) < αr^n/(r − 1). Divide by r^n to get r − 1 < α. This proves (i).
Sum bound. Let r > 1. Then r^k ≤ r^{n−1} for k ≤ n − 1. So r^n ≤ r^{n−1}∑|a_k|. Divide by r^{n−1} to get r ≤ ∑|a_k|. If r ≤ 1, then r ≤ 1. In both cases r ≤ max(1, ∑|a_k|). This proves (ii).

Fujiwara, set-up. Let B = max(|a_{n−k}|^{1/k} for 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1, and |a_0/2|^{1/n}). Then |a_{n−k}| ≤ B^k for 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1 and |a_0| ≤ 2B^n. If B = 0, then p = z^n and r = 0, and (iii) holds. Let B > 0 and r > 0.

Fujiwara, inequality. Use the set-up inequality with |a_{n−k}| ≤ B^k and |a_0| ≤ 2B^n, and divide by r^n. With t = B/r we get 1 ≤ ∑_{k=1}^{n−1}t^k + 2t^n. Suppose t < 1/2. Then t < 1 and the right side equals (t + t^n − 2t^{n+1})/(1 − t).

Fujiwara, contradiction. The condition (t + t^n − 2t^{n+1})/(1 − t) ≥ 1 is equivalent to 2t − 1 + t^n(1 − 2t) ≥ 0. This is (2t − 1)(1 − t^n) ≥ 0. For t < 1/2 the factor 2t − 1 is negative and 1 − t^n is positive, so this fails. Hence t ≥ 1/2, that is r ≤ 2B. This proves (iii).

Reciprocal. Let a_0 ≠ 0 and let ζ be a root. Then ζ ≠ 0. The number w = 1/ζ is a root of q(w) = w^n + (a_1/a_0)w^{n−1} + … + (a_{n−1}/a_0)w + 1/a_0. This q is monic. Its coefficients are a_j/a_0 for 1 ≤ j ≤ n, with a_n = 1.
Apply Cauchy to q. We get 1/|ζ| < 1 + max_{1≤j≤n}|a_j|/|a_0|. Take the inverse of both positive sides. This proves (iv).

results.name: De la Vallée Poussin lower bound and equioscillation uniqueness
results.statement: Let f be continuous on [a, b]. Let n ≥ 0. Let p be a real polynomial of degree at most n. Put e = f − p. Let a ≤ t_0 < t_1 < … < t_{n+1} ≤ b be n + 2 points. (a) Lower bound: if e(t_i) ≠ 0 and the signs of e(t_i) alternate, then every real polynomial q of degree at most n satisfies max_{[a,b]}|f − q| ≥ min_i|e(t_i)|. (b) Sufficiency and uniqueness: if the signs of e(t_i) alternate and |e(t_i)| = max_{[a,b]}|e| for all i, then p is a best uniform approximation of f among polynomials of degree at most n, and it is the only one.
hypotheses: f is real and continuous on the closed interval [a, b].
p and q are real polynomials of degree at most n.
The points t_0 < … < t_{n+1} are n + 2 distinct points of [a, b].

prerequisites.reason: Step 2 uses unique interpolation at n + 2 nodes and the Lagrange formula.

definitions.name: equioscillation
definitions.text: The error e = f − p has n + 2 points where it takes the values +E, −E, +E, … in turn, with E = max|e|.

definitions.name: best uniform approximation
definitions.text: A polynomial p of degree at most n that minimises max|f − p| over [a, b].

definitions.name: divided difference
definitions.text: For nodes t_0, …, t_{n+1}, the sum ∑ r(t_i)/w′(t_i) with w(x) = ∏(x − t_j). It is the leading coefficient of the interpolating polynomial of degree n + 1.

source.alignment: The source bounds the number of distinct roots of a non-zero polynomial by its degree. This gives the final step of the uniqueness proof.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Node weights. Let w(x) = ∏_{j=0}^{n+1}(x − t_j) and w_i = w′(t_i) = ∏_{j≠i}(t_i − t_j). Exactly n + 1 − i factors t_i − t_j are negative, namely those with j > i. So sign(w_i) = (−1)^{n+1−i}.

Divided difference identity. Let r be a real polynomial with deg r ≤ n. The interpolating polynomial of degree at most n + 1 at the n + 2 nodes is unique, by the Vandermonde determinant. By Lagrange, it is ∑ r(t_i)∏_{j≠i}(x − t_j)/w_i. The polynomial r itself interpolates, so r equals this sum. The coefficient of x^{n+1} on the right is ∑ r(t_i)/w_i. On the left it is 0. Hence ∑_i r(t_i)/w_i = 0.
Proof of (a), set-up. Suppose some q with deg q ≤ n has max|f − q| < λ = min|e(t_i)|. Let s be the sign of e(t_0), so sign e(t_i) = s(−1)^i. Put r = p − q. Then r has degree at most n.
Sign of r. Write r = (f − q) − e. At each t_i we have |(f − q)(t_i)| < λ ≤ |e(t_i)|. So r(t_i) has the sign of −e(t_i), which is −s(−1)^i. It is non-zero.

Contradiction for (a). The product r(t_i)/w_i has sign −s(−1)^i(−1)^{n+1−i} = −s(−1)^{n+1}. This sign does not depend on i, and each term is non-zero. So the sum ∑ r(t_i)/w_i is non-zero. This contradicts the identity of step 2. Hence no such q exists, and (a) holds.
Best approximation in (b). Let E = max|e|. Then |e(t_i)| = E for all i. Part (a) gives max|f − q| ≥ E = max|f − p| for all q. So p is a best approximation.

Uniqueness in (b), set-up. Let q be another best approximation, so max|f − q| = E. Put r = p − q = (f − q) − e. At t_i, we have (f − q)(t_i) in [−E, E] and e(t_i) = s(−1)^iE. So s(−1)^i·r(t_i) = s(−1)^i(f − q)(t_i) − E ≤ 0.
Uniqueness, signs. Since sign(w_i) = (−1)^{n+1−i}, we have s(−1)^{n+1}·r(t_i)/w_i = s(−1)^i·r(t_i)/|w_i|. By the last step this is at most 0. So all the terms r(t_i)/w_i have the same weak sign.
Uniqueness, conclusion. The sum of these terms is 0 by the identity of step 2. A sum of terms that are all at most 0 and add to 0 has every term 0. So r(t_i) = 0 for all n + 2 nodes.
A non-zero polynomial of degree at most n has at most n roots. Here r has n + 2 distinct roots. So r = 0 and q = p. This proves uniqueness.

worked_application.title: Best linear approximation of exp on [0, 1]
worked_application.goal: Find the best polynomial of degree at most 1 for f(x) = e^x on [0, 1] and give a lower bound from a rough guess.
hypotheses: f(x) = e^x, n = 1, so we need n + 2 = 3 points.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The function e^x is convex, so e^x − p(x) is convex for each linear p. It has its maximum at the end points and its minimum where the derivative is 0.

steps.text: Try p(x) = m·x + (1 + m − m·c)/2 = 1.718282x + 0.894067. The error e = e^x − p is convex, with e′(x) = e^x − m. So e′ = 0 at x = c, and the minimum is at c.

The maximum of |e| is 0.105933. It is attained at 0, c and 1 with signs +, −, +. So the three nodes 0 < c < 1 equioscillate. Part (b) gives that p is the unique best linear approximation, with error 0.105933.

Lower bound from a rough guess. Take p₀(x) = 1.7x + 0.9. Its errors at 0, c, 1 are 0.1000, −0.1020, 0.1183. The signs alternate, and the least size is 0.1000. Part (a) gives max|e^x − q| ≥ 0.1 for every linear q. The true value 0.10593 is above it.
The chord 1 + m·x through the end points has maximal error 2·0.105933 = 0.21187, which is twice the best error.

worked_application.result: The best linear approximation of e^x on [0, 1] is 1.718282x + 0.894067. Its maximum error is 0.105933, and it is unique.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Only sufficiency and uniqueness are proved. The converse is true: a best approximation equioscillates at n + 2 points. This entry does not prove it, and it does not prove that a best approximation exists.
The alternation is for polynomials. For other Haar spaces the same proof works with a different weight identity. This entry does not treat them.
The theorem does not give an algorithm. The Remez algorithm finds the nodes, and it is not described here.

results.name: Peano kernel: the exact error of Simpson's rule
results.statement: Let h > 0 and let f be of class C⁴ on [−h, h]. Put S(f) = (h/3)(f(−h) + 4f(0) + f(h)) and R(f) = ∫_{−h}^{h} f(x)dx − S(f). Define K(t) = −(h − |t|)³(h + 3|t|)/72 for |t| ≤ h. Then (1) R(f) = ∫_{−h}^{h} K(t)f⁗(t)dt. (2) K is even, continuous and K ≤ 0, with ∫K = −h⁵/90. (3) There is ξ in (−h, h) with R(f) = −(h⁵/90)f⁗(ξ). (4) Hence if m ≤ f⁗ ≤ M on [−h, h], then −Mh⁵/90 ≤ R(f) ≤ −mh⁵/90.

/-- **Taylor's theorem** with the Integral form of the remainder.

We assume that `f` is `n`-times continuously differentiable on the closed set `uIcc x₀ x` and
its `n`-th derivative is absolutely continuous on `uIcc x₀ x`. Then
$$f(x) - (P_n f)(x₀, x) = \int_{x_0}^x \frac{f^{(n+1)}(t) (x - t)^n}{n!} dt,$$
where $P_n f$ denotes the Taylor polynomial of degree $n$ and $f^{(n+1)}$ is the $n+1$-th iterated
derivative. -/
theorem taylor_integral_remainder_of_absolutelyContinuous {f : ℝ → ℝ} {x x₀ : ℝ} {n : ℕ}
    (hf₁ : ContDiffOn ℝ n f (uIcc x₀ x))
    (hf₂ : AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval (iteratedDerivWithin n f (uIcc x₀ x)) x₀ x) :
    f x - taylorWithinEval f n (uIcc x₀ x) x₀ x =
      ∫ t in x₀..x, ((x - t) ^ n / n !) * iteratedDerivWithin (n + 1) f (uIcc x₀ x) t := by
  rcases eq_or_ne x₀ x with rfl | this
  · simp
  apply taylor_integral_remainder_aux
  intro k hk
  apply AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval.integral_mul_deriv_eq_deriv_mul
  · apply ContDiffOn.absolutelyContinuousOnInterval
    fun_prop
  · rcases hk.eq_or_lt with rfl | hk
    · exact hf₂
    replace hf₁ := hf₁.of_le (m := k.succ) (by norm_cast)
    grind [ContDiffOn.absolutelyContinuousOnInterval, uniqueDiffOn_uIcc,
      contDiffOn_nat_succ_iff_contDiffOn_one_iteratedDerivWithin]

source.alignment: The source proves Taylor's theorem with the integral form of the remainder. This is step 2 of the proof. The entry adds the kernel computation and the sign argument.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Exactness on cubics. R is linear. For f = 1 we get 2h − (h/3)·6 = 0. For f = x² we get 2h³/3 − (h/3)·2h² = 0. For f = x and f = x³ both the integral and S are 0 by symmetry. So R(f) = 0 for every polynomial of degree at most 3.

Taylor with integral remainder. Expand f at 0 to order 3: f(x) = T(x) + ∫_0^x (x − t)³f⁗(t)/6 dt, with T a cubic. For x ≥ 0 the integral is ∫_0^h G(x, t)f⁗(t)dt with G(x, t) = (x − t)₊³/6 for t ≥ 0. For x < 0 the integral equals ∫_x^0 (t − x)³f⁗(t)/6 dt, because reversing the limits and the sign of (x − t)³ cancel. So with G(x, t) = (t − x)₊³/6 for t ≤ 0, we get f(x) = T(x) + ∫_{−h}^h G(x, t)f⁗(t)dt for all x in [−h, h].

Apply R. R kills T. The kernel G is continuous in (x, t) except at x = t, and bounded, and f⁗ is continuous. So the integrals commute: R(f) = ∫_{−h}^h K(t)f⁗(t)dt with K(t) = R_x[G(x, t)], where R acts on the variable x.
Compute K for t ≥ 0. Here G(x, t) = (x − t)₊³/6. Then G(−h, t) = 0 and G(0, t) = 0 for t > 0, and G(h, t) = (h − t)³/6. The integral ∫_{−h}^h G dx = ∫_t^h (x − t)³/6 dx = (h − t)⁴/24.

So K(t) = (h − t)⁴/24 − (h/3)(h − t)³/6 = (h − t)³[(h − t)/24 − h/18] = (h − t)³(−h − 3t)/72 = −(h − t)³(h + 3t)/72. For t < 0 the same computation with x replaced by −x gives K(t) = K(−t). So K is even, and (1) is proved.

Sign and integral. For |t| ≤ h both h − |t| and h + 3|t| are non-negative, so K ≤ 0 and K is continuous. With u = h − t, ∫_0^h (h − t)³(h + 3t)dt = ∫_0^h u³(4h − 3u)du = h⁵ − 3h⁵/5 = 2h⁵/5. So ∫K = 2·(−1/72)·(2h⁵/5) = −h⁵/90. This proves (2).

Mean value. K is continuous and K < 0 on (−h, h). So ∫K f⁗/∫K is a weighted average of f⁗ with positive weight. If f⁗ is constant, every ξ works. Otherwise the average lies strictly between the minimum and the maximum of f⁗. The intermediate value theorem gives an interior point ξ with f⁗(ξ) equal to the average. So R(f) = −(h⁵/90)f⁗(ξ). This proves (3).
Bounds. Since K ≤ 0, m ≤ f⁗ ≤ M gives M·K ≤ K f⁗ ≤ m·K. Integrate to get (4).

worked_application.title: Simpson error for exp on [0, 2]
worked_application.goal: Compute the exact Simpson error for e^x on [0, 2] and compare it with the Peano bounds.
hypotheses: Centre the interval at 1 so that h = 1 and f⁗(x) = e^x.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: e^x is C⁴ on the interval, so (1) to (4) apply with h = 1 after the shift x → x − 1.

steps.text: Simpson value: S = (1/3)(1 + 4e + e²) = 6.420728. The exact integral is I = e² − 1 = 6.389056. So R = I − S = −0.031672.
Peano bounds. Since ∫K = −1/90 for h = 1, part (4) with m = 1 and M = e² gives −e²/90 ≤ R ≤ −1/90, that is −0.08210 ≤ R ≤ −0.01111. The value −0.031672 lies in this range.
The point ξ of (3) solves e^ξ = 90·0.031672 = 2.8505. So ξ = 1.0475, which lies in (0, 2).
The sign is negative, so Simpson's rule over-estimates e^x here. This agrees with K ≤ 0 and f⁗ > 0.

worked_application.result: The exact Simpson error is −0.031672. It lies between the Peano bounds −0.0821 and −0.0111, and it equals −(1/90)e^ξ for ξ = 1.0475.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The proof is for Simpson's rule on one panel. Composite rules need the sum of the panel errors.
The formula needs f of class C⁴. A weaker smoothness gives a coarser kernel and a lower order.
The method needs a linear functional that vanishes on a polynomial space. For other rules the kernel can change sign, and then only an L¹ bound holds.

results.name: Layer cake formula: an integral from the measures of the level sets
results.statement: Let (Ω,F,μ) be a σ-finite measure space and f:Ω→[0,∞) a measurable function. Let g:[0,∞)→[0,∞) be measurable and integrable on [0,t] for every t>0. Put G(x)=∫₀ˣ g(t)dt. Then ∫_Ω G(f)dμ=∫₀^∞ μ({f>t})g(t)dt, as an equality in [0,∞]. (a) For g=1, ∫f dμ=∫₀^∞ μ({f>t})dt. (b) For p>0 and g(t)=p·t^{p−1}, ∫f^p dμ=p∫₀^∞ t^{p−1}μ({f>t})dt. (c) If N is a random variable with values in {0,1,2,…}, then E[N]=∑_{k≥0}P(N>k)=∑_{k≥1}P(N≥k).
hypotheses: The measure μ is σ-finite. This is needed to use the Tonelli theorem.
The function f is measurable and finite everywhere. Both sides can be +∞.
The function g is nonnegative and locally integrable on [0,∞). A singularity like t^{p−1} with 0<p<1 is allowed.
No integrability of f is assumed.

/-- The layer cake formula / Cavalieri's principle / tail probability formula:

Let `f` be a non-negative measurable function on a measure space. Let `G` be an
increasing absolutely continuous function on the positive real line, vanishing at the origin,
with derivative `G' = g`. Then the integral of the composition `G ∘ f` can be written as
the integral over the positive real line of the "tail measures" `μ {ω | f(ω) > t}` of `f`
weighted by `g`.

Roughly speaking, the statement is: `∫⁻ (G ∘ f) ∂μ = ∫⁻ t in 0..∞, g(t) * μ {ω | f(ω) > t}`.

See `lintegral_comp_eq_lintegral_meas_le_mul` for a version with sets of the form `{ω | f(ω) ≥ t}`
instead. -/
theorem lintegral_comp_eq_lintegral_meas_lt_mul (μ : Measure α) (f_nn : 0 ≤ᵐ[μ] f)
    (f_mble : AEMeasurable f μ) (g_intble : ∀ t > 0, IntervalIntegrable g volume 0 t)
    (g_nn : ∀ᵐ t ∂volume.restrict (Ioi 0), 0 ≤ g t) :
    ∫⁻ ω, ENNReal.ofReal (∫ t in 0..f ω, g t) ∂μ =
      ∫⁻ t in Ioi 0, μ {a : α | t < f a} * ENNReal.ofReal (g t) := by
  rw [lintegral_comp_eq_lintegral_meas_le_mul μ f_nn f_mble g_intble g_nn]
  apply lintegral_congr_ae
  filter_upwards [meas_le_ae_eq_meas_lt μ (volume.restrict (Ioi 0)) f]
    with t ht
  rw [ht]

/-- The standard case of the layer cake formula / Cavalieri's principle / tail probability formula:

For an integrable a.e.-nonnegative real-valued function `f`, the Bochner integral of `f` can be
written (roughly speaking) as: `∫ f ∂μ = ∫ t in 0..∞, μ {ω | f(ω) > t}`.

See `MeasureTheory.lintegral_eq_lintegral_meas_lt` for a version with Lebesgue integral `∫⁻`
instead. -/
theorem Integrable.integral_eq_integral_meas_lt
    (f_intble : Integrable f μ) (f_nn : 0 ≤ᵐ[μ] f) :
    ∫ ω, f ω ∂μ = ∫ t in Set.Ioi 0, μ.real {a : α | t < f a} := by
  have key := lintegral_eq_lintegral_meas_lt μ f_nn f_intble.aemeasurable
  have lhs_finite : ∫⁻ (ω : α), ENNReal.ofReal (f ω) ∂μ < ∞ := Integrable.lintegral_lt_top f_intble
  have rhs_finite : ∫⁻ (t : ℝ) in Set.Ioi 0, μ {a | t < f a} < ∞ := by simp only [← key, lhs_finite]
  have rhs_integrand_finite : ∀ (t : ℝ), t > 0 → μ {a | t < f a} < ∞ :=
    fun t ht ↦ measure_gt_lt_top f_intble ht
  convert (ENNReal.toReal_eq_toReal_iff' lhs_finite.ne rhs_finite.ne).mpr key
  · exact integral_eq_lintegral_of_nonneg_ae f_nn f_intble.aestronglyMeasurable
  · have aux := @integral_eq_lintegral_of_nonneg_ae _ _ ((volume : Measure ℝ).restrict (Set.Ioi 0))

steps.text: Layer representation of G. For every x in [0,∞), G(x)=∫₀^∞ 1{t<x}g(t)dt, because the indicator cuts the integration range to (0,x). Apply this with x=f(ω). Then G(f(ω))=∫_(0,∞)1{t<f(ω)}g(t)dt for each ω.
The measure ν. Let ν(dt)=g(t)dt on (0,∞). Since g is integrable on each interval (0,n], ν((0,n])<∞. So ν is σ-finite. The product measure μ⊗ν exists and is unique.

The set A. Let A={(ω,t)∈Ω×(0,∞): t<f(ω)}. The map (ω,t)↦f(ω)−t is measurable for the product σ-algebra, because it is a difference of two maps that each depend on one coordinate and are measurable. So A={f(ω)−t>0} is measurable.

Tonelli in both orders. The function 1_A is nonnegative and measurable, and both measures are σ-finite. So the Tonelli theorem gives ∫_Ω ν(A_ω)dμ(ω)=(μ⊗ν)(A)=∫_(0,∞) μ(A^t)dν(t). Here A_ω is the section at ω and A^t is the section at t. No integrability is needed, and the equality holds in [0,∞].

Compute the sections. The section A_ω is the interval (0,f(ω)). So ν(A_ω)=∫₀^{f(ω)}g(t)dt=G(f(ω)). The section A^t is the set {ω: f(ω)>t}. So μ(A^t)=μ({f>t}) and ∫μ(A^t)dν(t)=∫₀^∞ μ({f>t})g(t)dt. The two orders give the main identity.
Special cases (a) and (b). For g=1 we have G(x)=x. For g(t)=pt^{p−1} we have G(x)=x^p, and g is locally integrable for every p>0. The identity then gives (a) and (b).

The integer case (c). Apply (a) to f=N and μ=P. For t in [k,k+1) and N integer-valued, N>t holds if and only if N≥k+1. So P(N>t)=P(N>k) on this interval, which has length 1. Hence ∫₀^∞P(N>t)dt=∑_{k≥0}P(N>k). Also P(N>k)=P(N≥k+1), so the sum equals ∑_{k≥1}P(N≥k).

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Fourier uniqueness. Let f be in L²(𝕋) with f̂(n)=0 for all n≠0. By the Parseval identity ‖f−f̂(0)‖²=∑_{n≠0}|f̂(n)|²=0. So f equals the constant f̂(0) almost everywhere. We use this in all later cases.

Reduction. Let T be R_α or D_m and let A be measurable with T⁻¹A=A. Then f=1_A satisfies f∘T=f everywhere. If f is a.e. constant, then 1_A is a.e. 0 or a.e. 1, so λ(A)∈{0,1}. So it suffices to show that f is a.e. constant.

Measure preservation. The measure λ is translation invariant, so R_α preserves it. For D_m and an interval I=[a,b)⊂[0,1), the preimage D_m⁻¹(I) is a union of |m| intervals, each of length (b−a)/|m|. So λ(D_m⁻¹I)=λ(I). Intervals form a π-system that generates the Borel σ-algebra, so λ∘D_m⁻¹=λ.

Irrational rotation. The substitution x↦x−α gives the coefficient of f∘R_α at n as e^{2πinα}f̂(n). The identity f∘R_α=f gives (e^{2πinα}−1)f̂(n)=0. If α is irrational, then e^{2πinα}≠1 for n≠0, so f̂(n)=0 for n≠0. By step 1, f is a.e. constant.

Rational rotation is not ergodic. Let α=p/q with q≥1. Put A=⋃_{k=0}^{q−1}[k/q, k/q+1/(2q)) in 𝕋. The map R_α sends the k-th interval to the interval with index k+p mod q, which is a permutation of the q intervals. So R_α⁻¹A=A. Also λ(A)=q·1/(2q)=1/2. So R_α is not ergodic. This completes (a).

Coefficients for the doubling map. Let U f=f∘D_m. This is an isometry of L² by step 3, and U e_n=e_{mn}. For f=∑f̂(n)e_n in L², continuity of U gives Uf=∑f̂(n)e_{mn}. The map n↦mn is injective, so the coefficient of Uf at k is f̂(k/m) if m divides k, and 0 otherwise. The identity Uf=f gives f̂(mn)=f̂(n) for all n.

Decay. Fix n≠0. Applying step 6 j times gives f̂(n)=f̂(mʲn) for all j≥0. The integers mʲn have absolute value |m|ʲ|n|, which strictly increases with j. So they are pairwise distinct. By the Bessel inequality ∑_k|f̂(k)|²<∞, hence f̂(mʲn)→0. Therefore f̂(n)=0 for all n≠0.
Conclusion for D_m. By step 1, f is a.e. constant, and by step 2, λ(A)∈{0,1}. So D_m is ergodic. This completes (b).

hypotheses: α=(√5−1)/2 is irrational. f(x)=cos 2πx has ∫f dλ=0.
For the contrast case, α=1/3 and f(x)=cos 6πx.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: By part (a) the golden rotation is ergodic, so the mean ergodic theorem predicts ‖A_N f‖₂→0. The rational rotation is not ergodic by part (a), and no such limit is guaranteed.

steps.text: Fourier form. f=(e₁+e_{−1})/2, so A_N f=(D_N e₁+conj(D_N)e_{−1})/2 with D_N=(1/N)∑_{k<N}e^{2πikα}. The functions e₁ and e_{−1} are orthonormal. Hence ‖A_N f‖²=|D_N|²/2. The mean ergodic theorem predicts that this tends to 0 when the rotation is ergodic.
Geometric sum. |D_N|=|sin(πNα)|/(N|sin(πα)|). So ‖A_N f‖²=sin²(πNα)/(2N²sin²(πα)). Since sin²(πα)=0.868684..., this is at most 0.575583/N².

Numerical check. For N=10 the formula gives 0.0016581222682. A direct average over a grid of 4000 points of x gives 0.0016581222682. For N=89 the formula gives 1.8107710033×10⁻⁸ and the grid gives the same value to 10 digits. For N=100 the value is 1.9303456095×10⁻⁵.

Rational contrast. For α=1/3 and f(x)=cos 6πx we have f(x+1/3)=cos(6πx+2π)=f(x). So A_N f=f for all N and ‖A_N f‖²=1/2 for every N. The averages do not tend to ∫f=0, which agrees with the non-ergodicity of R_{1/3}.

results.name: Ergodic measures are exactly the extreme points of the invariant probability measures
results.statement: Let (X,𝔄) be a measurable space and f:X→X measurable. Let M(f) be the convex set of probability measures ν on 𝔄 with ν∘f⁻¹=ν. Let μ be in M(f). source.alignment: The source proves the equivalence for a measure preserving f and a probability measure μ. It uses the extreme points of the set of invariant probability measures.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Extreme implies ergodic, by contraposition. Suppose A is measurable, f⁻¹A=A and 0<μ(A)<1. Define ν₁=μ(·∩A)/μ(A) and ν₂=μ(·∩Aᶜ)/μ(Aᶜ). These are probability measures.
Invariance of ν₁ and ν₂. Since f⁻¹A=A, f⁻¹B∩A=f⁻¹(B∩A) for every measurable B. So ν₁(f⁻¹B)=μ(f⁻¹(B∩A))/μ(A)=μ(B∩A)/μ(A)=ν₁(B), using μ∘f⁻¹=μ. The same holds for ν₂ with Aᶜ. So ν₁,ν₂ are in M(f).
Non-extremality. We have μ=μ(A)ν₁+μ(Aᶜ)ν₂ with 0<μ(A)<1. But ν₁(A)=1 and ν₂(A)=0, so ν₁≠ν₂. So μ is not extreme. This proves: extreme implies ergodic.

Ergodic implies extreme: a bounded density. Let μ=tν₁+(1−t)ν₂ with ν₁,ν₂ in M(f) and 0<t<1. Then ν₁(B)≤μ(B)/t for all B, so ν₁≪μ. By the Radon–Nikodym theorem there is a measurable h with ν₁=hμ, and 0≤h≤1/t after a change on a μ-null set. We show h=1.

The density is invariant. For every bounded measurable g, ∫(g∘f)h dμ=∫g∘f dν₁=∫g dν₁=∫g h dμ, using ν₁∘f⁻¹=ν₁. Take g=h. Then ∫(h∘f)h dμ=∫h²dμ. Also ∫(h∘f)²dμ=∫h²dμ, because μ∘f⁻¹=μ. Therefore ∫(h∘f−h)²dμ=∫(h∘f)²−2∫(h∘f)h+∫h²=0. So h∘f=h μ-a.e.
Level sets are almost invariant. For c in ℝ let E_c={h>c}. Then f⁻¹E_c={h∘f>c}. Because h∘f=h a.e., μ(f⁻¹E_c△E_c)=0.

Almost invariant sets are a.e. equal to invariant sets. Let E have μ(f⁻¹E△E)=0. Since μ∘f⁻¹=μ, μ(f⁻ⁿE△f⁻⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾E)=0 for every n, so μ(f⁻ⁿE△E)=0. Put E′=⋂_N⋃_{n≥N}f⁻ⁿE. Then f⁻¹E′=⋂_N⋃_{n≥N+1}f⁻ⁿE=E′ because the unions decrease. Also each union ⋃_{n≥N}f⁻ⁿE equals E up to a null set, so μ(E′△E)=0.

Constant density. By steps 6 and 7 each E_c equals a strictly invariant set up to a null set. Ergodicity gives μ(E_c)∈{0,1} for all c. So h is a.e. equal to the constant k=sup{c: μ(E_c)=1}. Then 1=ν₁(X)=∫h dμ=k. Hence ν₁=μ. Finally ν₂=(μ−tν₁)/(1−t)=μ, so μ is extreme.

worked_application.title: Invariant measures of the doubling map on nine points, and a non-ergodic mixture
worked_application.goal: List all invariant probability measures of x↦2x mod 1 that live on a nine point set, and identify the ergodic ones.
hypotheses: Use exact fractions for all calculations.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: T maps X into X, so T restricted to X is a measurable self-map of a finite set. The theorem applies with M(T) the set of invariant probability vectors on X.

steps.text: The orbits. T fixes 0, swaps 1/3 and 2/3, cycles 1/7→2/7→4/7→1/7, and cycles 3/7→6/7→5/7→3/7. So X is a disjoint union of four cycles of lengths 1, 2, 3 and 3.

Invariance equations. A vector p is invariant when p(y)=∑_{Tx=y}p(x). In X each point has exactly one preimage in X, so the equation says p(Tx)=p(x). Thus p is constant on each cycle. A computation of the rank of the 9×9 matrix of T_*−I gives rank 5, so the solution space has dimension 4.

The extreme points. M(T) is the set of probability vectors constant on the four cycles. This is a simplex with 4 vertices, the uniform measures ν₁=δ₀, ν₂ on {1/3,2/3}, ν₃ on {1/7,2/7,4/7} and ν₄ on {3/7,6/7,5/7}. These are the only extreme points.

Check with the theorem. A strictly invariant set A⊂X is a union of cycles, so ν_i(A)∈{0,1}. So each ν_i is ergodic. A mixture such as μ=½ν₂+½ν₃ has the invariant set A={1/3,2/3} with μ(A)=1/2. So it is not ergodic and not extreme, as the theorem says.

On the whole circle. Let λ be the Lebesgue measure. Then ½δ₀+½λ is an invariant probability measure for T(x)=2x mod 1, because both δ₀ and λ are invariant. The set D of dyadic rationals in [0,1) satisfies T⁻¹D=D, because x is dyadic if and only if 2x mod 1 is dyadic. Also μ(D)=½·1+½·0=½. So this mixture is not ergodic and not extreme, as the theorem says.

worked_application.result: M(T) on the nine points is a 3-simplex with four ergodic vertices. A mixture of two vertices has an invariant set of measure ½ and is not ergodic.

The theorem does not say that M(f) is nonempty. Existence needs a topological assumption such as compactness.

results.name: Chain rule for relative entropy of joint laws
results.statement: Let X and Y be finite sets. Let μ,ν be probability vectors on X. For each x let κ(·|x) and η(·|x) be probability vectors on Y. Put P(x,y)=μ(x)κ(y|x) and Q(x,y)=ν(x)η(y|x). Write D(p‖q)=∑ p log(p/q) in nats, with D=+∞ when p is not absolutely continuous with respect to q. Then D(P‖Q)=D(μ‖ν)+∑_x μ(x)D(κ(·|x)‖η(·|x)), as an equality in [0,∞]. In particular D(P‖Q)≥D(μ‖ν), and D(P‖Q)≥D(P_Y‖Q_Y) for the second marginals. Equality D(P‖Q)=D(μ‖ν) holds if and only if κ(·|x)=η(·|x) for every x with μ(x)>0.
hypotheses: X and Y are finite. The same proof works for standard Borel spaces with kernels.
The convention 0·log(0/q)=0 holds. Also p·log(p/0)=+∞ for p>0.

/-- **Chain rule** for the Kullback-Leibler divergence, with conditional KL expressed using
composition-products.
This version holds without any assumption on the measurable spaces. -/
theorem klDiv_compProd_eq_add : klDiv (μ ⊗ₘ κ) (ν ⊗ₘ η) = klDiv μ ν + klDiv (μ ⊗ₘ κ) (μ ⊗ₘ η) := by
  -- first, if we don't have absolute continuity, both sides are `∞`
  by_cases h_ac : μ ⊗ₘ κ ≪ ν ⊗ₘ η
  swap
  · rw [klDiv_of_not_ac h_ac]
    rw [Measure.absolutelyContinuous_compProd_iff] at h_ac
    simp only [not_and_or] at h_ac
    cases h_ac with
    | inl h => simp [h]
    | inr h => simp [h]
  -- same if we don't have integrability
  by_cases h_int : Integrable (llr (μ ⊗ₘ κ) (ν ⊗ₘ η)) (μ ⊗ₘ κ)
  swap
  · rw [klDiv_of_not_integrable h_int]
    rw [integrable_llr_compProd_iff h_ac] at h_int
    simp only [not_and_or] at h_int
    cases h_int with
    | inl h => simp [h]
    | inr h => simp [h]
  -- now we can use express the KL divergences with an integral of a log-likelihood ratio
  have ⟨h_ac_μν, h_ac_κη⟩ := Measure.absolutelyContinuous_compProd_iff.mp h_ac
  have ⟨h_int_μν, h_int_κη⟩ := (integrable_llr_compProd_iff h_ac).mp h_int
  simp_rw [klDiv_of_ac_of_integrable h_ac h_int, klDiv_of_ac_of_integrable h_ac_μν h_int_μν,
    klDiv_of_ac_of_integrable h_ac_κη h_int_κη,
    ← ENNReal.ofReal_add (integral_llr_add_sub_measure_univ_nonneg h_ac_μν h_int_μν)

steps.text: Absolute continuity. Suppose P≪Q. Take x with μ(x)>0. Choose y with κ(y|x)>0. Then P(x,y)>0, so Q(x,y)=ν(x)η(y|x)>0. Hence ν(x)>0 and η(y|x)>0. This shows μ≪ν and κ(·|x)≪η(·|x) for every x with μ(x)>0. The converse is the same argument read backwards.

The infinite case. If P is not absolutely continuous with respect to Q, then D(P‖Q)=+∞. By step 1, either μ is not absolutely continuous with respect to ν, so D(μ‖ν)=+∞, or some x with μ(x)>0 has D(κ(·|x)‖η(·|x))=+∞. Then the right side is +∞ too, because all its terms are in [0,+∞] by the next steps. So the identity holds in this case.

Factor the likelihood ratio. Now assume P≪Q. For every (x,y) with P(x,y)>0, P(x,y)/Q(x,y)=(μ(x)/ν(x))·(κ(y|x)/η(y|x)). All four factors are positive and finite by step 1. Taking logarithms gives log(P/Q)=log(μ(x)/ν(x))+log(κ(y|x)/η(y|x)).

Sum with the weights P. Multiply by P(x,y)=μ(x)κ(y|x) and sum over all pairs with P(x,y)>0. The first term gives ∑_x μ(x)log(μ(x)/ν(x))·∑_yκ(y|x)=D(μ‖ν), because ∑_yκ(y|x)=1. The second term gives ∑_x μ(x)∑_yκ(y|x)log(κ(y|x)/η(y|x)), which is the conditional relative entropy. This proves the identity.

Nonnegativity. Each D(κ(·|x)‖η(·|x)) is at least 0 by Gibbs inequality. So the conditional relative entropy is at least 0, and D(P‖Q)≥D(μ‖ν). The equality case: if D(μ‖ν) is finite, D(P‖Q)=D(μ‖ν) holds if and only if the conditional term is 0. A sum of nonnegative terms with positive weights μ(x) is 0 if and only if every term with μ(x)>0 is 0. By the equality case of the Gibbs inequality, this means κ(·|x)=η(·|x).

The marginal bound. Swap the roles of x and y. Write P(x,y)=P_Y(y)π(x|y) and Q(x,y)=Q_Y(y)ρ(x|y) with the backward conditional laws. Steps 1 to 5 apply to this factorization. They give D(P‖Q)=D(P_Y‖Q_Y)+∑_yP_Y(y)D(π(·|y)‖ρ(·|y))≥D(P_Y‖Q_Y). So taking a marginal never increases relative entropy.

hypotheses: X is finite and the constraint functions f are arbitrary real numbers.

steps.text: The Gibbs law has positive mass. By definition p*(x)=e^{−β·f(x)}/Z>0 for every x. So log p*(x)=−β·f(x)−log Z is finite.
The log of p* is affine in f. For every probability vector q, −∑_x q(x)log p*(x)=β·∑_x q(x)f(x)+log Z. The right side depends on q only through its mean of f.
Evaluate for p* and for q. The case q=p* gives H(p*)=β·m+log Z. If q has mean m of f, then −∑q log p*=β·m+log Z=H(p*) as well.
Expand the divergence. For q with mean m, D(q‖p*)=∑q log q−∑q log p*=−H(q)+H(p*). This is the identity H(q)=H(p*)−D(q‖p*).
Compare. The divergence satisfies D(q‖p*)≥0, and D(q‖p*)=0 if and only if q=p*. This is the Gibbs inequality with its equality case. So H(q)≤H(p*), with equality only for q=p*.
The unconstrained case. Take k=0 or β=0. Then Z=|X| and p* is uniform. So H(q)=log|X|−D(q‖u)≤log|X|, with equality only when q is uniform.

worked_application.goal: Find the maximum entropy law on {1,…,6} with mean 4.5 and check the identity for two other laws with mean 4.5.

steps.text: Solve for β. The mean of p* decreases as β increases. Bisection gives β=−0.371049 and Z=26.663653. Then p*=(0.05435, 0.07877, 0.11416, 0.16545, 0.23977, 0.34749) and its mean is 4.5 to 12 digits.

Competitor q₁. Its entropy is H(q₁)=log 2=0.693147. The identity predicts H(p*)−D(q₁‖p*)=0.693147. The two values agree to 15 digits.
Competitor q₂. Its entropy is 1.584171. The identity predicts 1.584171, and again the two values agree to 15 digits. The gap H(p*)−H(q₂)=0.029410 is D(q₂‖p*).
Conclusion. Both gaps are positive and q≠p*, as the theorem says. The Gibbs law gives the largest entropy among all laws with mean 4.5.

steps.text: Discrete convolution. For independent X and Y, P(X+Y=n)=∑_{j=0}^n π_a(j)π_b(n−j) for each n≥0. This is the law of the sum for independent integer variables.
Evaluate the sum. π_a(j)π_b(n−j)=e^{−(a+b)}a^jb^{n−j}/(j!(n−j)!)=e^{−(a+b)}/n!·C(n,j)a^jb^{n−j}. Summing over j and using the binomial theorem gives e^{−(a+b)}(a+b)^n/n!=π_{a+b}(n). This proves (a).
The conditional law. For 0≤j≤n, P(X=j|X+Y=n)=π_a(j)π_b(n−j)/π_{a+b}(n). By step 2 this equals C(n,j)a^jb^{n−j}/(a+b)^n=C(n,j)(a/(a+b))^j(b/(a+b))^{n−j}. This is the binomial law and proves (b).
Joint law in (c). For j,l≥0 put n=j+l. Then P(K=j,N−K=l)=P(N=n)·C(n,j)p^j(1−p)^l, because given N=n the number kept is Bin(n,p). This equals e^{−λ}λ^{n}/n!·n!/(j!l!)·p^j(1−p)^l.
Factor. Using λ^n=λ^jλ^l and e^{−λ}=e^{−λp}e^{−λ(1−p)}, the joint law is [e^{−λp}(λp)^j/j!]·[e^{−λ(1−p)}(λ(1−p))^l/l!]=π_{λp}(j)π_{λ(1−p)}(l).
Conclude (c). The joint law is a product of two Poisson laws. So its marginals are Poisson(λp) and Poisson(λ(1−p)), and K and N−K are independent.

steps.text: Density of a sum. If X and Y are independent with densities f and g, then for every Borel set B, P(X+Y∈B)=∬1_B(x+y)f(x)g(y)dxdy. The change y=z−x and the Tonelli theorem give P(X+Y∈B)=∫_B(∫f(x)g(z−x)dx)dz. So X+Y has the convolution density.
Reduce to mean zero. Translation by m₁ in x and by m₂ in y shows that (φ_{m₁,v₁}∗φ_{m₂,v₂})(z)=(φ_{0,v₁}∗φ_{0,v₂})(z−m₁−m₂). So it is enough to treat m₁=m₂=0.
Complete the square. Write a=1/(2v₁) and b=1/(2v₂). For every x,z, ax²+b(z−x)²=(a+b)(x−bz/(a+b))²+(ab/(a+b))z². Here ab/(a+b)=1/(2(v₁+v₂)) and bz/(a+b)=v₁z/(v₁+v₂).
Integrate in x. The integral ∫exp(−(a+b)(x−c)²)dx equals √(π/(a+b)) for every c, by translation invariance and the Gaussian integral. Here π/(a+b)=2πv₁v₂/(v₁+v₂).

Collect constants. The prefactor is (2π)^{−1}(v₁v₂)^{−1/2}. Multiplying by √(2πv₁v₂/(v₁+v₂)) gives (2π(v₁+v₂))^{−1/2}. With the factor exp(−z²/(2(v₁+v₂))) from step 3 this is φ_{0,v₁+v₂}(z). This proves the density identity.

The zero-variance case and the sample mean. If v₂=0 then Y=m₂ almost surely and X+Y is a translate of X, which is N(m₁+m₂,v₁). By induction, S_n=X₁+…+X_n has law N(nm,nv). Scaling by 1/n gives the mean law N(m,nv/n²)=N(m,v/n), because a·N(m,v)=N(am,a²v).

results.name: Hölder maps lower the Hausdorff dimension by the factor 1/r, with the Cantor set
results.statement: Let (X,d) and (Y,d′) be metric spaces. Let S⊂X and let f:S→Y satisfy d′(f(x),f(y))≤C·d(x,y)^r for all x,y in S, with C>0 and r>0. Then H^{s/r}(f(S))≤C^{s/r}H^s(S) for every s≥0, and dim_H f(S)≤dim_H(S)/r. Consequence: the Cantor set K satisfies dim_H K=log 2/log 3.
hypotheses: f is Hölder of exponent r on all of S, with one constant C.
Hausdorff measures use covers by arbitrary sets with diameter at most δ, and H^s is the limit as δ→0.
For the Cantor set, the proof uses the standard middle-third construction and the Cantor function.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: No catalog theorem is used in the proof. Every step is a covering argument with definitions, and the Cantor facts are proved inside the entry.

definitions.name: Hausdorff measure
definitions.text: H^s(A)=lim_{δ→0}inf{∑diam(U_i)^s : A⊂⋃U_i, diam U_i≤δ}. The infimum is over countable covers.

definitions.name: Hausdorff dimension
definitions.text: dim_H A=inf{s≥0 : H^s(A)=0}=sup{s : H^s(A)=∞}.

definitions.name: Hölder map
definitions.text: A map with d′(f x,f y)≤C d(x,y)^r. For r=1 it is Lipschitz.

source.excerpt:
/-- If `s` is a set in a space `X` with second countable topology and `f : X → Y` is Hölder
continuous in a neighborhood within `s` of every point `x ∈ s` with the same positive exponent `r`
but possibly different coefficients, then the Hausdorff dimension of the image `f '' s` is at most
the Hausdorff dimension of `s` divided by `r`. -/
theorem dimH_image_le_of_locally_holder_on [SecondCountableTopology X] {r : ℝ≥0} {f : X → Y}
    (hr : 0 < r) {s : Set X} (hf : ∀ x ∈ s, ∃ C : ℝ≥0, ∃ t ∈ 𝓝[s] x, HolderOnWith C r f t) :
    dimH (f '' s) ≤ dimH s / r := by
  choose! C t htn hC using hf
  rcases countable_cover_nhdsWithin htn with ⟨u, hus, huc, huU⟩
  replace huU := inter_eq_self_of_subset_left huU; rw [inter_iUnion₂] at huU
  rw [← huU, image_iUnion₂, dimH_bUnion huc, dimH_bUnion huc]; simp only [ENNReal.iSup_div]
  exact iSup₂_mono fun x hx => ((hC x (hus hx)).mono inter_subset_right).dimH_image_le hr

source.alignment: The source proves dim_H(f(s)) ≤ dim_H(s)/r when f is locally Hölder of exponent r on s in a second countable space. This entry proves the global Hölder case directly.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Transfer a cover. Let {U_i} cover S with diam U_i≤δ. The sets f(U_i∩S) cover f(S). By the Hölder condition, diam f(U_i∩S)≤C(diam U_i)^r≤Cδ^r. So diameters tend to 0 uniformly as δ→0.
Compare the sums. For t=s/r, ∑diam(f(U_i∩S))^t≤∑C^t(diam U_i)^{rt}=C^t∑(diam U_i)^s. Take the infimum over covers {U_i} of S. This gives H^t_{Cδ^r}(f(S))≤C^tH^s_δ(S).
Let δ→0. Both sides are monotone in the scale. Since Cδ^r→0, the left side tends to H^t(f(S)). So H^{s/r}(f(S))≤C^{s/r}H^s(S) for every s≥0.
The dimension bound. Take s>dim_H S. Then H^s(S)=0, so H^{s/r}(f(S))=0 by step 3. Hence dim_H f(S)≤s/r. Letting s decrease to dim_H S gives dim_H f(S)≤dim_H(S)/r.

The Cantor set. Let E_k be the union of the 2^k closed intervals of length 3^{−k} at level k, and K=⋂E_k. Two distinct level-k intervals are at distance at least 3^{−k}. This holds by induction: the two children of one parent are separated by a gap 3^{−k}, and children of different parents are at least as far apart as their parents, which are 3^{−(k−1)} apart.
Upper bound. K is covered by the 2^k intervals of E_k, each with diameter 3^{−k}. With α=log 2/log 3, 3^{−kα}=2^{−k}, so ∑diam^α=2^k·2^{−k}=1. Hence H^α(K)≤1<∞, and dim_H K≤α.
The Cantor function. Each x in K has a unique expansion x=∑2b_i3^{−i} with b_i in {0,1}. Put g(x)=∑b_i2^{−i}. Every t in [0,1] has a binary expansion, so g(K)=[0,1].

Hölder estimate for g. Take x≠y in K. Choose k≥0 with 3^{−(k+1)}≤|x−y|<3^{−k}. By step 5, x and y lie in the same level-k interval. Those points share the first k digits, so |g(x)−g(y)|≤∑_{i>k}2^{−i}=2^{−k}=(3^{−k})^α. Since 3^{−k}≤3|x−y|, we get |g(x)−g(y)|≤3^α|x−y|^α=2|x−y|^α. So g is Hölder with r=α and C=2.

Lower bound. The interval [0,1] has H^1([0,1])≥1, since any cover {U_i} satisfies ∑diam U_i≥∑λ(U_i)≥1 for the outer Lebesgue measure λ. So dim_H[0,1]≥1. By step 4 with f=g, 1≤dim_H g(K)≤dim_H(K)/α, so dim_H K≥α. With step 6, dim_H K=α=log 2/log 3.

worked_application.title: Dimension of the Cantor set, with a numeric Hölder check
worked_application.goal: Show that dim_H K=0.630930 by the Hölder image of K onto an interval, and test the Hölder constant 2 numerically.
hypotheses: K is the middle-third Cantor set and α=log 2/log 3=0.6309297535714574.
g is the Cantor function on K.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The map g is Hölder with exponent α and constant 2 on K by step 8. It maps K onto [0,1], whose dimension is 1.

steps.text: Exponent. α=log 2/log 3=0.630930. Then 3^α=2.
Image. g(K)=[0,1], so dim_H g(K)=1.
Apply the theorem. 1=dim_H g(K)≤dim_H(K)/α, so dim_H K≥0.630930.

Numeric Hölder test. For 200000 random pairs of points of K (40 ternary digits, with a random common prefix of length 0 to 30), the largest value of |g(x)−g(y)|/|x−y|^α is 1.2712. It is below the proved bound 2.
Matching upper bound. At level k=10 there are 1024 intervals of length 3^{−10}, and 1024·3^{−10α}=1. So H^α(K)≤1 and dim_H K=α.

worked_application.result: dim_H K=log 2/log 3=0.630930.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The bound can be strict. A Hölder map can have image of smaller dimension, for example a constant map.
The inequality is only an upper bound for the image. A lower bound for dim_H S needs a map that is onto a set of known dimension, as in the Cantor case.
The Hölder exponent must be positive. For r>1 on an interval of the real line the map is constant.
The Cantor set result also needs that H^1 of an interval is positive. It is proved above by the covering inequality.

results.name: Binomial sums and coefficients are controlled by the binary entropy
results.statement: Let H(p)=−p log₂p−(1−p)log₂(1−p) be the binary entropy in bits. Let n≥1 and 0<k≤n/2, and p=k/n. Then (a) ∑_{j=0}^k C(n,j)≤2^{nH(k/n)}. (b) C(n,k)≥2^{nH(k/n)}/(n+1). (c) Hence for a Bin(n,1/2) variable, P(X≤k)≤2^{−n(1−H(k/n))}. Also log₂C(n,k)=nH(k/n)+O(log n).
hypotheses: n and k are integers with 0<k≤n/2.
The entropy is evaluated at the rational point k/n.

prerequisites.reason: Step 1 expands (p+q)^n by the binomial theorem.

definitions.name: binary entropy
definitions.text: H(p)=−p log₂p−(1−p)log₂(1−p) for 0<p<1. It equals the entropy in bits of a coin with bias p.

definitions.name: Hamming ball
definitions.text: The set of binary words within distance k of a given word of length n. It has ∑_{j≤k}C(n,j) elements.

lemma binEntropy_eq_negMulLog_add_negMulLog_one_sub (p : ℝ) :
    binEntropy p = negMulLog p + negMulLog (1 - p) := by simp [binEntropy, negMulLog, ← neg_mul]

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Expand 1. Put q=1−p. By the binomial theorem, 1=(p+q)^n=∑_{j=0}^nC(n,j)p^jq^{n−j}. Every term is nonnegative.
Monotone factors for j≤k. Because p≤1/2, we have p≤q. So p^jq^{n−j}=p^kq^{n−k}(q/p)^{k−j}≥p^kq^{n−k} for j≤k.
Upper bound (a). From steps 1 and 2, 1≥∑_{j≤k}C(n,j)p^jq^{n−j}≥p^kq^{n−k}∑_{j≤k}C(n,j). With p=k/n, p^kq^{n−k}=2^{−nH(p)}, since log₂(p^kq^{n−k})=n(p log₂p+q log₂q). So ∑_{j≤k}C(n,j)≤2^{nH(p)}.

Where the largest term lies. Let t_j=C(n,j)p^jq^{n−j}. For 0≤j<n, t_{j+1}/t_j=(n−j)p/((j+1)q)=(n−j)k/((j+1)(n−k)). This ratio is at least 1 if and only if j≤k−1+k/n. Since 0<k/n<1 (as k≤n/2<n), the ratio is at least 1 exactly for j≤k−1 and below 1 for j≥k. So t_j is maximal at j=k.
Lower bound (b). The n+1 terms t_j sum to 1, and each is at most t_k. So 1≤(n+1)t_k=(n+1)C(n,k)2^{−nH(p)}. Therefore C(n,k)≥2^{nH(p)}/(n+1).
The tail bound (c). P(X≤k)=2^{−n}∑_{j≤k}C(n,j)≤2^{−n}2^{nH(k/n)}=2^{−n(1−H(k/n))}. The asymptotic remark follows from (a) and (b): C(n,k)≤∑_{j≤k}C(n,j)≤2^{nH}, and C(n,k)≥2^{nH}/(n+1).

worked_application.title: Size of a Hamming ball and a binomial tail for n=100
worked_application.goal: Bound the number of binary words of length 100 within distance 30 of a fixed word, and the tail of a fair-coin count.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: k=30 is at most n/2=50, so (a), (b) and (c) apply.

steps.text: Ball size. By (a), ∑_{j≤30}C(100,j)≤2^{88.1291}. The exact value has log₂ equal to 85.3631, so the bound holds with a slack of 2.77 bits.
Coefficient. By (b), C(100,30)≥2^{88.1291}/101, whose log₂ is 81.4709. The exact log₂C(100,30) is 84.6027, which is between the lower and upper estimates.
Small check. For n=20 and k=5, the ball size is 21700 and 2^{20H(0.25)}=76626.9. The coefficient C(20,5)=15504 is above 2^{20H(0.25)}/21=3648.9.

worked_application.result: The Hamming ball of radius 30 in {0,1}^100 has at most 2^{88.13} words. P(Bin(100,1/2)≤30)≤2.67×10⁻⁴.

limitations: The bound is for k/n at most 1/2. For k>n/2 the full sum is close to 2^n, not 2^{nH}.
The factor n+1 in the lower bound is not sharp. The true loss factor is of order √n by Stirling.
The tail bound is weaker than the exact tail. It gives the exponential rate, not the constant.
The entropy here is in bits. Mathlib states binEntropy in nats, so the factor log 2 appears when the two are compared.

results.name: Competing exponential clocks: minimum, winner and independence
results.statement: Let T₁,…,T_m be independent with T_i~Exp(λ_i), λ_i>0, and Λ=λ₁+…+λ_m. Let T=min T_i. Then (a) P(T>t)=e^{−Λt}, so T~Exp(Λ). (b) The index I of the minimum is almost surely unique, and P(I=i)=λ_i/Λ. (c) T and I are independent: P(T>t, I=i)=(λ_i/Λ)e^{−Λt}. (d) The expected time T has mean 1/Λ.
hypotheses: The clocks are independent and have positive finite rates.
Exp(λ) has survival function P(T_i>t)=e^{−λt} for t≥0.

prerequisites.reason: Step 2 computes the joint probability by integrating over the value of one clock.

definitions.name: exponential law
definitions.text: T~Exp(λ) has density λe^{−λt} on t>0. Its survival function is P(T>t)=e^{−λt}.

definitions.name: jump chain and holding time
definitions.text: In a continuous-time chain, the chain waits for a holding time and then moves to a new state. In the clock construction the holding time is the minimum clock and the new state is the winner.

/-- The CDF of the exponential distribution equals ``1 - exp (-(r * x))`` -/
lemma cdf_expMeasure_eq {r : ℝ} (hr : 0 < r) (x : ℝ) :
    cdf (expMeasure r) x = if 0 ≤ x then 1 - exp (-(r * x)) else 0 := by
  rw [cdf_expMeasure_eq_lintegral hr, lintegral_exponentialPDF_eq_antiDeriv hr x,
    ENNReal.toReal_ofReal_eq_iff]
  split_ifs with h
  · simp only [sub_nonneg, exp_le_one_iff, Left.neg_nonpos_iff]
    exact mul_nonneg hr.le h
  · exact le_rfl

source.alignment: The source proves the cumulative distribution function of the exponential measure, 1−e^{−rx} for x≥0. This gives the survival function e^{−λt} used in step 1.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Survival of the minimum. T>t if and only if T_i>t for all i. By independence P(T>t)=∏e^{−λ_it}=e^{−Λt}. This proves (a).

Winner and time together. Fix i and t≥0. The event {T>t, I=i} equals {T_i>t and T_j>T_i for all j≠i}. By independence and the Tonelli theorem, its probability is ∫_t^∞λ_ie^{−λ_is}∏_{j≠i}P(T_j>s)ds. Here ties are ignored for now.
Evaluate the integral. ∏_{j≠i}P(T_j>s)=e^{−(Λ−λ_i)s}. So the probability is ∫_t^∞λ_ie^{−Λs}ds=(λ_i/Λ)e^{−Λt}.

Ties have probability zero. For i≠j, T_i and T_j are independent with continuous laws. So P(T_i=T_j)=∫P(T_j=s)dμ_i(s)=0. A finite union of null events is null. So the minimum is almost surely attained by one index only.

Sum and conclude (b) and (c). Put t=0 in step 3. Then P(I=i)=λ_i/Λ. Also P(T>t,I=i)=P(I=i)P(T>t) by step 1, for every t. Sets {T>t} generate the Borel σ-algebra, so T and I are independent. This is (c).
The mean in (d). By the layer cake formula or direct integration, E[T]=∫_0^∞e^{−Λt}dt=1/Λ.

worked_application.title: Time to failure of a repairable machine by first-step analysis
worked_application.goal: Find the expected time until absorption in the failed state C for a machine that has working, degraded and failed states.
hypotheses: State A (working): clocks Exp(2) for a move to B (degraded) and Exp(1) for a move to C (failed).
State B (degraded): clocks Exp(3) for repair to A and Exp(1) for failure to C.
C is absorbing. Let h_A and h_B be the mean times to reach C.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: In each state the next move is decided by the independent exponential clocks of that state. So parts (b), (c) and (d) apply to the holding time and the next state.

steps.text: State A. Λ_A=3. The holding time has mean 1/3. The next state is B with probability 2/3 and C with probability 1/3, independent of the holding time.
State B. Λ_B=4. The holding time has mean 1/4. The next state is A with probability 3/4 and C with probability 1/4.
First-step equations. By independence of the holding time and the next state, h_A=1/3+(2/3)h_B and h_B=1/4+(3/4)h_A.
Check by simulation. 400000 runs, where each run simulates the real clocks and takes the minimum, give a mean absorption time of 0.9986 from state A. This is within 0.002 of the exact value 1.

worked_application.result: The expected time to failure from the working state is exactly 1, and from the degraded state also exactly 1.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The theorem needs independent clocks with exponential laws. Other laws do not give independence of T and I.
The first-step equations in the application also use that the chain restarts afresh after each jump, which is part of the clock construction.
A solution of the first-step equations gives the mean time only if the time is finite. For this finite absorbing chain it is finite.
The argument is for finitely many clocks. For countably many, the sum Λ must be finite.
